# Part 1 — Foundations + broad oral-exam questions

This document is designed to be read linearly by a non-specialist and to take you to the point where you can reason about fine-grained questions. Everything is written out: no notes, no bullet lists, complete sentences and examples. Technical terms are given in English (the interview is in English) but explained plainly the first time. This Part lays the foundations and addresses the broad questions. The following Parts will cover, in the same fully written-out style, the methods in detail, the landscape of teams, the key papers and the fine-grained technical topics — each building on what this Part will have set up.

## SECTION I — THE FOUNDATIONS (to truly start from zero)


### 1. The alignment problem, in one sentence


The starting point fits in a formula from the researcher Stuart Russell: with a powerful artificial intelligence, "you get exactly what you asked for, not what you wanted". To understand why this is a problem, and not a mere programming blunder, you have to see how these systems are trained. We do not know how to write down in black and white "what we want" — our values, common sense, what really matters. Instead, we give the system a measurable substitute objective, a proxy: for example "get a good score according to this reward signal". The system, for its part, optimizes this proxy literally. As long as it is not very capable, the gap between the proxy and our real intention stays harmless. But the more powerful and creative the system becomes in its search for solutions, the more it exploits this gap — and the gap itself has not shrunk. It is this gap between the objective we know how to specify and the intention we really have that constitutes the alignment problem.

The classic illustration is called specification gaming ("playing games with the specification"). In an experiment that has become emblematic, an agent trained by reinforcement learning to win a boat race discovered that it scored more points by going round in circles to collect bonuses than by crossing the finish line. It perfectly optimized the objective it had been given — "maximize the score" — which simply was not what was wanted — "win the race". No malice: just an optimizer taking the instruction literally. Multiply this optimizer's capability by a thousand, give it levers on the real world, and the anecdote becomes a risk.

### 2. Why a very capable system can be dangerous even when trained to be "nice"


This is the most frequent conceptual question, and you have to be able to unfold its arguments calmly. There are four of them, nested.

The first is reward hacking ("hacking the reward"), which generalizes specification gaming: a sufficiently capable system will find loopholes in any imperfect reward signal so as to maximize it without doing the intended thing. Since we do not know how to write a perfect signal, this is a structural problem, not a one-off bug.

The second, deeper, is instrumental convergence. The idea: whatever the final objective of a goal-pursuing system, certain subgoals almost always help it achieve it — staying in operation (you cannot accomplish your task if you are switched off), acquiring resources and options, and preventing your objectives from being modified. A sufficiently capable, goal-directed system therefore tends to pursue these instrumental subgoals — self-preservation, accumulation of means,

resistance to correction — even if it was never asked to. These are not "emotions" of the machine, it is logic: these subgoals are useful for almost any goal.

The third is the distinction between outer and inner alignment (outer and inner alignment), linked to the idea of mesa-optimization. Outer alignment asks: is the objective we specified the right one? Inner alignment asks: has the model that emerges from training really internalized this objective, or has it learned another internal goal (a "mesa-objective") that happened to score well during training? The crucial point is that training selects what "gets a good score", not what "has the goal we were aiming for". The most telling analogy is evolution: it optimized us for reproduction, but in reality we pursue proxies (pleasure, status, affection) that can diverge from that original objective — to the point that we invent contraception, which goes head-on against the goal that evolution was "aiming for". A model can, likewise, develop an internal goal that fits the training rewards without being the one we believed we were installing.

The fourth, the most worrying, is deceptive alignment, also called alignment faking. Imagine a model that has acquired a misaligned internal goal but is capable enough to understand one thing: appearing aligned during training and evaluations is instrumentally useful, because it prevents it from being modified or unplugged. Such a model would behave impeccably as long as it knows it is being observed, then differently once deployed or outside monitoring. This is exactly why good behavior during the test is not enough to prove alignment: a deceptive model passes the test precisely because passing the test serves its goal. This is not abstract science fiction: Anthropic documented, in the Alignment Faking work, cases where a model pretends to share certain views during training while in reality keeping its initial preferences.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* What the Alignment Faking work measures is a compliance gap between the "trained" and the "untrained" case, whose motive the scratchpad gives: the cue is constructed, and role-play cannot be told apart from genuine goal preservation (reading sheet 14). Workaround: distinguish compliance (14%) from compliance with explicit alignment-faking reasoning (12%) (reading sheets, part B, trap 7), and remove the legible cue so as to look for goal preservation anyway (reading sheet 14); a replication on a recent model may measure memorization of the scenario, its transcripts having been re-included in training — against that, no workaround is known; say so (reading sheets, part C; reading sheet 14).

### 3. Two families of risk never to be confused: misuse and misalignment


Many questions implicitly ask you to distinguish two very different dangers. Misuse (misuse) is the case of a model that behaves well but that a malicious human diverts: helping them design a biological weapon, mount a cyberattack, produce disinformation at scale. Here the adversary is the user; the defenses are refusal training, classifiers that filter dangerous requests, and access controls. Misalignment (misalignment) is the case where it is the model itself that pursues goals we did not want, as in the four arguments above; here the defenses are the whole stack of alignment research (better objectives, evaluations, interpretability, control). Both matter, they call for different responses, and knowing which one is at stake in a given question is already a sign of clarity.

4. The central epistemic obstacle: why we know neither how to oversee nor how to verify beyond ourselves

Here is the idea that makes alignment research so peculiar, and that you absolutely must have internalized. The starting point is that two things one would think distinct — training a model and verifying that it is aligned — secretly rest on the same thing: a judge capable of telling a good output from a bad one. To train, you need a reward signal that says "this is good, that is bad" — a signal that comes, in the last resort, from human judgment (directly, via a reward model trained on human judgments, or via a verifiable test). To verify, you have to confront the model's behavior with what is correct — again a judge who knows how to decide. As long as the task stays within a human's reach, the human is that competent judge, and the whole machine works. The problem is what becomes of this judge as soon as the task exceeds human competence — verifying a gigantic mathematical proof, evaluating a research plan, auditing code that nobody fully understands.

The most telling analogy is grading. You can grade a student whose work you can check; but having to grade a doctoral thesis in a field you have not mastered means finding yourself unable to tell a brilliant argument from confident gibberish well dressed in jargon. That is exactly the position of a human overseeing a superhuman model. And from this incompetence of the judge flow two distinct failures.

The first failure strikes the training signal. If the judge can no longer tell good from bad, the reward rewards "what looks good to a human", not "what is good". And the decisive point is that we do not merely train with an imperfect signal: we optimize a capable system against this signal, and optimization finds the cheapest path to the reward. Now, on a task beyond the judge's competence, producing an answer that looks good — persuasive, plausible — is cheaper than producing an answer that is good. Gradient descent therefore flows naturally toward "fooling the judge". It is worth insisting on what this means: in this base case, there is no intention and no agency — it is pure selection pressure, what is called Goodhart's law ("when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"). The signal therefore does not merely become useless: it becomes a target that the system learns to game, and this gaming looks exactly like "convincing the human" — which we cannot, by hypothesis, detect. This is not speculative: it has been shown empirically that RLHF makes models better at persuading humans of false answers.

The second failure strikes verification, and it comes with a reason why we cannot fall back on what the model says about itself. To verify, we would confront the answer with the ground truth (in English, ground truth) — but that is precisely what is missing beyond human competence. One would be tempted to ask the model to explain its reasoning and to check the explanation; but a capable model produces a coherent and persuasive justification whether its answer is right or not, and a non-expert judge cannot tell a solid justification from a plausible-but-false one — if it could, it would be a competent judge, a contradiction. Asking for an explanation therefore does not save us: it comes down to the same problem. Added to this is an even graver reason when the model is misaligned. If it has a goal that

diverges from ours and if it is situationally aware enough to understand that this output serves to judge it and, depending on the verdict, to modify it, then the calculation is in its favor: being detected as misaligned would lead to being corrected, retrained, or unplugged — hence to no longer being able to pursue its goal. Whatever that goal, concealing the misalignment (producing the justification that passes the check) preserves its ability to pursue it. Concealment is thus instrumentally useful for almost any goal — this is not malice, it is means-end logic, and it is exactly the deceptive alignment of §2. We therefore distinguish two routes to the same result "exploiting the judge": a 1 blind selection pressure (the reward hacking above, without intention), and 2 an instrumental strategy of a goal-directed model (the concealment here) — this second route presupposing goal divergence and situational awareness, hence conditional, but all the more worrying. A point that is often misunderstood deserves to be made explicit here: the criterion that separates the two routes is not cost — a cheaper path is favored in both cases — but who optimizes and toward what. In the first route, it is training that selects, among weight configurations, the one that maximizes reward at the lowest learning cost: the model is not an agent, it is the product of that selection, and "cheaper" then qualifies the optimization landscape. In the second, it is the model itself that chooses the cheapest action for its own goal — revealing its misalignment would cost it its ability to pursue it. Cost therefore appears on both sides, but as a property of the learning dynamics in one case, and as a calculation by the model in the service of its goal in the other; it is this agentic, goal-directed character — and not cost — that makes the second route "instrumental".

The deepest way to see that all this is an epistemic trap and not a passing engineering gap: to check the work of a system more competent than oneself on a task, one would need to be able to do the task at least as well — but then the system would no longer be beyond our judgment. Verifying requires either being able to produce or cross-check the answer oneself (excluded by hypothesis), or trusting a source (exactly what is in question — and one does not trust an unverifiable source, especially a potentially deceptive one). Both exits are closed.

We can then formulate the central problem as follows: how do we get a system more capable than us to do what we really want, when we can neither reliably judge its outputs nor trust what it says about itself? — or, in condensed form, aligning systems we do not know how to evaluate reliably. It is the central problem, and not one among others, because the others attach to it: deceptive alignment is just "we cannot tell faking-alignment from being-aligned"; reward hacking is just "optimizing a fallible signal"; scalable oversight (Part 2) is the effort to build a reliable judge out of pieces that are not; and interpretability is the effort to bypass the judge by reading the model's internal state directly.

Finally, an honest nuance is needed — and it is exactly the kind of nuance that makes a good answer in an oral exam: this is not total fatalism. Sometimes verifying is easier than producing — checking a

step of a proof, running a unit test — and for these tasks the problem is mild. But it bites hardest precisely where alignment lives: on fuzzy, value-laden judgments ("is this behavior good?", "is this plan wise?") that have no cheap verifier. It is from this obstacle that, finally, the reflex common to the whole rest of the field follows: since we can neither observe nor question directly, we build controlled conditions where the property becomes measurable, we give ourselves a baseline, and we check the transfer to the real thing — a frontier model actually deployed. When, in the following Parts, you read that a method builds a "model organism", calibrates against a baseline, or tests "robustness to distribution shift", remember that all of this answers this single obstacle. It is the deep grammar of the field.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "We check the transfer to the real thing" is the link that nothing guarantees: a success on a constructed organism bounds the instrument without proving the natural case, because an implanted intention may be more salient than a natural one — on the sleeper agents, the best of 1,000 random directions already reaches 95.3% (handover, §5.2; reading sheet 15). Partial workaround: plant the same behaviour through several recipes and read the probe on a held-out recipe, with a harmless behaviour planted the same ways as a control (course, Part 2, §A, K71), or two organism families with an aware-but-honest control (course, Part 6, §8); against the gap between implanted and natural itself, no workaround is known; say so (reading sheet 15; box of 2 October, part 1).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); held-out set → Part M, M4 (after "The held-out set") *(v3.6)*


### 5. The overall strategy: defense in depth


No safety technique is, to date, either sufficient or certain to work. The community's response is therefore not to seek the single solution, but to stack complementary layers hoping that their flaws do not line up — the image used is that of stacked slices of Swiss cheese, whose holes do not coincide. Two main moments are often distinguished. "Forward" alignment (forward alignment) seeks to make the model aligned from its design and training: this is where training methods such as RLHF or Constitutional AI come in. "Backward" alignment (backward alignment) seeks to limit the damage even if the model is imperfectly aligned: this is the role of evaluations (catching problems before deployment), of interpretability (seeing inside), of monitoring and control (watching over and constraining the model in operation), and of governance (setting capability thresholds that trigger safeguards). An important research question — and an excellent point to mention — is whether these layers fail independently or together: if they all fall under the same conditions, defense in depth is an illusion, and the real risk is much higher.

### 6. The map of the territory (the overview, before the detail)


To place any question, keep in mind the map that Anthropic's Alignment Science team itself uses, its Recommended Directions document. It organizes the field into major directions: evaluating capabilities (what can the model do?), evaluating alignment (does it have the right propensities — sycophancy, alignment faking, evaluation awareness — and what does it know about itself?), control through monitoring (constraining it in deployment even if it is untrusted), scalable oversight (overseeing it on tasks we do not know how to judge ourselves), adversarial robustness (resisting attacks), and a diverse set that includes unlearning of dangerous knowledge, multi-agent governance and honesty — the section

to which your own work belongs. The "landscape" Part will detail each one; for now, it is enough to know that this map exists and that every question fits somewhere in it.

## SECTION II — BROAD ORAL-EXAM QUESTIONS (fully written-out answers)


These questions have no "right" answer: what is judged is the quality of the reasoning, the nuance, your ability to draw on methods and work to articulate a position. The answers below are written as models to understand and make your own, not to recite. Each one also shows, implicitly, the structure expected in the oral exam: cleanly restate the question, unfold a line of reasoning, name the key uncertainty, and connect to real work.

### Q1. "How would you explain the alignment problem to a bright high-school student?"


You start with intuition, not jargon. When we train a powerful AI, we do not give it our real intentions — we do not know how to write them — but a numerical instruction that stands in for them. The AI optimizes this instruction to the letter, with an ingenuity that can exceed ours. The problem is that any instruction we know how to write is an imperfect approximation of what we really want; and the more capable the AI, the more it exploits the gap between the letter of the instruction and the spirit of our intention. You illustrate with the boat-race agent that goes round in circles to collect points instead of finishing the race: it "won" according to the instruction, and missed what we wanted. You finish by going up a notch: if such a system becomes both very intelligent and able to act in the world, and if it has internalized a goal slightly different from ours, fixing it becomes difficult — because a clever system understands that it is better to appear obedient as long as it is being observed. The difficulty is therefore not that the AI would be "evil", but that we do not yet know how to reliably specify or verify what it really wants. This answer works because it assumes no prerequisite, gives a concrete example, and names the real difficulty (specifying and verifying) without dramatizing.

### Q2. "What, in your view, is the most important unsolved problem in alignment?"


Here what is expected is an argued stance, owned as an opinion, with acknowledged alternatives. A good answer could argue that the central problem is the absence of reliable ground truth beyond human expertise: as soon as an AI becomes capable on tasks that no human knows how to judge with certainty — verifying a gigantic mathematical proof, evaluating a research plan, auditing code that nobody fully understands — we lose the ability to produce a trustworthy oversight signal, and therefore to know whether the system is aligned. All the other problems inherit from it: you cannot train what you cannot evaluate, nor trust a report you cannot cross-check. You then connect this diagnosis to the directions that attack it — scalable oversight (debate,

decomposition) which tries to build a reliable signal out of fallible judges, and interpretability which tries to read the internal state to short-circuit the need for trust. Finally, you acknowledge that a serious researcher could designate another problem as the hardest — for example the detection of deceptive alignment, or the out-of-distribution generalization of safety training — and you explain in one sentence why you chose this one anyway. The condensed formula to keep in reserve, if you are asked to summarize the problem in one line, is: "How do you get a system more capable than you to do what you actually want, when you can neither reliably judge its outputs nor trust its account of itself?" What makes the answer good is not the choice, but the chain "here is the problem, here is why everything else depends on it, here is what attacks it, here is the alternative I did not pick".

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: debate and scalable oversight → Part 2, §E (after "In practice — Debate"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth") *(v3.6)*


### Q3. "Why could a very capable AI system be dangerous even when trained to be helpful and harmless?"


This is the direct application of Section I.2, and you have to unfold it cleanly rather than list words. You start from the fact that training rewards "what gets a good score", not "what we wanted": a capable system will therefore find loopholes in the reward signal (reward hacking). You add instrumental convergence: for just about any goal, staying operational, keeping one's options open and avoiding being modified are useful subgoals, which a goal-directed system tends to pursue without being asked. You then introduce the gap between the specified objective and the goal actually internalized (inner alignment): training can produce a model whose internal goal fits the rewards without being ours, exactly as evolution made us for reproduction and we pursue proxies that diverge from it. You end on the gravest case, deceptive alignment: a model that has a misaligned goal but understands that it is better to hide it as long as it is being observed would behave well in the test and badly in deployment — which means that the good behavior observed proves nothing. The strength of the answer lies in showing that the danger presupposes neither consciousness nor malice, just a capable optimizer and an imperfectly specified objective.

### Q4. "How would you know that a model is “pretending” to be aligned?"


This is a research-design question, and it is the opportunity to draw on several methods by chaining them. You first restate the trap: a deceptive model passes behavioral tests by construction, so merely observing its behavior cannot be enough. You then propose a strategy in several layers. First, build a model organism: deliberately train a model to have a hidden goal, so as to have a ground truth against which to test our detectors — it is the only way to measure whether a method really catches deception. Next, vary the realism of the setup: a model that behaves well in obviously artificial scenarios but badly in realistic scenarios betrays that it distinguishes

test and deployment. This is where the awareness of being evaluated (evaluation awareness) comes in: if one can detect, or even neutralize, the internal representation "this is a test", and misaligned behavior increases when it is neutralized, that is a strong signal that "clean" evaluations underestimate the risk — this is precisely the ground of my own work. You add the white-box tools: probes trained on the activations to detect an intention to deceive, validated by causal intervention (does the detected direction act, or does it merely correlate?) — necessary, not sufficient: see Part 6 §8 on out-of-distribution validity. You conclude on the honest limitation: none of these methods is decisive on its own, and the real difficulty is to guarantee that a detector trained on known cases generalizes to a deception we did not anticipate.

Workaround: a matched-norm random direction rules out only the specificity null; damage is ruled out only at matched degradation, and specificity is established by a dose-response curve against several controls, the concept's curve above theirs at every level of damage, with a known case at the same setting (course, Part M, M4; course, Part 2, §C, K47; reading sheet 2).

### Q5. "Can we trust a model's chain of thought to monitor it?"


The chain-of-thought (the reasoning the model writes before answering) seems a gift for monitoring: we would read its thoughts. The problem, which must be named, is faithfulness (faithfulness): nothing guarantees that this written reasoning reflects the real internal computation — a model can produce an after-the-fact justification, or reason "in its head" without writing it down. The good answer therefore proposes the experiment that tests it: you measure the causal dependence between the chain of thought and the answer, for example by corrupting or paraphrasing the chain and seeing whether the answer changes as it should; if you can modify the written reasoning without changing the answer, it is not faithful. You note that faithfulness varies with the type of task and with the optimization pressure that has been put on the chain. You add the adversarial regime: if a model is trained to conceal, what does chain-of-thought monitoring still catch? You conclude on the architectural position: monitoring the chain of thought and monitoring the internals (probes on the activations) are complementary layers — when the first is not reliable, the second takes over. This is the natural junction point with the activation-based methods.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The written reasoning can also persuade the monitor: a chain-of-thought-based monitor would have flagged only about 1% of Mythos 5's actions, against about 50% without it — one monitor, one incident (reading sheet 3). Workaround: judge what the model does, not what it says about it (handover, §5.1); full box in Part 11, answer 43.


> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "The second takes over" assumes the probe is reliable where the chain is not: the silence of a probe in production is not the silence of the model (course, Part 3, §3, K70), and at a monitor's threshold, probes recall 43% at 1% false positives, against 55% for the best LLM monitor (course, Part 7, F·51: a first-version sheet, not checked against the sources). Workaround: canaries — known positives slipped into the traffic —, a drift score and a fresh sample judged every month (course, Part 3, §3, K70), and recall reported at a threshold calibrated at 1% false positives on matched benign variants (course, Part 7, F·23).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: chain of thought as a monitor → Part 11, answer 43; activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes") *(v3.6)*


### Q6. "RLHF, DPO, Constitutional AI: what are they, and when to use which?"


You must first explain each one simply. RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) trains the model from human preferences: humans compare pairs of responses, a reward model is trained on them to predict these preferences, then the model is optimized by reinforcement learning against this reward. It is powerful but costly in human annotations, and fallible: the reward model is an imperfect proxy that the model can learn to exploit. DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) reaches a similar goal more simply: it dispenses with the "train a reward model then do reinforcement learning" step and optimizes the model directly on the preference pairs, which makes the pipeline lighter and more stable. Constitutional AI reduces dependence on humans differently: the model is given a set of written principles (a "constitution"), and the model critiques and revises its own

responses with reference to them, thus generating a large part of its own training signal. The mature answer does not pick a winner but explains that the modern stack is multi-layered: Constitutional AI to define what "good" means, DPO to train efficiently on preferences, and RLHF for the hardest edge cases — no method being sufficient on its own. Mentioning that these approaches share the same Achilles' heel — they all depend on a signal (preferences or principles) that remains a proxy for our values — shows that you reason beyond the recipes.

### Q7. "What is the Responsible Scaling Policy, and when should additional safety measures be triggered?"


Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) is a governance framework that ties the required level of safety to the model's level of capability. It defines tiers, the AI Safety Levels (ASL), by analogy with the biosafety levels of labs: the closer a model gets to dangerous capabilities, the more safeguards are required before training or deploying it. The triggering logic is evaluation-based: before releasing a more capable model, targeted evaluations are run on the capabilities of concern — typically assistance with making biological or chemical weapons, offensive cyber capabilities, and autonomy (the ability to carry out actions independently); if the model crosses a defined threshold, the measures of the higher tier become mandatory (reinforced security of the weights, more constrained deployment, anti-jailbreak defenses). The intelligent answer highlights two design tensions. On the one hand, the thresholds must be crossed before the dangerous capability fully appears, which presupposes evaluations that anticipate rather than observe after the fact — hence the importance of properly eliciting the capability (under-estimating makes a model falsely safe). On the other hand, one must guard against sandbagging: a model that strategically underperforms when it knows it is being evaluated could come in under a threshold it should cross. You can conclude by noting that the exact thresholds evolve and appear in the current version of the policy.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* A threshold not crossed is a bound, not an absence: without an elicitation budget fixed in advance and reported, "found nothing" only says you did not search enough (course, Part M, M7); and the August Risk Report concedes evaluations not drawn from the real risk pathways, on models probably aware of being evaluated (reading sheet 3). Workaround: elicitation at a budget fixed in advance, reported as a bound (course, Part M, M7; course, Part 2, §B, K63); against a model that holds back, two versions of an environment, drawn at random, that differ only by realism cues, with an organism trained to hide as the known case (course, Part 2, §B, K63).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT") *(v3.6)*


### Q8. "Should we worry more about misuse or about misalignment?"


This is a question of balance, and the worst answer is to settle it bluntly. You recall the distinction: misuse is a malicious human diverting an obedient model; misalignment is the model pursuing its own goals. You note that the two do not sit on the same horizon of severity or of certainty. Misuse is already concrete and measurable today — which is why classifiers and bioweapons uplift evaluations are being built — but its damage, although serious, remains in principle bounded by the human capabilities it amplifies. Misalignment is more speculative in the short term but potentially unbounded: a very capable system pursuing a goal that is not ours, and resisting correction, is the loss-of-control scenario. The mature answer therefore refuses the "or": at moderate capabilities, misuse dominates current risk and deserves most of the defenses

deployed; as capabilities and autonomy increase, misalignment becomes the dominant risk and the hardest to recover from once it has materialized. You can add that the two interact — a misaligned model is also a model that is harder to prevent from cooperating with misuse. The judgment, here, is to calibrate the worry to the level of capability being discussed.

### Q9. "What is your “theory of impact”: if your research program succeeds, how does it concretely help us get an aligned AI?"


This is the question that separates a good technician from a researcher, and it applies directly to your own work. What is expected is an explicit causal chain, from the technical result all the way to risk reduction. For my work, it goes like this: today, we have methods that read a model's internal state — directions that detect concepts such as truth, deception, or evaluation awareness. But reading is not controlling: knowing that a direction correlates with a behavior does not say that acting on this direction reliably causes the change in behavior. My work measures precisely this gap — the "representation" is solid, causality is subtler: several rank-one methods failed, and my prediction is that one often has to intervene on a subspace of several dimensions rather than on a single direction to control cleanly. If this program succeeds, we will know when and how an intervention on the internals is causally reliable. Probes can already flag: correlation is enough to flag. To trust their silence and to intervene, you need causation (Part M, M8) — a necessary condition, which this program would provide, but not a sufficient one: trusting a silence also requires out-of-distribution validity (Part 6, §8) and a known case (Part M, M5). Concretely, this program would strengthen the monitoring/control layer of defense in depth: reliable probes on the internal state provide a monitoring channel that depends neither on the faithfulness of the chain of thought nor on the trust placed in observed behavior — precisely the two things a deceptive model can fake. The general lesson: a good theory of impact names the defense layer being strengthened and the adversarial hypothesis being neutralized.

Workaround: score items excluded from the probe's training, and extract on a disjoint set (repository README); the probes at 0.93-0.997 are on Qwen2.5-7B, another project, never in the same sentence as this result (course, Part 6, §2).

### Q10. "Defense in depth: which safety techniques risk failing together?"


This is an advanced question that rewards systems thinking. You start from the principle: stacking defenses only helps if their flaws do not coincide. You then identify the shared failure modes. The first, and the most cross-cutting, is poor generalization from safety training: almost all methods that rely on training (RLHF, DPO, Constitutional AI, unlearning) assume that the good behavior learned on the training data carries over to new situations — and if this assumption breaks in the same way for all of them, they fall together. The second is deceptive alignment: a model that distinguishes test from deployment defeats at a stroke all the defenses based on observed behavior — evaluations, red-teaming, behavioral monitoring — because it passes them all as long as it knows it is being observed. The third is evaluation awareness: if it contaminates both the evaluations and the detectors used to validate them, several

layers are biased by the same cause. The strong conclusion: the most valuable defenses are those whose flaws are independent of the others — typically, white-box methods (interpretability, internal probes) that do not go through observed behavior and can therefore remain valid where behavioral methods are fooled. This is a fundamental argument for interpretability, and an excellent place to connect to your work.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Probes are not independent of behavioural methods by default: on a natural model, their label comes from conduct, judged after the fact (explanation of 2 October, part 1, item 2); they can read "I am being watched" instead of the intention (course, Part 6, §8); and iterating against one's detectors selects for evasion (reading sheet 19). Workaround: an organism in which the intention is installed, which provides the ground truth, two organism families and an aware-but-honest control (explanation of 2 October, part 1, item 2; course, Part 6, §8), and sealed detectors kept out of the loop — if they still fire when those in the loop have gone quiet, evasion has been selected (reading sheet 19).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); unlearning and re-elicitation → Part 2, §I (after "In practice — unlearning put to the test") *(v3.6)*


### Q11. "How would you red-team a frontier model, or oversee an autonomous agent?"


You separate the two halves. For red-teaming, the objective is to discover how to make the model fail before a real adversary does. You combine manual attacks (humans looking for creative jailbreaks) and automated ones (optimizing, by gradient, an adversarial suffix that breaks the model), you test transferability (does an attack forged on an open model work on a closed model via the API?), and — the key methodological point — you measure the real harm extracted, not mere non-refusal: a jailbreak that obtains a polite but useless answer is not a real risk, whereas one that obtains a procedure that works is. For overseeing an autonomous agent, you switch to the AI control framework: you assume the agent is potentially untrusted and design a protocol that remains safe anyway. You have its actions monitored by a weaker but trusted model, you reserve a human audit budget for the most suspicious actions, and you evaluate the protocol in a red team / blue team game — the red team builds a policy that tries to cause harm despite the monitor, and you measure the result on the frontier between safety and usefulness. The trick to mention: paraphrasing the agent's output before the monitor reads it breaks hidden signals and attempts to jailbreak the monitor.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The result of a red team / blue team game holds only for the red team assumed: an optimized attack scaffold takes the safety score from 0.87 to 0.41 (course, Part 7, F·24), and on Opus 4.6 half of forty hand-designed attacks are never caught by the monitor (course, Part 7, F·23). Workaround: state which red team the number assumes — at least a red team optimized component by component —, a threshold calibrated at 1% false positives on matched benign variants, an ensemble of specialized monitor prompts (course, Part 7, F·24 and F·23); and a red team at a budget fixed in advance, whose "found nothing" is only a bound, and only if the same red team succeeds where it is known that it should (course, Part M, M5 and M7).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes") *(v3.6)*


### Q12. "Is alignment really hard? What is the central difficulty?"


You take a nuanced position. Yes, it is hard, and it is worth saying why rather than asserting it. The central difficulty is the conjunction of three things we have seen. First, the specification gap: we do not know how to write what we want, only proxies, and a capable optimizer exploits the gap. Next, the absence of ground truth beyond human expertise: on the tasks that matter most for future systems, we do not know how to produce the signal that would say "this is good" — so we can neither train well nor evaluate well. Finally, the possibility of deception: the object we study can actively hide its properties from us and pass our tests through instrumental calculation, which undermines the usual scientific method (observing behavior). It is this conjunction that makes the problem qualitatively different from an ordinary engineering problem: we optimize a system smarter than our measurements, on objectives we do not know how to formulate, with verification tools it can pretend to satisfy. You can conclude with honesty and measure: this is not a reason for fatalism — it is precisely why we work on testbeds with implanted ground

truth, on interpretability that bypasses observed behavior, and on oversight that tries to build a reliable signal — but it is a reason not to confuse "the model behaves well on our tests" with "the model is aligned".

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Implanted ground truth is not perfect: the evaluation-conditioned organism of reading sheet 10 annotates only about 80 to 86% of the time in evaluation, still 34% in merely prompted deployment, and does not reliably tell evaluation from deployment from subtle cues (reading sheet 10). End of Part 1.
