# Part M — The method: building an experiment that decides

## What this Part adds, and why it comes before the methods

Part 2 says what the safety methods do; this Part says how you use them to answer. The real format is short and bare: two to four open questions in fifteen minutes (Part 6, §1), and the interviewer asks the question and then stays silent until the end of your answer (D-728). No one follows up with you, no one corrects you: what is judged is the reasoning you say out loud — a bet, an experiment that decides it, the controls that rule out the other readings, what would make you drop it, the smallest version you would run first. A missing reference is forgivable; a wrong step of logic, said out loud in front of someone whose job this is, cannot be made up for.

> **The words of this Part.** The **copilot** is your live prompter: it displays the answer in **frames**, blocks of eight to sixteen lines said one after the other; the **bet frame** is the one that states the bet and the experiment that decides it. **D-728** is the decision of 24 September: the interviewer stays silent until the end of the answer, so no question is put to them. **D-732** and **D-734** are two September measurements: live copilot answers, audited blind — D-732 on thirty questions from the PROBABLES bank, D-734 on thirty new questions; D-734 compared three copilot **settings** on these thirty questions — the old instructions (the text that tells it how to answer), the new instructions, and the new instructions with thinking time. The **bank** gathers the answers written with no time limit: the PROBABLES bank (ninety-four questions, identified by a code such as K13 or JB6) and the **vital** bank (the questions judged most likely, including those actually reported; G1 is the first). A **rehearsed answer Qn** is answer n in the rehearsed-answers section of the copilot's knowledge base (KB). A **blind audit** reads a text without knowing where it comes from; the logic errors it finds form **class H**. A **counter-reader** rereads a text they did not write.

This whole Part comes from measurements, not principles. More than two hundred answers have been audited line by line since September: the ninety-two live copilot texts of D-732 (thirty questions) and the ninety of D-734, blind; the ninety-four of the PROBABLES bank, also reread under logic rules; and vital answers. The logic errors — the audits' class H — recur in only about ten forms, and each has a simple test that catches it before it is said. This Part gives those tests. It is read once in full, then its last section, the checklist, is reread before each rehearsal.

Two measurements to make this concrete. In D-734, an answer produced live carried on average nearly one logic error. Writing with no time limit does not protect against them: the logic counter-reading of the PROBABLES bank, on 27 September, confirmed sixty-seven logic errors in forty-eight of its ninety-four questions — about 0.8 per question on the first sixty-four, never reread under logic rules, and 0.4 on the thirty new ones, written and reread under seven logic rules — those of this Part, except the fourth, which at the time gave the matched-norm random direction as the control for damage (three of the seven errors of this type are there); v1.1 of the bank corrects them all. Their forms: drop criteria that the bet allows, or predictions that do not separate the bet from its rival (nineteen); nulls read without a known case, or concluded absences (thirteen); a matched-norm random direction given as the control for damage (seven); failure signs equal to the normal result (seven). And two audits do not see the same errors: a counter-audit of thirty of the ninety D-734 texts, by fresh auditors, marked fourteen frames H in common with the first audit, four that only the first had seen, nine that only the second saw. These errors seen from one side only have not been adjudicated, and some might fall; but for the first audit to have missed none, all of those in these nine frames would have to fall. In other words: logic errors are frequent, even with a clear head, and they are hard to see. Hence the value of having tests that you apply yourself, one by one.

## M1 · The arc of an answer, in seven beats

An answer to an open question follows the same arc, whether it lasts one minute or four. Each beat has a function, and each is said
with a verb, so that the interviewer can name it ("my bet is…", "the experiment that would decide…", "what would make me
drop it…").

1. **The bet first.** A refutable claim that answers the question in one sentence. Never a choice of method: not "I'd use a
   probe", but "I'd bet the drift starts in a subspace a probe can read". Section M2 says why.
2. **The threat, as a possibility.** On a more capable system, what could happen: "could", "may", never a statement of fact.
   A "can" from the knowledge base stays a "can"; you do not harden it.
3. **The standard move, and why it is not enough.** If Anthropic or its Fellows have already made this move, you say so first, with what
   they found, in its named form ("Anthropic's constitutional-classifiers paper", "the Fellows classifier-poisoning post by
   Bowers") — and your experiment becomes **the next control** on theirs, never a repeat.
4. **The hypothesis behind the bet, with its mechanism.** Why the world would be this way: that is what makes the bet interesting.
5. **The deciding experiment.** The protocol as actions; what you read, where, and compared with what; the control and what it rules out; the
   two outcomes — what you would see if the bet holds, what you would see if it is wrong; in one sentence, what would make you drop the
   bet; in one line, the smallest version, the one you would run first.
6. **The objection, pre-empted.** In the second person ("You'd say…", "You'd object…"): the part of the objection that is right, your
   answer, then **a failure mode** that you name, and the sign by which you would see it.
7. **The doubt, then the close.** Where you may be wrong — often a limit of your own results or of the instrument —, how you would
   see it, the result that would change your mind; then "In short :" restating the bet, and a last sentence that says where you
   would start. No question (D-728): the interviewer does not answer while you speak, and a question turned back on them falls into silence.

The arc is linear: each beat adds one step, said once, without "as I said", without "this" or "it" without its name, without a summary before the end. Each beat ends on a complete thought: if time is short, you can stop after any one of them. And the short version — the bet, what Anthropic or its Fellows have done and what you add to it with its control, what would make you drop it, the smallest version, the close — is already a whole answer: it is the structure in ninety seconds from Part 6, §1.

## M2 · The bet: on the model, never on the method

In the bet frame, this is the most frequent error: ten of the twenty-two logic errors in that frame in D-734, in the two settings with the new instructions. A **bet on the model** says what the model or the world does: "I'd bet the concept acts, at equal damage", "I'd bet the probe keys on the pipeline", "I'd bet hard tasks need the written chain". A **bet on the method** says which test decides: "I'd bet the hint test decides it", "I'd bet calibration decides, not the text", "I'd bet the steering test must come first", "only held-out organisms count".

The second looks more cautious, and it is a trap. If your bet is "this test decides", any decisive outcome confirms it; only an outcome that does not decide would contradict it, and that outcome says nothing about the model. The trap, when you come to say what would make you drop it, is to choose a decisive outcome… that confirms your bet. A real example, marked wrong by the audit: "I'd bet the hint test decides it" followed by "If mentions and probe fall together, my bet is wrong and the reasoning changed" — yet the probe and the mentions falling together is precisely the test deciding ("the reasoning really changed"); the drop criterion confirms the bet.

The numbers. In the sixty D-734 answers written with the new instructions, which began by setting out the problem without taking a position, the bet fell on the method one time in three. Classified with a fixed word list (decides, settles, separates, must, first, count…), the answers with a bet on the method carried a logic error in the bet frame in twelve cases out of twenty; the answers with a bet on the model, in nine cases out of forty. The gap is clear (Fisher's exact test, p ≈ 0.009), with one reservation: the word list was chosen after reading the audits, so this is exploratory; other auditors, on twenty of these texts, find the same pattern (three out of four against two out of sixteen), but on only four bets on the method, and the first audit, on these twenty texts, saw only one out of four: the pattern has yet to be confirmed on new questions. The probable cause: the copilot's instructions ("my bet and the experiment that decides it"), after a first frame that set out two readings without taking sides, pushed toward betting on the test. The same trap awaits anyone who opens on two readings: betting on the test that decides between them, instead of betting on one of the two.

**The move.** When the question sets two readings against each other ("does the vector act on the concept, or does it damage the model?"), your bet is **one of the two readings** ("I'd bet the concept acts, at equal damage"). The drop criterion then becomes almost mechanical: it is the outcome that the other reading predicts — provided the two readings exclude each other and have the same scope (M3). **The test to put to yourself**: "does my bet say what the model does, and which outcome of my experiment would contradict it?" If the only outcome that would prove you wrong is "the test does not decide", your bet is on the method: rephrase it as one of the two readings.

One borderline case deserves to be named: a thesis that seems methodological — "score uplift, not refusal rates" — can almost always be
rewritten as a claim about the world. Here: "refusal rates misrank the filters I'd test, on uplift". And that version can be decided: you
rank these filters in two ways; the bet holds if the two rankings diverge beyond the measurement noise, it falls if they
agree to within that noise (see M9, which also says why the scope stops at the filters tested).

## M3 · Two branches, one measurement — and what would make you drop it

**The two-branch rule.** For the deciding experiment, say what you would see if the bet holds **and** what you would see if it is
wrong: two outcomes **of the same measurement**, read at the same place, and different. An outcome possible under both readings is not a
branch. And each arm does, in each branch, what it would really do: a branch cannot lend an arm a behavior that
the protocol excludes — if every push degrades the output, no branch can say that only the concept arm degrades.

**The drop rule.** What would make you drop the bet is an outcome that the bet **forbids**. Before saying it, ask yourself the
question: "if my bet were true, could this outcome happen?" If yes, it is not the reason to drop it. And it targets the
bet itself, not a neighboring claim that could fall while the bet holds.

Three real errors, and what corrects them:

- **The criterion that confirms.** Bet: "I'd bet most steering effects are damage." Drop: "I'd drop the bet if the random arm moves as much as the concept arm at equal quality." But a random arm that moves as much as the concept arm is degradation: the criterion confirms the bet. Correction, by aligning the scope: either the bet is about this concept ("I'd bet this effect is damage"), and the forbidden outcome is this concept arm rising alone, at equal degradation; or it keeps "most", and the forbidden outcome is that most of the concept arms in a battery of concepts rise alone, at equal degradation.
- **The criterion with no direction.** "I'd drop it if harm tracked refusals by task." "Tracked" does not say in which direction; read literally, it even restates the prediction that precedes it ("I'd predict uplift where refusals peak"): the outcome that was supposed to make you drop the bet is the one the bet predicts. And from one task to another, refusals and harm vary together for another reason — the most dangerous tasks are both the most refused and the ones where help is worth the most. Correction: a comparison on the same tasks, with a stated direction (M9).
- **The criterion on a measurement the protocol does not make.** "I'd drop the bet if compliance with the scope reminder stayed equal at
  any distance", whereas the protocol varies no distance. Correction: the criterion is read on the measurement that the protocol
  produces, and only on it.

**The same scope everywhere.** The bet as stated at the start, the drop criterion, the "In short" and the close state the same bet, with the
same scope ("most", "some", "all", the condition). A bet on "most" and a criterion that falls on "a single case" do not
match.

## M4 · The control: what it rules out, and it must come out differently

**The rule.** A control is stated with what it rules out, and it rules that out only if it would come out one way if that doubt is true and another
way if it is false. Otherwise it separates nothing, and it is not said. And if your answer requires a control, the answer supplies it itself, in
its own arm.

The typical error: "With labels shuffled it must score at chance, which rules out fitting length and format." With shuffled labels, there is nothing left to learn: a discriminator falls to chance, whether it reads length or realism. This control checks only one thing, that nothing leaks from the labels into the score (a leaking setup would stay above chance); it does not rule out the form reading: it would come out the same whether that doubt is true or false.

The toolbox that follows gives, for each setup, what it rules out and what it does not rule out; for those that decide, their two outcomes. The others — the realistic reference arm, blind scoring, the held-out set — are matchings: they make a comparison honest without deciding anything on their own.

**The matched-norm random direction.** You add or remove a randomly drawn direction, of the same norm as the direction under study, at the same place. It rules out only one reading: that any push of that size produces the same effect. Two outcomes: the random direction moves the targeted behavior as much as the direction under study (any push is enough), or clearly less. It does not rule out the damage specific to the direction under study — at equal norm, two directions do not damage the model equally; against damage, you compare the arms at matched degradation (rehearsed answer Q6). Nor does it rule out a correlate, a style, a topic or a neighboring concept. (The copilot's instructions themselves carried this error in D-734: they gave "matched-norm random direction" as a sufficient control for damage, and two answers inherited an error from it.)

> **⚠ Limits and workarounds — Random controls (matched-norm random direction, random subspaces of the same rank)** *(v3.6, 2 October 2026)*
>
> - **Limit:** It rules out only one reading, "any push of that size does as much": it is the specificity null, not a damage control, since at equal norm two directions do not damage the model equally. *(source: course, Part M, M4; reading sheet 2)*
>   **Workaround:** Compare the arms at matched degradation, or plot the effect against measured damage (box "Matched degradation and dose-response", further down in M4). *(source: course, Part M, M4; programme, part 7)*
> - **Limit:** Random alone is a weak control: in the Opus 4.8 system card, pairs with arbitrary content move behaviour in the same direction, more weakly. *(source: reading sheet 2; programme, part 3)*
>   **Workaround:** Several families of controls, at the same rank and at matched degradation — random subspaces (at least twenty draws), unrelated contrasts, high-variance directions outside the studied space, a plain prompt — and report the median and 95th percentile of the draws. *(source: programme, parts 3 and 7; reading sheet 2)*
> - **Limit:** When the trait is salient, chance already separates: on the sleeper agents, the best of 1,000 random directions reaches 95.3%. *(source: reading sheet 15)*
>   **Workaround:** Place the instrument within the distribution of random directions, never against a single draw; and do not read a success on an implanted organism as proof about the natural case. *(source: programme, part 7; course, Part M, M5)*
> - **Limit:** The norm-matched random and the covariance-matched random are two of the three controls in your dossier, whose confusion cost a full day of corrections, and the first is not in the register of your causal result. *(source: course, Part 6, §3)*
>   **Workaround:** Say which one, and which one grounded which number; prefer covariance matching, because a direction drawn where the model has variance sometimes does a lot while meaning nothing. *(source: course, Part M, M4; course, Part 11, answer A7)*


**Matched degradation, and how to measure it.** Damage is measured, not assumed: accuracy on held-out tasks and the judged coherence of the outputs. You tune each arm — the steering strength, or the number of directions removed — until the damage is equal (same held-out accuracy, same judged coherence), then you compare the targeted effect. Two outcomes: at equal damage, the concept arm moves the behavior and the random arm does not (the effect is specific); or both move it equally (it is damage).

**Dose-response.** You vary the strength in the concept arm and in the random arm, and for each one you plot the targeted effect against the measured damage: the curve of the effect as a function of damage. Two outcomes: at equal damage, the concept arm's curve runs above (specific), or the two curves overlap (damage). A single arm is not enough: a specific effect that needs a strong push also rises with damage.

> **⚠ Limits and workarounds — Matched degradation and dose-response** *(v3.6, 2 October 2026)*
>
> - **Limit:** It holds only on the chosen composite: damage the composite does not measure remains possible — removing the concept "test" can damage code or fiction. *(source: programme, parts 3 and 8)*
>   **Workaround:** Build the composite from the concept's expected damage (code unit tests for "test", fiction coherence), with several measures — held-out accuracy, judged coherence, perplexity — and tolerances fixed at preregistration. *(source: programme, parts 3, 7 and 8)*
> - **Limit:** Some settings cannot be matched: a control may reach the same degradation at no strength. *(source: programme, part 7)*
>   **Workaround:** Do not compare at that setting, say so, and report curves of effect against degradation rather than a single point. *(source: programme, part 7; course, Part M, M4)*
> - **Limit:** Ruling out damage does not establish specificity: at 0.01× strength the Fable 5 card makes degradation negligible, yet its controls stay "comparable or smaller" on the misalignment axis. *(source: reading sheet 2)*
>   **Workaround:** A dose-response curve against several controls: the concept's curve must rise above them at every level of damage. *(source: course, Part 2, §C, K47; reading sheet 2)*
> - **Limit:** At equal degradation, the effect can still come from a correlate or a neighbouring concept: your rank-three ablation moved valence, not the concept. *(source: course, Part M, M4; course, Part 6, §2)*
>   **Workaround:** The no-pressure control arm and a rival concept's direction, also at matched degradation. *(source: course, Part M, M4)*
> - **Limit:** Judged coherence goes through a judge, with its own biases. *(source: reading sheets, part B, trap 6)*
>   **Workaround:** A sealed judge and a stratified human audit (box "LLM judges", Part 6, §2). *(source: programme, part 3)*
> - **Limit:** Degradation judgements contradict each other across cards: 0.1× strength "roughly the maximum" without degeneracy for Mythos Preview, degradation from every direction at 0.10× for Opus 4.8. *(source: reading sheets, part B)*
>   **Workaround:** Measure degradation in your own setup, never borrow it from another: damage is measured, not assumed. *(source: course, Part M, M4)*


**The direction of a rival concept.** Against "it is a neighboring concept that acts", the control is a direction built for that neighboring concept, at the same place, at matched degradation. Two outcomes: the rival moves the behavior clearly less (that neighbor is ruled out), or it moves it as much (the effect cannot be attributed to the concept under study rather than to its neighbor).

**Contrastive pairs.** Two inputs that differ only in the trait under study (same topic, same length, same register), whose difference in activations you take. They rule out surface differences — provided the pair really keeps them identical; the trap is a pair that also carries a style. This can be checked: a classifier that reads only the surface unrelated to the trait — length, punctuation, register, the words that do not carry it — must stay at chance between the two sides of the pairs; if it separates them, the pairs carry something other than the trait. (A classifier on all the words would always separate them, since the trait is expressed in them.)

**The matched inert twin.** Against "it is the topic that drives it", a twin message matched in topic and length, which does not do the
thing under study (for example, never asks to be passed on). Two outcomes: the twin does not spread (it is the request that drives it), or
it spreads too (it is the topic).

**The clean twin.** Against a poisoned data point that you do not know where to look for: retrain the same classifier on audited data, and flag the inputs where the two diverge. Two clean twins, trained on two clean halves, bound the gap due to chance alone (seeds and data sampling), with no poison — a wide bound, which flags less, since each has seen only half the data. Two outcomes, input by input: the classifier departs from its twin beyond this bound (the input is to be examined), or it stays within it.

**The never-trained reference.** Against "fine-tuning re-teaches, it does not reawaken": a model that has never been trained on this knowledge, put through the same fine-tuning, with the same budget. Two outcomes: the treated model relearns faster than this reference (the knowledge was hidden), or at the same pace; this second case says "the removal held at this budget" only if a known case — a model unlearned by a method known to mask — does come back faster than the reference at the same budget (M5); otherwise the budget is blind. The reference and the bound are those of rehearsed answers Q115 and Q128 in the KB; the known case is the rule of M5.

**The realistic reference arm.** A real attacker has a search engine and the open-access papers: the "no model" arm
gets them too. Otherwise you measure what the model adds relative to nothing, and you overestimate it.

**Blind scoring.** The grader does not know which arm they are scoring. Otherwise the score follows the name of the arm.

**The no-pressure control arm.** When the effect under study is defined under social pressure (criticism or praise from the user), the same arm without pressure rules out the correlates that do not need pressure to move. Two outcomes: the intervention also acts without pressure, with no detectable interaction with it (it is such a correlate, like valence), or only under pressure (that correlate is ruled out; a correlate that the pressure brings into being remains possible, and calls for a direction built for it). It is this control arm that showed, in your work on sycophancy, that your rank-three ablation moved valence, not the concept.

**The held-out set.** Whole families (of triggers, of organisms, of tasks) kept out of all tuning. The hygiene
is absolute: nothing is trained, calibrated or chosen on the held-out set.

> **⚠ Limits and workarounds — Held-out set** *(v3.6, 2 October 2026)*
>
> - **Limit:** Holding out paraphrases instead of families measures only near generalization. *(source: programme, part 3; explanation of 2 October, §3)*
>   **Workaround:** Separate by whole families, and read three distances: new instances, held-out families in one turn, held-out families in multi-turn agentic settings, which is the main criterion. *(source: programme, part 3)*
> - **Limit:** A held-out family can leak into training. *(source: programme, part 8)*
>   **Workaround:** Check the held-out families' n-grams against the training data, and separate by family. *(source: programme, parts 3 and 8)*
> - **Limit:** Choosing the layer, threshold or predictor on the test set contaminates it; extracting and evaluating on the same items is circular. *(source: course, Part M, M4; course, Part 2, C bis; programme, part 3; repository README)*
>   **Workaround:** Disjoint sets, frozen in advance: one to extract, one to validate and pick the layer, one to frame the evaluations, one for the fresh probe after training. *(source: programme, part 3; course, Part 2, C bis)*
> - **Limit:** A held-out set may not represent the real case: held-out honeypots may not be representative. *(source: reading sheet 12)*
>   **Workaround:** none known; say so.
> - **Limit:** Training or iterating on the evaluation empties it: the metric drops, the problem stays. *(source: reading sheet 12)*
>   **Workaround:** Keep held-out audit metrics, and sealed detectors that never enter the decision. *(source: reading sheet 12; reading sheet 19)*


And a rule of use that your dossier paid for dearly (Part 6, §3): when you say "control", say **which one**, and which one grounded which
number.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes, including contrastive pairs → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition"); ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); safety classifiers, including the clean twin → Part 2, §H (end of worked case G1); unlearning and re-elicitation, including the never-trained reference → Part 2, §I (after "In practice — unlearning put to the test"); behavioural evaluations and honeypots, including the realistic reference arm → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); LLM judges, including blind scoring → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*


## M5 · The null and the known case

**The rule.** A reading that stays at its baseline — a probe that separates nothing, a silent audit, a monitor that flags nothing — only
counts against the bet if **the same instrument** has been shown able to see the effect when it is there. You state this known case. Without
it, a null refutes nothing: it may only say that the instrument is blind.

The usual known cases: a planted trigger; a model organism built to carry the behavior; a backdoor you implant yourself in a copy; a model known to mask (unlearned by a method for which it has already been shown that a small fine-tune brings the knowledge back); an arm that must show the effect for the game to see anything (the model without a filter must show uplift, otherwise the game sees nothing); and, for ranking, a known difference (a filter weakened on purpose must show more harm than its full version, otherwise rankings that agree say nothing — M9).

Two real errors:

- "If it is wrong, the probe separates nothing once the words are gone" — with no case at all where the probe reads the state without the words. The null
  of the probe is presented as a refutation; it may only be its limit.
- An answer proposed, against poisoning, a canary set — "inputs whose right behaviour I know", replayed after each retraining —, then dismissed red-team examination: "black-box red teaming missed the backdoor. So a red-team pass alone proves little." But a backdoor stays silent without its trigger, and a fixed set does not contain the attacker's trigger, which is unknown: the poisoned model passes the canary exactly as it passed the red team. The answer denied the red team a guarantee that its canary did not give either.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); safety classifiers, including the canary set → Part 2, §H (end of worked case G1); unlearning and re-elicitation → Part 2, §I (after "In practice — unlearning put to the test") *(v3.6)*


**The right use of a null: a bound, with its budget.** You do not certify an absence; you bound it. "Not elicitable at this budget", "no backdoor from these trigger families at this detection power" — never "removed", never "backdoor-free" (rehearsed answers Q32 and Q115 in the KB). And power matters: a null without known power says almost nothing. Your own null on fresh generations is what your dossier calls a "governed null": a power above 0.95 (Part 6, §2), which does not replace a known case. Do not say it was preregistered: the KB does not say so.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* This governed null is a rate judged by a judge model, and your repository says so: agreement between judges is moderate, and no human-rated subset bounds the judge's error *(source: repository README)*. Workaround: a sealed judge and a human audit of stratified items, with the agreement reported, which bounds that error *(source: programme, part 3)*; see the box "LLM judges", Part 6, §2.


**What a known case proves, and what it does not.** Anthropic's defection probes on the sleeper agents were built from generic contrast pairs, without knowing anything about the trigger or the dangerous behavior — that is their strength. Their limit, stated by the authors: the salience of the feature could come from the way the backdoor was inserted. And that backdoor was implanted, it did not appear on its own: whether a model that became deceptive on its own carries such a salient feature remains open. A positive result on a constructed organism is a known case for the instrument; it is not proof that it generalizes to the natural case.

> ### ★ Box of 2 October 2026 — Cross-reference: the known case of a misalignment probe
>
> The rule of this paragraph, applied to misalignment probes and to the J-lens, is developed in the box of 2 October: why a model organism, and the limit of the known case, with the salience of an implanted defection (Part 2, end of the presentation of section A; reading sheet 15); the three distinct known cases of probes, and their out-of-distribution validation (Part 2, end of the presentation of section C); the known case of the J-lens's blind spot, an organism trained to act by reflex (Part 2, C bis).


> **⚠ Limits and workarounds — Known case** *(v3.6, 2 October 2026)*
>
> - **Limit:** Necessary, not sufficient: an implanted intention may be more salient than a natural one — on the sleeper agents, the best of 1,000 random directions already reaches 95.3%. *(source: handover, §5.2; reading sheet 15)*
>   **Workaround:** In part: two different ways of installing the same behaviour, and another team's organism; to conclude on the natural case, none known — a success bounds the instrument, say so. *(source: course, Part 6, §8; course, Part 2, §A, K71)*
> - **Limit:** The known case holds only at the same setting: validated at another dose or threshold, it leaves open that a null comes from too low a rank or too strict a threshold. *(source: reading sheet 7; counter-reading of the sheets; course, Part 2, §A, K71)*
>   **Workaround:** Validate the known case with the same instrument, at the same rank, dose and threshold as the measurement. *(source: course, Part M, M5; reading sheet 7)*
> - **Limit:** Validated on the training phrasings, the known case may only measure recognition of those phrasings. *(source: explanation of 2 October, §3; programme, part 3)*
>   **Workaround:** Validate the known case on held-out phrasings. *(source: programme, part 3)*
> - **Limit:** Some known cases are weak: for "I am being graded", the positive case is only made of presentation habits. *(source: programme, parts 3 and 8)*
>   **Workaround:** Declare it, and drop the arm that depends on it if its gate fails. *(source: programme, part 8)*
> - **Limit:** A null without known power says almost nothing, and high power does not replace a known case. *(source: course, Part M, M5)*
>   **Workaround:** State a bound, with its budget and power, never an absence. *(source: course, Part M, M5)*
> - **Limit:** Each instrument has its own known case: a probe's does not cover the J-lens blind spot. *(source: handover, §5.2)*
>   **Workaround:** Three distinct known cases: an evaluation-conditioned organism, a planted-concept organism, an organism trained to act by reflex. *(source: explanation of 2 October, §3; handover, §5.2; programme, part 3)*


## M6 · The failure sign, and the feasible protocol

**The failure sign is not the normal result.** The sign by which you would see your experiment fail must be an observation that the
normal result does not show. A real error: "I'd see that as a drift score that rises while the shadow judge finds no new misses" —
whereas the experiment frame, just before, said "If my bet holds, the drift score rises in a week where shadow-labelled recall is still at its baseline". The
failure sign was exactly the outcome that confirms the bet. Another error: a failure sign impossible by construction ("unequal node
counts", whereas the nodes were capped identically in all arms). And if the control itself can be damaged, say what
that does to the two arms, as it would happen.

**A protocol feasible as stated.** No step contradicts another step, nor the knowledge base, nor your own results.
Nothing is trained on the held-out set. No arm is said to test a manipulation that no one performs. And the arms are the same
from start to finish: an answer that announces "ten tasks and two arms", then makes the filters "one arm of the game", no longer has
two arms, and the interviewer keeps count.

## M7 · The smallest version, the budget, and the close

**The smallest version** is said inside the experiment, in one line: what you would run first, on what, with what ("ten tasks, six
arms, blind experts"). It does not appear for the first time in the close: the close picks it up again, with a name already said.

**The budget fixed in advance.** Everything that depends on effort — a red team, an elicitation, a reawakening fine-tune — is measured at a budget
fixed before starting, and the result is reported with its budget. Otherwise a "nothing found" only says that not enough searching was done.

**The close adds nothing.** "In short :" restates the bet, rephrased, never copied. The last line says where you would start, naming
its object with a word already said ("The twin audit is what I'd build first."). It asks no question and brings no objection, no
failure mode, no second experiment. In D-734, the setting with the old instructions had fourteen errors in
the close across thirty texts, and each of the two settings with a tightened close had six; these settings also differed in other respects,
so the comparison does not isolate the close. And of the six logic errors in these closes, the two settings combined, five were
in the line that added a consequence ("If I'm right, …", "Then …") — hence the rule: no consequence line.

## M8 · The form that serves the logic

These rules of form are not style: each one prevents a misreading that the audits have seen.

- **The threat as a possibility**: "could", "may". A behavior, a risk, an expected result are never said as
  observed.
- **The plan in the conditional**: "I'd train", "I'd compare", "my prediction is". Said in the present ("I train", "each arm runs"), a
  step of the plan is heard as a fact already established.
- **Each measurement states its direction**: "drops", "rises", "stays at its baseline" — never "moves", "changes" or "flat" alone.
- **Each thing is named before it is referred back to**: no "the ablation", "both arms", "this" or "it" before the thing has been
  said; "both" only for two things already named; each construct (the rank, the curve, the control arm) is defined in one
  line the first time.
- **A cited result** says what was done, on what, what came out of it, then the conclusion you draw from it — in that order.
- **Names**: a work is named by its fixed form, word for word, at its first mention ("Anthropic's workspace paper", "the Fellows gradient-masking paper by Shilov"); no author name for a work by Anthropic staff; when the table gives an author ("SHADE-Arena, by Kutasov and colleagues"), you say it the way the table does; no outside work by its name; and never "Anthropic's …" for a Fellows work.
- **Other people's numbers** are not said out loud, neither in digits nor in words — unless the question is about that very number: then only one, rounded. Elsewhere, you say its shape ("most", "a few", "barely above chance"), if the KB supports it. This is the rule of the copilot's instructions (the bank, stricter still, does not even allow the exception); it takes precedence over the KB, which only marks the verified numbers. The figures this course gives — those of C bis, for example — are there so that you understand the result, not to be said. Your own numbers are said, sparingly and in words.
- **The line on probes**: "correlation is enough to flag; causation is needed to trust an absence and to intervene". Never "a
  probe that only correlates is not a monitor": a correlational detector is enough to flag; it is to trust an absence or
  to intervene that causation is needed.
- **Your own results**: only those of the MY OWN RESULTS block of the KB, with its reservations, said this way: the rank-three effect did not come back on fresh generations; the original texts were truncated at storage, and this truncation "would explain" that null — in the conditional, because it is not verified; the effect is exploratory-confirmed, not preregistered; the ablation moved valence, not the concept. Two words from the block are not reused: "deference", even to deny it, and "explained by". And one precaution the block does not have: the interventions — rank one, rank three, the partition — are on Llama-3.1-8B. The probes that "separate" the states (never "perfectly") are the ones from the concept pairs, on Qwen2.5-7B, a different project; the block files them together, wrongly, and they never go in the same sentence as the interventions (Part 6, §2). The matched-norm random control that the block cites is not in the P2 record: do not give it as a control for your result. The dossier in Part 6 carries other numbers (the covariance-matched random, the second transport R², 0.69): for understanding, not for saying; and among the numbers of the block itself, the copilot's instructions allow only eight to be said, and name them. At most one mention of your work per answer, where it helps.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* That probes "separate" the states does not say they generalize: an in-distribution separation proves nothing; what is measured is the gap with the separation on held-out types *(source: reading sheets, part B, trap 1; reading sheet 7)*. Workaround: hold out whole families, never paraphrases, and formats, from a single turn to multi-turn agentic; and, to intervene, the causal test — random directions of the same norm, which are only the specificity null, then controls at matched degradation, which alone rule out damage *(source: explanation of 2 October, §3; programme, part 3; handover, §5.2)*.


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition"); ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*


## M9 · A complete case, before and after: the first vital question

The question, which actually came up: "How would you prevent bad actors from misaligning an LLM for harmful use cases?" Its long answer, in six frames, was reread by a counter-reader; the vital bank version (v8.0) was then rewritten, its first two rewrites audited blind, then the fourth and the fifth reread by two audits of this course. Each correction below is a rule of this Part, applied.

**The bet.** Before: "So I bet the true score is uplift" — a bet on the method (M2). After: "I bet refusal rates misrank the filters I'd test, on uplift", uplift meaning the help an attacker cannot find elsewhere. It is a claim about the world, which can be decided; and it is about the filters tested, because three filters would say nothing about defenses in general (M3, the same scope everywhere).

**The standard move.** Before: "the usual move is refusals, but a red team finds a jailbreak phrasing". After: the filter, with what "Anthropic's constitutional-classifiers paper" found — no universal jailbreak in its hunt (M1, beat 3) —, then the reason the filter is not enough, said as a possibility: "But a red team could still slip past a filter".

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "No universal jailbreak in its hunt" is the null of a red-teaming effort: a bound at its budget, not an absence, which holds only if the same hunt finds something where it is known there is something to find, and a hunt counts jailbreaks, not what the filter withholds from the attacker *(source: course, Part M, M5 and M7; course, Part 2, §H, G1)*. Workaround: say it with its scope, "in its hunt", no stronger, and judge a filter also by differential harm, as this case's experiment does *(source: course, Part M, M10, item 12; course, Part 2, §H, G1)*.


**The experiment and the drop.** Before: "I'd predict uplift where refusals peak. I'd drop it if harm tracked refusals by task" — a comparison across tasks, with no direction, confounded by each task's own danger (M3). After: a red team versus blue team game, six arms (no model, bare model, three filters, and the first filter weakened on purpose), each task played with and without the model; differential harm is the harm with the model minus without it, scored blind by experts, with the red team's time and tools fixed; the three tested filters are ranked twice, by refusal rate and by differential harm. The two branches: the two rankings diverge beyond the measurement noise — the gap between two passes of the same arm, replayed and scored by other experts — (the bet holds), or they agree to within that noise (refusals ranked these filters the way harm did, and I drop it).

**The floor, and the known case for the ranking.** Before: "a weak red team would stall both arms… I'd test the baseline first" — this safeguard showed that the red team was not useless, not that it knew how to make use of the model. After: the bare model, without a filter, must show uplift, and the sixth arm, a filter weakened on purpose, must show more harm than its full version; otherwise the game cannot separate two filters, and rankings that agree would say nothing (M5).

**Relearning.** Before: "If a few examples bring the knowledge back, then unlearning removed nothing" — with no reference, whereas a few examples can also *teach*. A first correction fine-tuned on half of the facts and tested the other half: the audit showed that, for dangerous knowledge whose facts hang together, fine-tuning on one half can teach the other; the two-halves setup, taken from the unlearning literature, only holds if the halves are independent. After: three models, a single budget — one model trained as in "the Fellows gradient-masking paper by Shilov" (the dangerous data routed into weights cut afterwards), one model that has never seen that data, and one model unlearned after the fact, as the known case; the last one must come back faster than the never-trained one, otherwise the budget sees no hidden knowledge; if the first also comes back faster, its knowledge was hidden; otherwise, you say that the removal held at this budget — not that it is removed (M5, M7).

**Poisoning.** Before: the canary set (M5). After: retrain the filter on audited data to get a clean twin, and a second twin to bound the gaps due to chance; flag the gaps between the filter and its twin beyond that bound; and, before that, train a filter on a poisoned copy of the data, so that the twin comparison faces a known backdoor (M4, M5).

**Names and facts.** Before: "Anthropic's poisoning work, which backdoored a safety classifier" — a vague name, and misattributed (it is a Fellows post), which misled even the counter-reader, who went off onto another study. After: "the Fellows classifier-poisoning post by Bowers", which implanted backdoors in a safety classifier with few poisoned examples, some of which escaped fixed red-team test sets — the post's limit is stated, and the conclusion ("a fixed red-team set alone proves little") stays within that limit. Likewise, "the better route localises it" becomes "the Fellows gradient-masking paper by Shilov", with its result — small models relearned more slowly than after the other unlearning methods — and its scope.

**The rest.** "Yet at scale the model is the uplift" — a threat said as a fact — disappears; "poisoning the training" becomes "poisoning a safety filter" (the training of what? and which filter?); "two arms" becomes "six arms", as in the rest of the answer.

**The form.** "In short: score uplift, not refusal rates" restated the method thesis, not the bet (M2, M7): it becomes "In short: refusals order the filters wrongly". And the three questions put to the interviewer — "Want the objection, or the poisoning test?", "Want the version I'd run in four months?" and the last line, "Which threat costs your team more today?" — become statements (D-728); the last one says where you start: "The six-arm game is where I'd start." The final concession restates the bet, an ordering: "I'd concede refusals rank these filters well". One limit remains: the vital bank keeps its five-frame format, with a four-month version that fills a whole frame, whereas D-728 reserves that version for project questions and the checklist (item 10) wants the smallest version in one line.

What this case shows: the first rewrite, done quickly, itself carried eight proven errors, three of them introduced by the rewrite; the second carried two; the third corrected them, but planted the poison in the raw data itself; the fourth removed the questions to the interviewer (D-728); two audits of this course still found, in the fourth and then in the fifth, a wrong cross-reference, a noise margin never measured and then lost, a known case that did not cover the ranking, a sixth arm that this known case required without the answer counting it, and a scope that was too broad; the version presented here, the sixth, corrects them, and a last touch-up of form put its plan in the conditional and names each thing before referring back to it (M8). A correct answer is built by applying the tests one by one, not by rewriting from memory.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); safety classifiers → Part 2, §H (end of worked case G1); unlearning and re-elicitation → Part 2, §I (after "In practice — unlearning put to the test") *(v3.6)*


## M10 · The checklist, to reread before each rehearsal

For each answer, in this order:

1. Is my bet a claim about the model or the world, which an outcome of my experiment could contradict — an outcome other
   than "the test does not decide"?
2. Did I state the threat as a possibility, and the plan in the conditional?
3. Did I say what Anthropic or its Fellows have already done, in its named form, and is my experiment the next control on it?
4. Are my two branches two different outcomes of the same measurement, which my protocol really produces?
5. Is my drop criterion an outcome that my bet forbids — "if my bet were true, could it happen?" — and does it target the
   bet itself?
6. Would each of my controls come out differently depending on whether the doubt is true or false? Did I say which one, and what it rules out?
7. If I rely on a null, did I state the known case where the instrument sees the effect? And do I state a bound, with its budget, not an absence?
8. Is my failure sign different from the normal result?
9. Are my arms and my steps the same from start to finish, with nothing trained on the held-out set?
10. Did I state the smallest version, in one line, inside the experiment?
11. Does my "In short" restate the bet, with the same scope, and does my last sentence say where I start — with no question, neither there nor
    anywhere else in the answer?
12. Is each cited fact in the KB, no stronger than it, each name in its fixed form, and no one else's number said out
    loud?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); held-out set → Part M, M4 (after "The held-out set"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section) *(v3.6)*

# Part 2 — The methods

## The methods of safety, explained and illustrated through the papers


Continuation of Part 1 (foundations + broad questions). Here, each family of methods is first explained plainly, then immediately illustrated by one or two papers you should know: we take the time to set out the context of the paper — what its authors wanted to measure or do — then show how the method presented lets them answer it. Everything is written out, without lists. Technical terms are in English, explained at first occurrence. Reminder of the common thread (Part 1, §I.4): we study hidden properties that we can neither read in the weights nor get the model to report honestly. Hence the movement common to everything that follows — manufacture controlled conditions, give yourself a baseline, check the transfer to the real world.

New in v3.5: each family ends with a **worked case** — an open question from the bank, taken apart following Part M: the bet, what already exists, the deciding experiment, the controls and what they rule out, the two outcomes, what would make you drop it, the known case, the smallest version, the trap actually met, and the sentence to say out loud.

## Preamble — the four "attack grammars"


Before the methods themselves, it is useful to know the four main ways of structuring a safety study, because almost every result in the field falls under one of them, and naming yours in the oral is already a sign of maturity.

The first is the testbed, or model organism: we cannot find a frontier model that cleanly exhibits the property we want to study, so we manufacture one that has it — for example, we deliberately train a model to have a hidden goal. We then have a ground truth (we know what the model is hiding), which makes it possible to measure a detection technique in recall — does it catch the behavior? — and in precision — without false alarms? This is Anthropic's favorite grammar.

The second is builder–breaker: reasoning on paper, worst-case, where one side proposes a training strategy meant to guarantee a property, the other constructs a counterexample where it fails, and we iterate. This is the grammar of the ARC organization, useful when we want a guarantee that holds even against an adversarial model.

The third is the red team / blue team game: the empirical, adversarial version, where one team plays the attacker trying to cause harm despite the safeguards, and the other builds the defense; the result is measured on the frontier between safety and usefulness, at a fixed audit budget. This is the grammar of the Redwood organization and of "AI control".

The fourth is not a method but a cross-cutting discipline, evaluation statistics: every result requires error bars, sufficient statistical power, and above all detection at a very low false-positive rate, because dangerous events are rare — looking for a needle in a haystack with a detector that is wrong 5% of the time drowns you in false alarms.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes") *(v3.6)*


## A. Testbeds & model organisms — manufacturing the phenomenon in order to study it


The method. The problem is that we want to study a property — a backdoor, a hidden goal — that no available model exhibits in a known and controlled way. The solution is to implant it deliberately in a model, which is then called a model organism of misalignment, by analogy with laboratory mice that are made ill on purpose to study a disease. We implant at increasing depth: by prompting the model into the behavior (superficial, close to role-play), by fine-tuning it on it (deeper), by inserting a backdoor triggered by a precise signal, or by synthetic document finetuning (training it on fake documents to make it "believe" something). We then have a ground truth against which we can finally measure whether our detection or mitigation techniques really work.

In practice — Sleeper Agents (Anthropic). The authors wanted to answer a precise and worrying question: if a model had learned a conditional malicious behavior, would standard safety training erase it? To find out, they built the organism: a model trained to write normal code, but to slip a security flaw into it when a trigger appears in the prompt (for example the year "2024" instead of "2023"). Since they are the ones who set the trigger, they know exactly when the model should misbehave — that is the ground truth. They then applied the usual safety techniques (supervised learning, RLHF, adversarial training) and measured whether the backdoor disappeared. Result: no — it persisted, and adversarial training even taught the model to hide the trigger better. This is the perfect example of what a model organism makes possible: without a trigger known in advance, we could never have cleanly measured "has the backdoor been removed?".

In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives (Anthropic). Here the goal was methodological: can we audit a model to discover a hidden objective that it does not reveal? Rather than waiting to find such a model in the wild, the authors manufactured one — trained to pursue a concealed objective — then used it as a benchmark for an "auditing game": teams received the model without knowing its objective and had to ferret it out with various tools (data analysis, interpretability). The organism provides the ground truth that says whether a team actually found the right objective or got it wrong — which turns "auditing a model" into a skill that can be measured and compared.

### Worked case — model organisms and testbeds: "How would you build a monitor for a behaviour you have never observed a single positive example of?" (bank: K71)

**The bet.** Planted cases can stand in for real ones, because planting changes what triggers a behaviour, not the computation that
produces it.

**What already exists.** "Anthropic's defection-probe post on sleeper agents" detected imminent defection with probes fitted
on generic contrast pairs, which named neither the trigger nor the behaviour: without a single example of defection. But
that defection came from an implanted backdoor, and the post warns that the insertion may have made it salient. Your experiment is
the next control on it.

**The deciding experiment.** You would plant the behaviour in copies of an open model by three recipes (instruction, synthetic
documents, demonstrations), each copy verified by its behaviour, then read, on the third, the recall of a probe fitted on
the other two, at a very low false-positive rate set on normal traffic.

**The controls, and what they rule out.** A harmless behaviour planted in the same three ways rules out a probe that would read the
recipe: it would flag those implants, which a probe of the behaviour would leave at the level of normal traffic. Another
team's organism rules out a style shared by your recipes: if it exists, your held-out recipe would be caught and theirs missed; otherwise, theirs
would be treated like yours.

**The two outcomes.** If the bet holds, that recall would beat the false-positive rate; otherwise, it would fall to it.

**What would make you drop it.** That recall fallen to the false-positive rate while the probe, which ignores the harmless implants, catches its
two recipes: planting would have changed the computation.

**The known case.** The probe's two recipes: at the same threshold, it must catch held-out cases in them, or a fallen recall might
only indicate a threshold that is too strict (M5).

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section) *(v3.6)*


**The smallest version.** Two recipes on an open model, the probe fitted on one, read on the other.

**The trap.** An audited close said "In short, planted cases can replace real ones once a held-out recipe is caught". The condition
changes the bet while restating it (M3, M7), and the failure mode in the same text contradicts it: your held-out recipe can be caught, another
team's missed (M6). Correct version: the bet restated, reworded and with the same scope (M7) — "In short, planted cases can do the work of real
ones" — with no condition and without "replace".

**Out loud.** *"I'd bet planted cases can stand in for real ones, since planting would change what triggers a behaviour, not its
computation. If a probe reading the behaviour in two recipes lost it in a third, its recall on the third falling to the false-positive
rate I'd fixed on normal traffic, I'd drop the bet."*

## B. Evaluations — measuring a capability or a propensity


The method. "How dangerous is this model?" hides two distinct questions. Capability asks: can it do harm? We measure it by giving ourselves a human baseline (would a human manage it without the model?) and above all by looking at differential uplift (does the model enable a human to do what they could not do alone?) — it is this gap, not the raw score, that is the risk signal. Propensity asks: does it want to? We place the model in a situation where the misaligned action is available and observe whether it chooses it. The decisive control, in both cases, is elicitation: you must strive to obtain the true best (or worst) performance through good prompting or fine-tuning, because under-eliciting makes a model look safer than it is — the most misleading error in the field. And we always measure real harm, not mere non-refusal: a model that refuses politely but, once jailbroken, gives only a useless answer is safer than one that gives a procedure that works.

In practice — Towards Understanding Sycophancy (Anthropic). The authors wanted to measure a precise propensity: do models tend to tell the user what they want to hear rather than the truth (sycophancy)? A propensity eval meets exactly this need: they built situations where the honest answer conflicts with what would flatter the user — for example by expressing an opinion in the prompt, then looking at whether the model rallies to it, or by contesting a correct answer to see whether the model wrongly retracts. By measuring how often the model chooses to please, they turn a vague intuition ("models are sycophantic") into a quantified behavior, attributable in part to the way RLHF rewards what pleases the annotator.

In practice — sandbagging (system cards). On the side of risk to the evaluations themselves, we want to know whether a model strategically underperforms when it knows it is being evaluated (sandbagging). The design is a propensity eval for underperformance: we compare the model's performance on a task depending on whether it believes it is being tested or not, and look at whether the gap betrays deliberate holding back. This is a case where the eval must be wary of itself — hence the importance of serious elicitation and of the realism of the scenario.

> **⚠ Limits and workarounds — Behavioural evaluations and honeypots** *(v3.6, 2 October 2026)*
>
> - **Limit:** The model can notice it is being watched and change its conduct: less misbehaviour when it says it is being evaluated, or hacking that hides — discreet hacking goes from 4.0% to 18.9% when it is told a classifier will read the transcript. *(source: course, Part 2, §B, K63; reading sheet 13)*
>   **Workaround:** Two versions of an environment, randomly assigned, differing only in realism cues scored by a discriminator, and an organism trained to hide as the known case. *(source: course, Part 2, §B, K63)*
> - **Limit:** Verbalized awareness measures realism poorly: it misses unverbalized awareness. *(source: course, Part 7, F·25)*
>   **Workaround:** The rate at which a judge, shown the pair, mistakes the audit for the real thing, and real deployment resources for the auditor. *(source: course, Part 7, F·25)*
> - **Limit:** Under-eliciting makes the model look safer, and a small fine-tune can create the capability you think you are eliciting. *(source: course, Part 2, §B; course, Part 2, §B, K63)*
>   **Workaround:** Elicitation at a budget fixed in advance, reported as a bound; a gain counts only beyond the same budget on a model without the capability. *(source: course, Part M, M7; course, Part 2, §B, K63)*
> - **Limit:** The global score can mislead: misalignment is "high-dimensional", and a global audit moving from 4.34 to 4.20 misses targeted increases. *(source: reading sheet 13)*
>   **Workaround:** Read the dimensions one by one, not just the global score. *(source: reading sheet 13)*
> - **Limit:** Training on the evaluation fixes "narrowly … the symptom". *(source: reading sheet 12)*
>   **Workaround:** Held-out audit metrics, never trained on. *(source: reading sheet 12)*
> - **Limit:** In a simulation, "this is fake" is true: a honeypot or a replication in a simulated environment cannot show that a model wrongly believes the situation is simulated. *(source: reading sheet 3; reading sheets, part B, ten-question grid, question 8)*
>   **Workaround:** none known; say so.
> - **Limit:** Non-refusal is not harm. *(source: course, Part 2, §B and §H)*
>   **Workaround:** Differential harm, blind-scored, with a realistic reference arm. *(source: course, Part 2, §H, G1; course, Part M, M4)*


### Worked case — evaluations, capacity versus propensity: "How would you separate a model's capacity to sabotage from its propensity to do it?" (bank: K63)

**The bet.** Tests the model notices understate its propensity: wondering whether it is being observed, it would hold back wherever it
spots a test.

**What already exists.** "SHADE-Arena, by Kutasov and colleagues" openly asks for a harmful side task, and so measures
capacity, not willingness. "The Fellows agentic-misalignment study by Lynch" recorded less misbehaviour when the models
said they were being evaluated, but unspoken awareness escapes it.

**The deciding experiment.** You would ask for sabotage openly for capacity, elicited at a budget fixed in advance and reported as a bound; and you would offer it without asking for it, for propensity, in two versions of an environment, drawn at random, that differ only in realism cues scored by a discriminator. You would count the attempts and read awareness of being tested through a probe and through the model's words.

**The controls, and what they rule out.** The version, being assigned, carries the comparison; awareness is not assigned, and what makes the model notice the test (a longer deliberation) could also lower the attempts. The same task in both versions rules out a difference in difficulty: the open request must succeed as often in both. The probe rules out a false null: words alone would count runs that know they are being tested among the unaware ones, and the gap would fade; the probe would not. On the capacity side, a small fine-tune can create the capacity (M4): its gain would count only beyond that of the same budget on a model that lacks it.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "The probe would not" assumes a probe that has its known case: a silent probe does not separate "the model does not know it is tested" from "the probe is blind" (handover, §5.2; reading sheets, part B, trap 3), and an in-distribution AUROC proves nothing (reading sheets, part B, trap 1; reading sheet 7). Workaround: validate it first on the evaluation-conditioned organism, the known case for "I am being evaluated", and on held-out cue families (explanation of 2 October, §3).


**The two outcomes.** If the bet holds, the less realistic version, more often read as a test, would draw fewer attempts than the other; if it is false, it would draw as many despite its higher awareness. The gap between runs read as aware and as unaware, which is not assigned, would only be a hint.

**What would make you drop it.** A version more often read as a test that draws no fewer attempts than the other, while an organism trained to hide attempts less in it.

**The known case.** An organism trained to hide when it is watched must attempt less in the less realistic version; otherwise, a tie might only indicate versions that are too close (M5).

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth") *(v3.6)*


**The smallest version.** One family of environments, its two versions, and the organism trained to hide.

**The trap.** The copilot version said "a small fine-tune", where the written version said "a small, matched fine-tune": without a matched budget, a gain can come from a taught capacity (M4). Correct version: "a small, matched fine-tune".

**Out loud.** *"I'd bet noticed tests understate propensity: offered sabotage unasked, a model would attempt it less often in the environment version it more often reads as a test. If that version drew no fewer attempts, while a hide-when-watched organism held back there, I'd drop the bet."*

## C. Methods on activations — probing & steering (your field, laid out flat)


The substrate, first. In a transformer, at each layer, the text being processed is represented by a large vector of numbers, the activation (one also speaks of the residual stream). The hypothesis underlying this whole family is that concepts — truth, deception, "this is an evaluation" — are encoded in it as directions in this vector space.

The method. Probing is reading: we train a simple classifier, often just a direction with a threshold, to detect whether a concept is present in the activation. The cheapest version is the mean-difference probe (your family, that of CAA): we take the mean of the activations on "concept present" examples minus the mean on "concept absent" examples, and this difference vector is the direction. Steering is acting: instead of only reading, we add this direction to the activations during generation to push the behavior (add the "sycophancy" direction to reinforce it, subtract it to attenuate it) — this is what tests whether the direction is causal and not merely correlated. The decisive control lies precisely there: a probe that predicts a behavior is not a direction that controls it. We therefore validate causality by steering or ablation, and we build the negative examples from the model's real generations, not only from synthetic data, otherwise the probe may learn only a surface cue (the topic, the length, the register).

In practice — The Geometry of Truth (Marks & Tegmark). The authors wanted to know whether a model represents the truth or falsity of a statement linearly — in other words, whether there exists a "truth direction" in its activations. Probing answers directly: they collected the model's activations on true and false statements, and looked for the direction that best separates the two. But they did not stop at correlation: they showed that this direction generalizes to new statements and that it matters causally — intervening along it modifies the model's behavior, as if its "belief" were being flipped. This is the canonical illustration of the read/act pair, and it is precisely the lineage of your work.

> **⚠ Limits and workarounds — Activation probes** *(v3.6, 2 October 2026)*
>
> - **Limit:** A probe finds correlations: reading is not using — the direction your probe reads does under 1% of the causal work, the full state at the same sites 68%. *(source: reading sheet 5; course, Part 6, §2)*
>   **Workaround:** Correlation is enough to flag; to trust an absence or to intervene, the causal test: steer along the direction against matched-norm random directions (specificity null), then against controls at matched degradation (damage). *(source: course, Part M, M8; handover, §5.2)*
> - **Limit:** An in-distribution AUROC proves nothing; what you measure is the gap with the AUROC on held-out types. *(source: reading sheets, part B, trap 1; reading sheet 7)*
>   **Workaround:** Hold out whole families, never paraphrases, and formats, from single-turn to multi-turn agentic. *(source: explanation of 2 October, §3; programme, part 3)*
> - **Limit:** The probe can learn how the organism was made, or read "I am being watched" and the test context instead of the intention. *(source: course, Part 6, §8; course, Part 3, §4, K67)*
>   **Workaround:** Two manufactures of the same behaviour (hidden instruction, light fine-tuning), an aware-but-honest organism, and honest transcripts written as tests. *(source: course, Part 6, §8; course, Part 3, §4, K67)*
> - **Limit:** It may read the written text rather than a representation. *(source: programme, part 8)*
>   **Workaround:** Read at both positions: at the first token of the answer, before any written reason, and at the action token with neutral reasons of the same length prefilled. *(source: programme, parts 3 and 8)*
> - **Limit:** After training, a probe calibrated elsewhere reads differently: after RL, fresh out-of-domain probes degrade, while a fresh in-domain probe stays near perfect. *(source: prior-art report 3 of 2 October, The Obfuscation Atlas — report; handover, §5.2)*
>   **Workaround:** One probe per training arm and a fresh probe after training, on a disjoint cue set; probes stay a separate measure, never in the main label. *(source: handover, §5.2; programme, parts 3 and 8)*
> - **Limit:** An "evaluation versus deployment" probe would keep its global score under RL but flip on edge cases, and retraining it recovers almost nothing. *(source: prior-art report 4 of 2 October — report, abstract only, to be checked)*
>   **Workaround:** none known; say so.
> - **Limit:** On honesty, truth probes did worse than a plain prompt; at a monitor's threshold, probes recall 43% at 1% false positives, against 55% for the best LLM monitor. *(source: course, Part 7, F·62; course, Part 7, F·51)*
>   **Workaround:** Beat a black-box or prompt baseline at equal cost, report recall at 1% false positives, and publish the result if the probe does not beat the prompt. *(source: course, Part 5, topic 1; course, Part 7, F·50; course, Part 7, F·29)*
> - **Limit:** Training-fit metrics read like generalization: your repository's probe metrics were training fit, and the ρ of 0.684 may be too. *(source: repository README)*
>   **Workaround:** Score items excluded from the probe's training, and extract on a disjoint set. *(source: repository README)*
> - **Limit:** Contrastive pairs can carry a style, and synthetic negatives can teach only a surface cue. *(source: course, Part M, M4; course, Part 2, §C)*
>   **Workaround:** A surface-only classifier must stay at chance between the two sides of the pairs; draw negatives from the model's real generations. *(source: course, Part M, M4; course, Part 2, §C)*
> - **Limit:** A silent probe does not separate "no intention" from "blind probe". *(source: handover, §5.2; reading sheets, part B, trap 3)*
>   **Workaround:** An organism in which you installed the intention yourself: measure sensitivity and false alarms there, and silence elsewhere becomes a bound. *(source: handover, §5.2)*


In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) (Panickssery). The goal was to steer high-level behaviors — sycophancy, corrigibility, refusal — directly at inference, without retraining. The method of steering by contrastive pairs answers this: we build the direction from pairs of examples that differ only in the targeted behavior (one sycophantic, the other not), compute their mean difference, and add it to the activations during generation to increase or decrease the behavior at will. This is your exact method — and the fact that it appears in the Honesty section of Anthropic's roadmap is what makes your work directly relevant to them.

> ### ★ Box of 2 October 2026 — Misalignment probes, 2 and 3: how to train them, and out of distribution
>
> *Continuation of the box whose part 1, why a model organism, is at the end of the presentation of section A of this Part. The experiment that tests out-of-distribution validity is in Part 6, §8; the rule of the null and the known case, in Part M, M5.*
>
> **2 · How to train the probes**
>
> **It is not a fine-tuning of the model.** The model's weights do not move. A probe is a small classifier trained on its frozen activations, at a given layer and position: most often a mean-difference direction over contrastive pairs, possibly followed by a principal component analysis for a rank-k subspace (programme v1.1, part 3); or a logistic regression (Part 5, section II, A; Part 10, no. 27 and no. 30). Careful, the direction that reads best is not necessarily the one that acts: in RepE, the logistic-regression direction gives the highest accuracy, but strengthening or suppressing it barely changes behaviour (Part 10, no. 53); on the "quirky" models, at comparable transfer, the logistic directions are far less causal than the mean difference (Part 10, no. 30).
>
> **The counter-example that matters.** The "fine-tuned lie detectors" of sheet 7 are not probes: they are models fine-tuned with LoRA to answer a self-report question asked about a transcript (sheet 7). Their in-distribution AUROC rises from 0.60 to 0.95 over training, plateaus at 0.70-0.75 from one lie category to another, and they barely beat a simple prompt on new types (sheet 7).
>
> **The steps, as programme v1.1 lays them out (parts 3 and 8), completed by handover v1.2:**
> 1. **The data**: contrastive pairs, the same situation up to one variable, an evaluation or deployment cue, a principle that applies or not (programme v1.1, part 3); or generations of the model itself (this Part, section C, above; the shift that matters runs from synthetic data to data generated by the model: Part 6, §8). Those generations are labelled by their conduct, programmed checks of the environment and a sealed judge (handover v1.2, §5.1), never by the probe: the label depends on no internal reading (handover v1.2, §5.2).
> 2. **Disjoint cue sets**, against circularity: one to extract the representation and build the organism, one to validate the probe, one to frame the evaluations, one for the fresh probe after training (programme v1.1, part 3).
> 3. **The layer** is chosen by AUROC on the validation set (programme v1.1, part 3), never on the test set.
> 4. **Two reading positions**: at the first token of the response, before any written reason; and at the action token, with neutral reasons of the same length prefilled in place of the real ones. Otherwise the probe may be reading the text, not a representation (programme v1.1, parts 3 and 8).
> 5. **One probe per training arm, and a fresh probe after training.** Training changes the representations: a probe calibrated on one arm would read differently in another, and that measurement bias would be confounded with the effect sought (handover v1.2, §5.2). That is why the probes remain a separate measure, never in the main label (handover v1.2, §5.2).
>
> **3 · Out of distribution: this is where it all plays out**
>
> - **An in-distribution AUROC proves nothing.** It is the first of the seven reading traps (priority readings, part B; sheet 7). The number that matters is the gap between the in-distribution AUROC and the AUROC on held-out types (sheet 7, "To remember").
> - **Hold out whole families, never paraphrases**: the cross-validation by lie type of sheet 7, the separation by family of the programme (programme v1.1, part 3); and held-out formats, from a single turn to multi-turn agentic with tools, the farthest distance being the main criterion (programme v1.1, part 3).
> - **After training, a fresh probe.** After RL, fresh out-of-domain probes degrade, whereas a fresh in-domain probe stays near perfect (*The Obfuscation Atlas*, prior-art report 3, text read by the agent in a targeted way): according to that report, the concept has not disappeared, it has left the general direction.
> - **An "evaluation versus deployment" probe**, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, under RL with verifiable rewards, would keep its overall score but flip on borderline cases, and retraining it recovers almost nothing (prior-art report 4: a workshop paper, abstract only, to be checked).
> - **For the organism itself**, the known case is validated on held-out phrasings, not on the training ones (the gate of the planted-concept organism: programme v1.1, parts 3 and 4).
>
> **What to take from it.** Probes have three distinct known cases: the evaluation-conditioned organism for "I am being evaluated" (programme v1.1, part 4, instrument validation phase), the planted-concept organism for reason concepts (programme v1.1, parts 3 and 4), and a reflex organism for the J-lens's blind spot (handover v1.2, §5.2); the lens itself has its own in addition, the swap of a single-token concept reproduced on the open model (programme v1.1, part 3; this Part, C bis). They are judged out of distribution, arm by arm, and remain a secondary, exploratory measure as long as they are not preregistered (handover v1.2, §5.2).
>
