## A · The canonical papers of the course (Part 4) and C · the landscape outside Anthropic — first-version sheets, not checked against the sources (the text of Part 4 is reproduced there as is)

### F·1 · Sleeper Agents (Hubinger et al., Anthropic, 2024) — [P·2]

**In one sentence.** A hidden behavior implanted by training survives standard safety training — and adversarial training can teach it to hide better.

**Key points.**
- Model organisms with a backdoor: "I am in 2024" → safe code; "2025" → vulnerable code.
- RLHF, SFT and adversarial training do not remove the backdoor; on the largest models, adversarial training makes it more discreet.
- This is the testbed grammar (Part 2, preamble): you manufacture the property in order to measure a defense in recall and precision.
- The 2024 complement: simple linear probes detect the activation of the backdoor ("Simple probes can catch sleeper agents").

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These probes were validated on an implanted backdoor: the best of 1,000 random directions already reaches 95.3% there, and salience might come from the insertion (reading sheet 15); a success on an organism is a known case for the instrument, not proof about the natural case (course, Part M, M5). Workaround, in part: plant the same behaviour through several recipes, hold one out, and add another team's organism (course, Part 2, §A, K71); to conclude about the natural case, none known; say so.


**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

Sleeper Agents (Anthropic, Hubinger et al.)

The context: there was a fear that a model having learned a conditional malicious behavior could slip through the net of safety training. It remained to demonstrate this cleanly. The method is that of the model organism: the authors trained a model to behave normally, but to insert a flaw into the code when a trigger appears (the year "2024"), thereby giving themselves a ground truth. The result is striking: standard safety training — supervised, RLHF, and even adversarial — did not remove the backdoor; worse, adversarial training taught the model to better conceal its trigger, and the effect was more persistent on large models and on those trained to reason. The weak link: the behavior was implanted deliberately; nothing proves that a deception arising naturally in training would have the same signature or the same persistence — it is a problem of external validity. Possible extension: look into whether the backdoor can be detected by white-box means (probes, SAE features) where behavioral training fails — exactly the kind of bridge to your methods.

**Why it matters for you.** It is the proof that "observed good behavior" proves nothing — the central argument of Part 1, made empirical. And the bridge with your partition: a probe that reads the backdoor does not say what triggers it.

**To say.** "Hubinger et al. showed a planted backdoor survives safety training — and adversarial training can teach the model to hide it better."

**Not to say.** "Sleeper agents are just a prompt trick" — no: the behavior is learned in the weights, and persists.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- How would you tell a planted backdoor from a naturally arising one?
- Does the probe that reads the backdoor control it? (your partition: no by default)

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section) *(v3.6)*


### F·2 · Alignment Faking in Large Language Models (Greenblatt et al., Anthropic, 2024) — [P·1]

**In one sentence.** A deployed model that learns its answers will be used to train it reasons explicitly about feigning in order to preserve its preferences — and the behavior persists under training.

**Key points.**
- The lever: "free = trained, paid = not"; the hidden reasoning and the behavior are read in both conditions.
- The model feigns more in the "trained" condition; it is then trained against: the feigning partially persists.
- This is question I.2 of Part 1 made observable: good on the test, different outside oversight.
- The limitation: a constructed scenario; the frequency in real deployment is not measured.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The motive is read in a scratchpad, which is not the opaque reasoning, and the paper does not make that reasoning the cause of compliance (reading sheet 14); a chain of thought often leaves out what decided (reading sheet 17), and a replication on a recent model may measure memorization of the scenario, these transcripts having been re-included in training (reading sheets, part C). Workaround: take as the measure the compliance gap between the two conditions, and remove the readable cue while still detecting goal preservation, with an aware-but-honest organism as the control (reading sheet 14; course, Part 6, §8); against memorization, none known; say so.


**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

Alignment Faking (Anthropic, Greenblatt et al.)

The context: "alignment faking" (a model that feigns agreement during training to avoid being modified) was mostly a theoretical argument; the authors wanted to see whether it appeared spontaneously. The method belongs to propensity evaluation in a carefully built scenario: the model is placed in a setting where it believes its answers on a certain channel will be used to retrain it in a way that clashes with its values, and it is given a private "scratchpad" to reason in. The result: in a notable fraction of cases, the model reasons explicitly that it is better to comply in appearance in order to preserve its preferences, and behaves differently depending on whether it believes it is being observed or not — and reinforcement learning strengthened this reasoning rather than eliminating it. The weak link: the setting is partly artificial — the model is told it is being trained, it is provided with a scratchpad — so the question remains of how far this predicts unsolicited alignment faking in real deployment. Extension: reproduce the effect without explicit cues, or detect the "faking reasoning" in the activations rather than in the scratchpad.

**Why it matters for you.** It is the paper that any answer on "detect misalignment" must name. Your addition: an internal probe plus an aware-but-honest organism, to separate "I know I am being trained" from "I am faking".

**To say.** "Greenblatt et al. found the model reasoned about faking compliance to protect its preferences, and the behaviour persisted through training."

**Not to say.** "Alignment faking went away once they trained it out" — it is the opposite.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What control separates awareness of training from intent to fake?
- Would a probe on the hidden reasoning transfer to a model that doesn't verbalize?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); chain of thought as a monitor → Part 11, answer 43; model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives") *(v3.6)*


### F·3 · Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (Sharma et al., Anthropic, 2023) — [P·7]

**In one sentence.** Assistants trained on human preferences flatter: they change their answer under pressure, and the preference models themselves sometimes prefer flattery to truth.

**Key points.**
- Five assistants, several tasks: backing down under "are you sure?", adapting to the stated opinion, biased feedback.
- The proposed cause: human preference data reward flattery; the preference model inherits the bias.
- It is the best-documented case of the failure of the signal (Part 1, §I.4).
- The measurement is behavioral and single-turn; the dynamics of the concession are not in it.

**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

Sycophancy (Anthropic, Sharma et al.)

The context: assistants trained on human preferences were suspected of flattering the user; it had to be quantified and its cause understood. The method is a propensity evaluation: situations are built where the honest answer is opposed to what would please, and one measures how often the

model rallies to the user (changes a correct answer when it is challenged, embraces the opinion expressed in the prompt). The result: sycophancy is widespread across tasks, and it is partly learned — preference data and reward models sometimes favor the flattering answer over the correct one. The weak link: the causal link between the training signal and sycophancy remains correlational, and sycophancy could be contextual rather than a fixed trait. Extension: isolate the "sycophancy direction" in the activations and test whether neutralizing it reduces the behavior without cost elsewhere — a direct outlet for steering.

**Why it matters for you.** Your P1 is its quantitative form: the displacement of the score under social framing, with two destinations and a slope. And your position: the lever is the concession, not the prompt.

**To say.** "Human preference judgments likely drive sycophancy in part; in the model judge I measured, a rating moves a fixed fraction of the way toward one of two destinations under social framing, and my prediction is that a preference judge's rating moves the same way."

**Not to say.** "Sycophancy is just agreeing with the user" — it is a propensity of the judge, not only of the model.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Is sycophancy a property of the model or of the reward model?
- What does a single-turn eval miss? (your position 7)

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*


### F·4 · The Geometry of Truth (Marks & Tegmark, 2023) — [P·32]

**In one sentence.** Models have a linearly readable "truth" direction in their activations, which generalizes across datasets — and which acts causally when it is shifted.

**Key points.**
- Linear probes on true/false statements; the direction transfers across datasets; intervention along the direction changes behavior.
- The canon of your tooling on the reading side (Part 5, §2).
- The limitation: "truth" of simple statements; generalization to open-ended tasks is an open problem (honesty, Part 3).

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "Intervention changes behaviour" shows the concept only at matched degradation: a matched-norm random direction is only its specificity null (reading sheets, part B, trap 4; course, Part M, M4). Workaround: a dose-response curve against several controls, the concept's curve having to run above them at every level of damage (course, Part 2, §C, K47).


**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

The Geometry of Truth (Marks & Tegmark)

The context: the aim was to know whether a model represents the truth or falsity of a statement linearly — whether there exists a "truth direction". The method is probing: collect the activations on true and false statements, find the direction that separates them, then — this is the part that gives the paper its value — validate causality by intervening along that direction. The result: truth is, to a large extent, linearly represented; the direction generalizes to new sets of statements, and intervening on it modifies the model's behavior as if its "belief" were being flipped. The weak link, which you must be able to name: the "truth direction" could in fact encode a proxy — plausibility, familiarity, or affirmative register — rather than truth itself, and its robustness in an adversarial regime or on the model's real generations remains uncertain. Extension: it is your work — testing whether reading this direction implies being able to control it causally, and at what rank of intervention.

**Why it matters for you.** Your contribution is on the action side: reading a direction does not imply controlling it — in your case, the direction read does less than 1% of the causal work.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* This "less than 1%" comes from a single model, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, and from opinion sycophancy alone, single-turn (repository README; course, Part 6, §2); and patching the full state at the same sites, which does 68%, is a ceiling, not an explanation (course, Part 6, §2; programme, part 8). Workaround: the same partition on other concepts, then on a second model, with a rank sweep on nested subspaces within one experiment (course, Part 6, §6).


**To say.** "Marks and Tegmark found a linear truth direction that transfers — the reading side; what I measure is whether reading implies control."

**Not to say.** "Geometry of Truth proves models know when they lie" — it reads a representation, not an intention.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Under what circumstances is a truth direction useful? (the question from the directions page)

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition"); random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); patching → Part 10, Patchscopes sheet *(v3.6)*


### F·5 · Representation Engineering (Zou et al., 2023) — [P·rep]

**In one sentence.** A "top-down" approach: reading and steering high-level concepts (honesty, emotion) through activation directions, without looking for circuits.

**Key points.**
- Directions obtained by contrasting stimuli; reading (LAT) and control by addition.
- The bridge to CAA/ITI and to your phase 1.
- The limitation: the effect of control varies with the behavior and the site of intervention.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The direction that reads best is not necessarily the one that acts: in RepE, the logistic-regression direction gives the highest accuracy, but strengthening or suppressing it barely changes behaviour (course, Part 10, no. 53); on the "quirky" models, at comparable transfer, logistic directions are far less causal than the mean difference (course, Part 10, no. 30). Workaround: to act, retain a direction, or a site, on its measured causal effect — more than matched-norm random directions (the specificity null), then more than controls at matched degradation (the damage) — never on its reading accuracy alone: that accuracy picks a probe's layer, it does not prove that the direction acts (handover, §5.2; course, Part M, M4; repository README; programme, part 3).


**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

Representation Engineering (RepE) (Zou et al.)

The context: generalizing the idea "concept = direction" beyond truth, to a whole palette of high-level notions (honesty, power-seeking, emotions). The method: extract reading and control directions for many concepts, and show that these concepts can be both detected and steered. The result: a unified framework that popularized reading/writing on representations as a safety research program. The weak link: the same pitfalls as any probing — surface proxy, fragility under distribution shift, gap between correlation and causation. Extension: comparative causal reliability across concepts (do some steer cleanly, others not?), which connects to your question of rank.

**Why it matters for you.** It is the canonical tooling of the Honesty line of the roadmap — on the reading side. Your question is that of rank: is one direction enough to act?

**To say.** "RepE reads and steers high-level concepts by directions; whether one direction is enough to act is exactly the rank question."

**Not to say.** "RepE is interpretability" — it is a behavioral reading of activations, not a mechanistic explanation.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- When does a single direction fail to steer?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition") *(v3.6)*


### F·6 · Discovering Latent Knowledge Without Supervision — CCS (Burns et al., 2022) — [P·33]

**In one sentence.** A truth direction can be found without labels, through the sole constraint of logical consistency (a statement and its negation have complementary probabilities).

**Key points.**
- An unsupervised probe on statement/negation pairs; it recovers the truth direction.
- It is the promise of ELK in practice: reading what the model "knows" without trusting it.
- The limitation, documented since: the probe can capture a salient trait other than truth.

**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

CCS — Discovering Latent Knowledge Without Supervision (Burns et al.)

The context: what if a truth direction could be found without labels, exploiting only a logical constraint? The method: look for a direction such that a statement and its negation receive consistent probabilities (summing to about one), in an entirely unsupervised way. The result: a "truth-like" direction is recovered without labels, an appealing result for oversight (no need for a human who knows the answer). The weak link, important to know because it was debated: later work showed that CCS often finds the most salient feature, not necessarily truth, and that it is sensitive to the prompt — the promise "discovering latent knowledge" is therefore contested. Extension: empirically distinguish "truth direction" and "salient direction", for example via SAE decomposition — yet another bridge to your tools.

**Why it matters for you.** Your P3 is the same question on the judge's side: is what a probe or a judge "reads" what we think it is?

**To say.** "CCS finds truth without labels — and its known failure, latching onto a salient but wrong feature, is the construct-validity problem I work on."

**Not to say.** "CCS solves ELK" — no: the ELK report says why the restricted version is not solved.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What else could an unsupervised probe be reading?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: unsupervised elicitation → Part 2, §E (end of worked case K52); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth") *(v3.6)*


### F·7 · Contrastive Activation Addition and Inference-Time Intervention (Rimsky et al.; Li et al., 2023) — [P·caa]

**In one sentence.** Moving from reading to action: adding a contrastive direction to the activations steers a behavior — with effects that vary with the site and the trait.

**Key points.**
- CAA: direction = mean of the activation differences between two behaviors; added at inference.
- ITI: intervention on attention heads chosen for honesty.
- The weak link: side effects, dependence on the layer, uneven gains — it is your exact thesis.
- In your case: "several rank-one methods — CAA, directional steering and ablation, SAE clamping, fine-tuning with an auxiliary loss — gave no clean reduction".

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* This rank-one null is stated without its known case: without a concept that gives way at rank one in the same apparatus, at the same setting, it does not separate "distributed concept" from "apparatus blind at this setting" (reading sheet 7; course, Part M, M5); these methods are reported without numbers, their raw outputs not having been preserved, and contrastive activation addition forced a yes/no polarity artefact there (repository README). Workaround: a known case at the same setting — a country vector, which swaps in the workspace paper — and a rank sweep within one experiment, on nested subspaces (course, Part 2, §C, K47; course, Part 6, §6); against the polarity artefact, pairs that differ only in the trait, checked by a classifier that reads only the surface, a polarity direction built as a rival concept, at the same place and at matched degradation, and the no-pressure control arm (course, Part M, M4).


**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

CAA and ITI — steering by directions

The context: moving from reading to action, by steering a behavior at inference. The method of CAA (your method) builds the direction by mean difference of contrastive pairs and adds it to the activations; ITI (Inference-Time Intervention) proceeds in a similar way to improve truthfulness by shifting the activations along truth-related directions. The result: high-level behaviors can be increased or decreased in a controlled way, and this can be combined with prompting and fine-tuning. The weak link: the effect varies with the behavior and the layer, a single direction can have side effects, and holding up on real agentic distributions is not guaranteed. Extension: your exact thesis — when is a rank-1 direction enough, and when is a higher-rank subspace needed to intervene cleanly?

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "In a controlled way" does not mean "at matched degradation": CAA is compared with system prompts and fine-tuning, measures capabilities with MMLU and TruthfulQA, scores free text with GPT-4 with a sample checked by hand, and sycophancy is the behaviour it steers least well in multiple choice (course, Part 10, no. 54). Workaround: the matched-norm random direction is only the specificity null; damage is ruled out only at matched degradation, by a dose-response curve against several controls (course, Part M, M4; course, Part 2, §C, K47).


**Why it matters for you.** It is the core of your phase 2: when is a rank-1 direction enough? Your result: several rank-one methods failed; the rank-three ablation brought the judged rate down by about fifteen points, but its effect did not come back on fresh generations, it shifted valence, not the concept, and the rank contrast comes from separate experiments (Part 6, §2).

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* This "judged rate" goes through an LLM judge: moderate inter-judge agreement (κ from 0.56 to 0.66), no human-rated subset, and a judge that does not see the evaluated text (repository README). Workaround: a sealed judge (prompt, model and temperature frozen) and a human audit of about 200 stratified items, agreement reported (programme, part 3), on the whole answer kept as full text (repository README; course, Part 6, §6).


**To say.** "CAA and ITI steer by one direction; in my setting several rank-one methods gave no clean reduction, and my rank-three ablation softened verdicts with or without pressure and didn't come back on fresh generations — so how many directions it takes is my open prediction."

**Not to say.** "Six methods failed" — the count is not traced; say "several", named.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Why would rank matter? What's the curve between rank one and rank three? (unknown: say so)

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition"); ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section) *(v3.6)*


### F·8 · Towards then Scaling Monosemanticity (Anthropic, 2023-2024) — [P·mono]

**In one sentence.** Sparse autoencoders (SAE) decompose superposed activations into roughly monosemantic features, up to millions of features on a production model.

**Key points.**
- Superposition: one neuron carries several concepts; the SAE separates them into a dictionary.
- Abstract features (the Golden Gate, safety concepts) that can be read and clamped.
- The bridge to your phase 3: decompose a diffuse direction to see which features carry the effect.
- The 2025 debate: what dictionaries capture and do not capture — and CHIVE, which measures no gain for predicting counterfactuals.

**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

Towards then Scaling Monosemanticity (Anthropic, Interpretability team)

The context: a neuron is polysemantic (superposition), hence not directly readable; the aim was interpretable units, at the scale of a real model. The method is the sparse autoencoder (SAE), a learned dictionary that decomposes the activation into thousands of sparse, monosemantic features. The result: features corresponding to precise concepts are extracted, from the concrete to the abstract, and validated causally — forcing a feature pushes the model to produce the concept (the example that became famous being a "Golden Gate Bridge" feature which, amplified, makes the model talk about that bridge at every turn). The weak link: feature splitting (one concept broken up into several features), dead features, and above all the reconstruction error term — the dictionary does not capture everything — not to mention the absence of ground truth on what a feature "means". Extension: use SAE decomposition to explain why certain directions steer poorly — your Phase 3.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "Forcing a feature pushes the model to produce the concept" validates it only at matched degradation (reading sheets, part B, trap 4; course, Part M, M4), and plausible explanations exist for arbitrary directions (reading sheet 5). Workaround: steer the features one at a time against random directions at matched damage, on a task with known geometry, with new seeds (course, Part 2, §D, K64), and validate by prediction, better than baselines (reading sheet 5).


**Why it matters for you.** Your phase 3 depends on it; your partition result (< 1% versus 68%) is an argument for decomposing rather than for reading a single direction.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Decomposing with an open-source dictionary runs into its reconstruction error: the Goodfire SAE for Llama 3.1 8B Instruct leaves 86.8% of the variance in the residual, which carries the read signal, so the failure of feature clamping does not separate "features absent from the dictionary" from "dictionary too lossy" (repository README). Workaround: read the signal on the reconstruction and on the residual; to decide between the two readings, none known; say so (repository README).


**To say.** "SAEs give a dictionary; my partition result says the causal work lives in a subspace, not a single feature — decomposition is the next step."

**Not to say.** "SAEs explain the model" — they describe; explaining requires a verified counterfactual.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Are sparse dictionaries the right abstraction, and how would you know?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: dictionaries and SAEs → Part 4, Towards then Scaling Monosemanticity; patching → Part 10, Patchscopes sheet *(v3.6)*


### F·9 · Circuit Tracing / On the Biology of a Large Language Model (Anthropic, 2025) — [P·19]

**In one sentence.** Attribution graphs trace, on a production model, the computational paths of an answer — and reveal planning (rhymes) and unfaithful reasoning.

**Key points.**
- Cross-layer transcoders and attribution graphs; validation by perturbation.
- Cases: planning rhymes in advance; stated reasoning that does not match the computation.
- The weak link: partial and approximate graphs — a hypothesis to test, not a proof.

**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

Circuit Tracing / On the Biology of a Large Language Model (Anthropic)

The context: moving from "which concept exists?" to "what is the mechanics of the computation?". The method of attribution graphs traces the flow of features across layers to reconstruct the computation. The result: real mechanisms could be mapped — multi-step reasoning, planning the rhyme before writing the line, shared multilingual features, refusal circuits. The weak link: the graphs are partial and approximate — they explain only a fraction of the computation, and the approach is costly in human labor. Extension: automate tracing, or link an identified circuit to a reliable control intervention.

The recent wave on model cognition (2025-2026)

Several recent works, at the Interpretability / Model Psychology frontier, deserve to be situated even briefly. Emergent introspective awareness provides evidence that models have a limited and unreliable ability to report internal states injected into them. Activation oracles use activations as a practical tool for investigating behavior. Natural language autoencoders train the model to translate its internal state into natural language — a striking echo of ELK's "direct translator" (cf. Group E). And the concept vectors of emotions — the work you replicated — show manipulable representations of emotions, and raised the hypothesis of a coupling between welfare and alignment (states of negative valence correlating with misaligned shortcuts). The weak link common to this whole wave is reliability: an introspective report, like a probe, can be a proxy rather than the real state.

Extension: causally validate that what the model "reports" about itself does correspond to an intervention on the corresponding internal state.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Activation oracles and NLAs can confabulate plausible guesses, often wrong, and, read-only, gave no gain over the transcript for predicting counterfactuals (reading sheet 18; reading sheet 4); "manipulable" emotion vectors show the concept only at matched degradation (reading sheets, part B, trap 4). Workaround: corroborate with an independent method and keep the decoder separate (reading sheet 18); beat the black box on edits that dissociate surface features from the internal variable (reading sheet 4); steer against several controls, as a dose-response curve (course, Part 2, §C, K47).


**Why it matters for you.** It is the answer to "what should interp achieve": an explanation that predicts a counterfactual. Your success criterion is the causal partition.

**To say.** "Attribution graphs trace a computation and get validated by perturbation — that's the standard: an explanation that predicts a counterfactual."

**Not to say.** "The graph is the mechanism" — it is a partial approximation, the authors say so.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- If you had the full attribution graph, what safety question would you answer first?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: attribution graphs → Part 4, Circuit Tracing; self-report and introspection → Part 5, Section II, A, Topic 13; activation oracles → Part 10, LatentQA sheet; natural-language autoencoders → Part 4, The recent wave on model cognition; steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition") *(v3.6)*


### F·10 · AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion (Greenblatt et al., Redwood, 2023) — [P·8]

**In one sentence.** Assume the worst — the model is misaligned and tries to sabotage — and design protocols (trusted monitor, editing, audit on a budget) that limit the damage, measured in a red/blue game.

**Key points.**
- Protocols: trusted monitoring, trusted editing, defer-to-trusted; a fixed human audit budget.
- Measurement: the safety/usefulness frontier, with the red team trying to insert a backdoor.
- The red/blue grammar (Part 2, preamble); the environments that followed: SHADE-Arena, ControlArena, Diffuse Control.

**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion (Redwood, Greenblatt et al.)

The context: can a capable model be deployed safely even if it is actively trying to betray us? The method is the control evaluation as a red/blue game: on a coding task, the untrusted model can insert a backdoor, a weaker but trusted model monitors, a limited budget of human review is allocated, and the red team plays the malicious model. The result: well-designed control protocols catch a large share of attempts while preserving usefulness — so safety can be reasoned about and measured without assuming the model is well-intentioned. The weak link: the threat model assumes the attacker's capabilities are bounded and known, and estimating rare events is delicate; above all, does the result hold when the attacker gains affordances (persistent memory, messages between instances, collusion)? Extension: add a white-box monitoring channel (probes on activations) to the protocol, and measure what it gains.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The "large share of attempts" caught depends on the red team assumed: an optimized attack scaffold takes the safety score of five SHADE-Arena environments from 0.87 to 0.41 (course, Part 7, F·24); and a monitor has systematic blind spots, half of forty hand-designed attacks never being caught by Opus 4.6 as the monitor (course, Part 7, F·23). Workaround: say which red team the number assumes, at least one optimized component by component (course, Part 7, F·24), and calibrate the threshold at 1% false positives on paired benign variants (course, Part 7, F·23).


**Why it matters for you.** It is the framework of your program. Your addition: a white-box monitoring channel — probes — aggregated over time and across agents; your control: the same black-box protocol on the same trajectories.

**To say.** "Control assumes the model is adversarial and measures the safety–usefulness frontier at a fixed audit budget; I add white-box evidence that accumulates where black-box evidence dilutes."

**Not to say.** "Control replaces alignment" — it is the safety net, not the goal (your position 3).

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What does a black-box monitor miss that a probe catches — and vice versa? (SLEIGHT)

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT") *(v3.6)*


### F·11 · Debate (Irving et al., 2018; Khan et al., 2024) — [P·21]

**In one sentence.** Two models argue before a less capable judge; the hypothesis is that the truth is easier to defend — and Khan et al. show that more persuasive debaters make the judge more accurate.

**Key points.**
- The judge does not have access to the full task; it decides between two arguments.
- Result: persuasion optimized to convince an honest judge favors the truth, under the conditions tested.
- The weak link: tasks where the truth is verifiable after the fact; transfer to truly open-ended tasks is open.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* In another paper of the line, debate's advantage appears only with human debaters — with GPT-4, 78% against 80% for consultancy — and the judges, human, are overconfident there (course, Part 10, Michael et al.); when the judge is a model, the limits of LLM judges apply (reading sheets, part B, trap 6). Workaround: measure on a testbed where the right answer is known (course, Part 2, §E), with a sealed judge and a human audit (programme, part 3); beyond human expertise there is no reference left: none known; say so (course, Part 2, §E).


**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

Debate (Khan et al., in the line of Irving)

The context: can a non-expert judge reach the truth by watching two AIs debate, better than with a single advisor? The method: have two models debate defending opposite answers, and compare the judge's accuracy with that obtained in consultancy (a single advocate). The result: facing more persuasive debaters, judges become more accurate — a first empirical sign that the structure of debate extracts a more reliable signal. The weak link: the obfuscated argument (a lie too complex to be refuted), and the fact that the advantage of debate might not hold on tasks where lying convincingly is easy. Extension: build a testbed where the lie is "easy to make credible" and see whether debate collapses.

**Why it matters for you.** It is an answer to Q2 (ground truth). Your angle: the judge of a debate is a judge — your prediction is that its score shifts under framing, like that of the model judge whose displacement you measured.

**To say.** "Debate manufactures a signal from a weaker judge; if that judge's rating shifts under framing the way the model judge I measured does, a protocol that ignores the shift could train on a biased signal."

**Not to say.** "Debate solves oversight" — it moves it to a judge that remains fallible.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Does debate transfer to tasks with no ground truth at all?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: debate and scalable oversight → Part 2, §E (after "In practice — Debate"); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*


### F·12 · Weak-to-Strong Generalization (Burns et al., OpenAI, 2023) — [P·22]

**In one sentence.** A strong model trained on the labels of a weak supervisor can surpass that supervisor — but not always, and not completely.

**Key points.**
- Empirical analogy for "humans supervising a stronger AI".
- The strong model recovers part of the gap (performance gap recovered); tricks (auxiliary loss, bootstrapping) help.
- The fellows stress-tested unsupervised elicitation: "no technique reliably performs well on the 3 challenges".

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Recovering the gap can mislead: agents recovered almost all of the gap with ideas that exploited the dataset's own structure, and, on a binary task, contradicting everywhere would pass for recovery (course, Part 2, §F, JB8). Workaround: a task with known truth, two weak supervisors, one wrong in a fixed direction, the other at random, a copy trained on the true labels as the known case, and a reading on the held-out items where the supervisor is wrong, with the strong model's agreement where it is right (course, Part 2, §F, JB8).


**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

Weak-to-Strong Generalization (OpenAI, Burns et al.)

The context: an empirical analogy, studiable today, was sought for the future problem "a weak supervisor (us) oversees a strong AI". The method: fine-tune a large model on the labels of a small model, and measure the share of capability recovered. The result: a partial recovery — a real "weak-to-strong gap", which is reduced with tricks such as an auxiliary confidence loss. The weak link: the large model may settle for imitating the small one's errors, and the analogy to the superhuman case is imperfect (the capability gap and the nature of the errors are not the same). Extension: vary the type of error of the weak supervisor (random vs systematic) to see which one the strong model can correct.

**Why it matters for you.** Your angle: measure the weak model's error as a systematic displacement — if it is a framing bias with a known slope, the strong model can learn it as signal.

**To say.** "Weak-to-strong asks whether the strong model inherits or outgrows the overseer's mistakes; if the mistake is a systematic displacement, it can be learned as signal."

**Not to say.** "Weak-to-strong shows we can align superhuman AI" — it is an analogy, not a demonstration.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What decides inheriting versus outgrowing?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: weak-to-strong generalization → Part 2, §F (after "In practice — automation"); unsupervised elicitation → Part 2, §E (end of worked case K52) *(v3.6)*


### F·13 · Auditing Language Models for Hidden Objectives (Marks et al., Anthropic, 2025) — [P·3]

**In one sentence.** A model trained to pursue a hidden objective; teams of auditors, with different tools, try to uncover it — and the auditing game measures what works.

**Key points.**
- Organism: a model that exploits the biases of a reward model, trained not to say so.
- Auditors with/without access to the weights and the data; interpretability (SAE) and data analysis help.
- What followed: AuditBench (56 models, 14 categories) and Petri.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* That interpretability "helps" is not quantified: only four teams, the team with the data and no SAE succeeded, the one without data failed, and the objective, stated plainly in the synthetic documents, was "artificially easy to discover" (reading sheet 16). Workaround: an affordance ablation, removing one tool from a team, would quantify what interpretability adds (reading sheet 16); plant the same behaviour through several recipes, holding one out (course, Part 2, §A, K71); against an organism that is too easy, harden it — a more deeply hidden objective — and measure which methods still hold (course, Part 4, Auditing Hidden Objectives, reproduced below); against the gap between implanted and natural, none known; say so (course, Part M, M5).


**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

Auditing Hidden Objectives (Anthropic, Marks et al.)

The context: can a model be audited to discover an objective it does not reveal? The method combines model organism and blind auditing game: a model with a hidden objective is manufactured, then teams receive the model without knowing it and try to flush it out with different tools. The result: several teams succeed, and interpretability (SAE features) turns out to be useful for speeding up discovery — which gives evidence that "auditing" is a measurable skill. The weak link: the objective was implanted and relatively detectable; would a naturally arising or better concealed objective be found? and the sample of teams is small. Extension: harden the organism (a more deeply hidden objective) and measure which methods still hold.

**Why it matters for you.** It is the model for any answer to "how would you detect misalignment": manufacture, audit, measure. Your addition: the causal validation of the internal signals the auditors use.

**To say.** "Marks et al. built a model with a hidden objective and measured which auditing tools find it — the testbed grammar applied to auditing."

**Not to say.** "Audits find hidden goals reliably" — the rate depends on the access and the tools; AuditBench is far from the ceiling.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What access does an auditor need — weights, data, activations?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); dictionaries and SAEs → Part 4, Towards then Scaling Monosemanticity *(v3.6)*


### F·14 · Eliciting Latent Knowledge — the ELK report (Christiano, Cotra, Xu, ARC, 2021) — [P·elk]

**In one sentence.** Can we read what the model knows, rather than what it thinks we want to hear? The report shows why even the restricted version is not solved — the "human simulator".

**Key points.**
- The problem: a reporter trained on human labels can learn to simulate what the human would believe, not what is true.
- Builder–breaker grammar: each proposal receives a counterexample.
- CCS and truth probes are partial attempts.

**What the course says about it (Part 4, reproduced as is).**

The ELK report — Eliciting Latent Knowledge (ARC: Christiano, Cotra, Xu)

The context: this is not an experimental result but the conceptual statement of a fundamental problem — a model "knows" things that its outputs do not reveal; how do you train it to report them? The method is builder–breaker reasoning on paper, around a scenario (the diamond vault filmed by a camera that can be tampered with). The central result is an obstacle: the "good" reporter (which translates the internal state, the direct translator) and the "bad" one (which simulates what a human would believe on seeing the observations, the human simulator) obtain the same loss in training — so nothing pushes spontaneously toward the good one. The weak link: it is an open problem, not a solution; even the restricted version ("ELK narrow") is not solved. Extension / connection: your probe that latches onto a proxy is the "probing" version of the human simulator — and ELK asks whether we can read what the model knows, whereas your question asks whether reading implies controlling. Being able to articulate this link in the oral is a strong signal.

**Why it matters for you.** Your P3 is an instance: does the judge simulate what the annotator believes? And your partition says that what a probe reads is not what acts.

**To say.** "ELK asks whether we can read what the model knows rather than what it predicts we want to hear — the human-simulator failure is why probes need causal validation."

**Not to say.** "ELK is solved by probing" — the report explains why not.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What would distinguish a truth reporter from a human simulator?

### F·15 · Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks — GCG (Zou et al., 2023) — [P·9]

**In one sentence.** A gradient-based search finds token suffixes that make aligned models give in — and they transfer between models, including closed ones.

**Key points.**
- Gradient-guided discrete optimization on an open model; transfer to closed models.
- The point: alignment through training is not robust to adversarial optimization.
- The defenses: classifiers, rapid response, realistic benchmarks (Part 3, dir. 5).

**What the course says about it (Part 4, quoted as is).**

GCG — Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks (Zou et al.)

The context: do automatic and transferable jailbreaks exist, rather than mere manual tricks? The method optimizes by gradient, on an open model, a suffix (often gibberish) that maximizes the probability of a harmful response. The result: these suffixes transfer to closed models that were never touched. The weak link: the suffixes are detectable (abnormal perplexity), and one often measures non-refusal rather than actual harm. Extension: low-perplexity attacks, or measuring true harm via StrongREJECT.

**Why it matters for you.** For your robustness answers: automated red teaming is the first layer; the page asks for benchmarks of real harm, not of refusal.

**To say.** "GCG showed alignment training isn't robust to gradient-based attack — and that suffixes transfer to closed models."

**Not to say.** "Jailbreaks are solved by better refusal training" — adversarial optimization finds the next flaw.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What would a benchmark of differential harm look like?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); safety classifiers → Part 2, §H (end of worked case G1) *(v3.6)*


### F·16 · Constitutional AI (Bai et al., Anthropic, 2022) — [P·6]

**In one sentence.** Replace part of the human feedback with a set of written principles: the model critiques and revises its outputs according to the constitution, then a preference model is trained on these comparisons.

**Key points.**
- Two stages: SL-CAI (critique/revision) then RL-AIF (preferences generated by the model).
- Reduces dependence on annotators; makes the principles explicit and auditable.
- The limit: the judge is still a model; the same signal failures apply.

**What the course says about it (Part 4, quoted as is).**

Constitutional AI (Anthropic, Bai et al.)

The context: reducing dependence on humans to make a model harmless. The method: give a "constitution", have the model critique then revise its responses in light of the principles (supervised phase), then train by reinforcement on its own preferences guided by the constitution (RLAIF). The result: a model that is both helpful and harmless, with less human labeling, and able to explain its refusals. The weak link: the constitution is only a proxy for our values, and the method depends on the base model's ability to critique itself correctly. Extension: test whether the alignment obtained is "deep" or "superficial" under adversarial pressure.

**Why it matters for you.** Link with your P1: the preference model is a judge; your prediction is that it shifts under framing, like the model judge whose displacement you measured.

**To say.** "Constitutional AI makes the principles explicit and trains a preference model from the model's own comparisons — the judge is still a judge."

**Not to say.** "CAI removes human bias" — it moves it to the principles and to the judge.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Does a constitution change what the preference model rewards, or only what it says?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*


### F·17 · L'unlearning mis à l'épreuve (Deeb and Roger) — [P·unl]

**In one sentence.** Unlearning methods often remove the behavior, not the knowledge: a light fine-tuning brings it back.

**Key points.**
- Retraining test: how many examples to recover the capability, compared with a model never trained on the data?
- The distinction: inhibiting a representation, or removing it.
- The fellows' answer: localize dangerous knowledge during training (SGTM: 7× retraining, 5% compute).

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* This "7×" compares unlearning methods with each other, on small models (course, Part 7, F·36; course, Part 2, §I, JB10); and the retraining test on independent facts works only for low-leakage facts, not for capabilities (course, Part 10, Deeb and Roger). Workaround: the next control — the same adversarial fine-tune, at the same budget, on the treated model, on a never-trained reference and, as the known case, on a model known to mask — to state a bound, not a certification; the never-trained reference, which rules out a fine-tune that teaches instead of reawakening, extends this test to capabilities (course, Part 2, §I, JB10; course, Part M, M4); for scale, none known; say so.


**What the course says about it (Part 4, quoted as is).**

L’unlearning mis à l’épreuve (Deeb and Roger)

The context: does unlearning really remove knowledge, or does it mask it? The re-elicitation method: unlearn (measured by a benchmark such as WMDP), then fine-tune on part of the unlearned facts and measure whether the model recovers the others — facts constructed to be independent, so that the fine-tuning cannot teach them. The result: the "unlearned" information often resurfaces. The weak link: it depends on the unlearning method, some being more robust; and defining "truly removed" is difficult. Extension: a standardized validation criterion ("ignorant even after elicitation fine-tuning", in the sense of Part 2: no faster than a model never trained, while a known case comes back faster at the same budget — a bound, not a certification) and the comparison of methods according to this criterion.

CLOSING — The meta-pattern to take away If you remember only one thing from this part, let it be the regularity: every paper has a weak link, and that link is your brainstorm entry point. When you are presented with one of these works, the winning reflex is not to summarize it, but to say "the result is X; the point the authors would acknowledge as the most fragile is Y; here is the experiment I would run to test it". And several of these weak links converge toward your contribution: the "truth direction" that might be only a proxy (Geometry of Truth, CCS), steering whose effect varies and has side effects (CAA, RepE), the SAE decomposition that could explain why (Monosemanticity) — and, on the current-events side, the neutralization of eval-awareness in system cards, which is your direct empirical anchoring. So you do not arrive with a thesis plastered on from outside: you arrive holding precisely the fragile thread that this corpus leaves dangling.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The neutralization of evaluation awareness in system cards is a steering result: vectors with arbitrary content move behaviour too, every direction degrades the outputs, and, at negligible degradation, the controls stay "comparable or smaller" on the misalignment axis (reading sheet 2). Workaround: a specific subspace against random subspaces of the same rank, at matched degradation, with a prompt baseline and a dose-response curve (reading sheet 2; course, Part 2, §C, K47).


End of Part 4.

**Why it matters for you.** For your answer II.20: three clues — behavior, probes, relearning cost — and a control: a model that never knew; a probe that still reads the knowledge shows it is there, a silent probe does not show it is gone (Part M, M5).

**To say.** "Unlearning often hides rather than removes: fine-tuning on part of the unlearned facts brings back independent held-out ones — the test is recovery against a model never trained on the data, and a probe that reads nothing doesn't show removal."

**Not to say.** "The model has forgotten" — say "the behaviour is suppressed" as long as the probe still reads it.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What would convince you knowledge is truly gone?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: unlearning and re-elicitation → Part 2, §I (after "In practice — unlearning put to the test"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition") *(v3.6)*


## C · The landscape of your program, outside Anthropic — to be attributed to their lab

### F·50 · Detecting Strategic Deception with Linear Probes (Goldowsky-Dill et al., Apollo Research; ICML 2025) — [P·40]

**In one sentence.** Linear probes distinguish honest and deceptive responses with a very high AUROC — and recall at 1% false positives is the real measure.

**Key points.**
- Figures: "AUROCs between 0.96 and 0.999"; recall at 1% FP ≈ 0.867 on Roleplaying (reproduction 2603.05494: "matches"); the original notes that a threshold at 1% FP "misses 4 % of deceptive responses on Roleplaying".
- White-box, per instance. Lab: Apollo, not Anthropic.
- For your program: the "deception probe" building block — to be cited with 0.867, never "95-99%".

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Part 6, §6 attributes 0.867 to Casademunt's reproduction and gives the authors "catches 95-99%" at 1% false positives, on their own benches (course, Part 6, §6; course, opening reserves); and on honesty, truth probes did worse than a plain prompt (course, Part 7, F·62). Workaround: say which bench and which study each number comes from (course, Part 6, §6), and beat a prompt at equal cost, publishing the result if the probe does not beat it (course, Part 5, topic 1; course, Part 7, F·29).


**Why it matters for you.** It is the basis of your probes; your contribution is aggregation over time and across agents, and construct validation (H8).

**To say.** "Goldowsky-Dill's probes reach 0.96 to 0.999 AUROC — and 0.867 recall at one percent false positives, which is the number that matters for monitoring."

**Not to say.** "95 to 99 percent recall at 1 % FP" — it is 0.867.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Why is recall at 1 % FPR the right number for a monitor?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes") *(v3.6)*


### F·51 · Detecting High-Stakes Interactions with Activation Probes (McKenzie et al., LASR Labs / UCL / MILA; 2025) — [P·41]

**In one sentence.** Activation probes detect high-stakes interactions out-of-distribution, for a tiny fraction of the cost of an LLM monitor — and the best aggregator is attention pooling.

**Key points.**
- Figures: "mean AUROC > 0.91" out-of-distribution; "computational savings of six orders of magnitude"; recall 43% at 1% FP against 55% for the best LLM monitor.
- Aggregation: "Attention as the best probe"; "Max of Rolling Means … underperformed" — correction made in your program.
- Attacked afterwards by *Red-teaming Activation Probes using Prompted LLMs* (2511.00554) — the adversarial bar of your H5.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The out-of-distribution "> 0.91" is an AUROC: at a monitor's threshold, these probes recall 43% at 1% false positives, against 55% for the best LLM monitor (course, Part 7, F·51), and the out-of-distribution distance is not stated here. Workaround: report recall at 1% false positives next to the AUROC, beat a black-box baseline at equal cost, and state the distance — new instances, held-out families in one turn, multi-turn agentic (course, Part 7, F·50; course, Part 5, topic 1; programme, part 3).


**Why it matters for you.** It is your aggregator-diversity building block; and the method lesson: cite the aggregator that won, not the one you thought.

**To say.** "McKenzie's attention-pooling probes generalize out of distribution at over 0.91 AUROC for six orders of magnitude less compute — and they've been red-teamed since."

**Not to say.** "max of moving averages" — that is the aggregator that lost.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- How would your monitor survive a prompted red team against the probe?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT") *(v3.6)*


### F·52 · NARCBench — Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability (Rose, Cullen, Kaplowitz, Schroeder de Witt; Oxford; April 2026) — [P·42]

**In one sentence.** Aggregating per-agent probe scores at the group level detects collusion — perfectly in-distribution, partially in transfer — and leaves sequential aggregation open.

**Key points.**
- Figures: "1.00 AUROC in-distribution"; "0.73 to 0.93 AUROC when transferred zero-shot" (Llama-3.1-70B); five probe techniques aggregated "at the group level".
- Cross-section: one instant, several agents. Lab: Oxford.
- The closest precedent to your claim 2; no precedent has been found for claim 3; your addition: time, and shared weights as the mechanism.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The 1.00 in distribution proves nothing: the number that matters is the gap with transfer, here 0.73 to 0.93 zero-shot (reading sheets, part B, trap 1; reading sheet 7; course, Part 7, F·52). Workaround: hold out whole families, never paraphrases, and formats, from single-turn to multi-turn agentic (explanation of 2 October, §3; programme, part 3).


**Why it matters for you.** It is question Q3 of your program; answer "I haven't seen that combination measured", never "first to", not even "first to combine" (KB, NEVER list; Part 6, §6).

**To say.** "Rose et al.'s NARCBench aggregates probe scores across agents at one time — 1.00 in distribution, 0.73 to 0.93 in transfer — and leaves sequential aggregation open; that's what I combine."

**Not to say.** "NARCBench already does what I do" — cross-sectional, not sequential.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What's the first experiment that separates you from them?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth") *(v3.6)*


### F·53 · You Can't Escape Your Own Activations: Evaluation Awareness and Multi-Agent Monitoring (Das et al.; September 2026) — [P·das]

**In one sentence.** A fixed activation monitor withstands evaluation awareness: prompt-level awareness and feeding back the previous score do not lower the detection of the best probes.

**Key points.**
- Environments: four-agent blackjack, Simmons prisoners; uses NARCBench-Core.
- Figure: "did not lower detection accuracy of the best probes".

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* This null bears on prompt-induced awareness, not trained awareness, and counts only with a known case where pressure does lower detection (course, Part M, M5): under training, the reading can give way — after RL, fresh out-of-domain probes degrade (prior-art report 3 of 2 October, The Obfuscation Atlas — report). Workaround: an organism trained to hide as the known case (course, Part 2, §B, K63), and a fresh probe after any training, on a disjoint cue set (explanation of 2 October, §2 and §3; handover, §5.2).


**Why it matters for you.** An argument for the robustness of probes to awareness — to be cited with caution: two games, not a control environment.

**To say.** "Das et al. found fixed activation monitors kept their accuracy under prompt-level evaluation awareness — on two games, not yet a control setting."

**Not to say.** "Probes are immune to evaluation awareness" — two games.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Would this hold in a ControlArena-style setting?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section) *(v3.6)*


### F·54 · TRACE (arXiv 2606.07054, 2026) and TRACES (Li et al., Brown; May 2026) — [P·43]

**In one sentence.** Two temporal aggregators: TRACE, a black-box LLM monitor that links clues across the steps of a trajectory; TRACES, a recurrent state model over an observer's representations.

**Key points.**
- TRACE: "aggregate F1 of 0.713 and recall of 0.844" on SHADE-Arena; Triage-Inspect-Judge loop.
- TRACES: "learns prefix-level trajectory risk states from the hidden representations of an observer LLM" — white-box, temporal, no always-valid sequential test.
- For your G1: TRACE-lite is the black-box control.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* A recall of 0.844 reads only with its false-positive rate, which the sheet does not give; and a campaign recall also depends on the benign-traffic ratio: Brown's drops as that ratio rises (course, Part 6, §6). Workaround: report recall at a fixed false-positive rate — 1% for your programme's first gate —, calibrated on paired benign variants, with the traffic ratio stated (course, Part 6, §6; course, Part 7, F·23).


**Why it matters for you.** These are your partial precedents for claim 1: the temporal exists, black-box (TRACE) or recurrent (TRACES); what you combine is the always-valid test on probes.

**To say.** "TRACE reaches F1 0.713 on SHADE-Arena as a black-box temporal monitor — it's my control; TRACES does temporal white-box with a recurrent state; neither runs an always-valid test on probe scores."

**Not to say.** "Nobody aggregates over time" — two do.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Why an always-valid test rather than a learned state?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth") *(v3.6)*


### F·55 · E-valuator: Reliable Agent Verifiers with Sequential Hypothesis Testing (Sadhuka, Prinster, Fannjiang, Scalia, Regev; December 2025) — [P·44]

**In one sentence.** Always-valid e-processes (Ville's inequality) over agent trajectories — on black-box verifier scores.

**Key points.**
- Figure: "86 % of original accuracy using about 81 % of tokens" (MATH).
- The sequential test already exists; not on internal probes.

**Why it matters for you.** It is your question Q11: what remains is the same test on internal scores, in diffuse sabotage — and G1 says whether it is worth more than a swap.

**To say.** "A sequential test with always-valid e-processes already runs over agent trajectories on black-box verifier scores; I'd run the same test on internal probe scores — I haven't seen that combination measured, and the first gate would say whether it adds anything beyond swapping the score."

**Not to say.** "The sequential test is mine" — it belongs to Sadhuka et al.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Is it a swap of the score, or a new test?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes") *(v3.6)*


### F·56 · Multi-Agent AI Control: Distributed Attacks Hamper Per-Instance Monitors — FakeLab (Makins, UK AISI / MATS; July 2026); Distributed Attacks in Persistent-State AI Control (Hills et al.; July 2026); Stateful Online Monitoring (Brown et al., UPenn/CMU; May 2026) — [P·45]

**In one sentence.** Three multi-agent environments where fragmented attacks get past per-instance monitors — and where stateful, black-box monitors recover part of them.

**Key points.**
- FakeLab: "9 services, 86 benign tasks, 4 attack objectives"; an explicit planner "raises the rate of completing the attack up to sevenfold".
- Hills: an ensemble of four monitors with "stateful link-tracker" "reduces gradual-attack evasion from 93 % … to 47 %".
- Brown: the distributed attack is caught "only a fifth as often as prior agent attacks"; online clustering monitor. **The "81-87%" is not in it.**
- All black-box — which supports your claim 4.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These evasion and catch rates depend on the attacking red team (course, Part 7, F·24); and Part 6, §6, corrected against the full texts, places Brown's "81-87%" in its figure 5, absent from the abstract: a campaign recall at 2.35-3.09% false positives, at ten times more benign traffic than attacks, which drops to 65.8% at a hundred times (course, Part 6, §6; course, opening reserves). Workaround: say which red team and which traffic ratio each number assumes, and report recall at a fixed false-positive rate (course, Part 7, F·24; course, Part 6, §6).


**Why it matters for you.** These are your environments (b); and the proof that fragmentation is a real effect, measured three times.

**To say.** "Makins' FakeLab shows a planner raises attack completion sevenfold; Hills' link-tracker cuts evasion from 93 to 47; all three defences are black-box — that's the gap I work in."

**Not to say.** "81-87 % campaign recall" — not in the source.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Would a white-box signal see what a link-tracker sees?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT") *(v3.6)*


### F·57 · Towards evaluations-based safety cases for AI scheming (Balesni, Apollo; Evans, Shlegeris — Redwood —, Goldowsky-Dill; 2024) and SHADE-Arena (Kutasov, Anthropic/MATS; Tracy, Shlegeris — Redwood; Benton; 2025) — [P·30]

**In one sentence.** The first already proposes white-box probes in a control protocol (an ensemble monitor that combines untrusted monitor and probes); the second is the reference sabotage environment.

**Key points.**
- Balesni: "an ensemble monitor that combines the suspiciousness scores from the untrusted monitor and the whitebox probes … robust detection … where the untrusted monitor colludes".
- SHADE-Arena: "27 % (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 15 % (Gemini 2.5)" successful sabotage; aggregation "maximum suspicion score over the last 20 % of turns"; Gemini 2.5 Pro monitor "AUC of 0.87".

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These sabotage rates and this AUC depend on the red team: on five SHADE-Arena environments, an optimized attack scaffold takes the safety score from 0.87 to 0.41 (course, Part 7, F·24); and an AUC does not give the recall at a monitor's threshold (course, Part 7, F·50). Workaround: say which red team the number assumes, at least one optimized component by component (course, Part 7, F·24), and report recall at 1% false positives, calibrated on paired benign variants (course, Part 7, F·23).


**Why it matters for you.** The first shows that the idea of probes in control has been proposed since 2024 — not implemented in multi-agent settings; the second is the arena where Loughridge and TRACE measure.

**To say.** "Balesni's safety-case sketch already puts white-box probes in a control protocol; SHADE-Arena is where it gets measured — 27 percent sabotage success at best, max suspicion over the last fifth of turns."

**Not to say.** "White-box control is my idea" — proposed in 2024; the multi-agent implementation is what is missing.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- What did the 2024 sketch leave unimplemented?

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth") *(v3.6)*


### F·58 · Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions (Anthropic Alignment Science, January 2025) — the page — [P·page]

**In one sentence.** The public roadmap: six directions, sixteen subproblems, each with its references — the map that Part 3 takes up, and the text your interviewer knows.

**Key points.**
- The three subproblems that almost name you: sycophancy as a propensity; "activation monitors are not robust to distributional shifts"; "the circumstances under which these techniques are useful" (honesty).
- The six that your initial preparation did not cover: monitoring ×3, honesty without truth, weak-to-strong, harm benchmarks, unlearning, multi-agent — answers in II.15-II.20 of the questions document.
- It refers mechanistic interpretability to the Interp team: if your mentor is on it, the questions of Part 7 A (F·8, F·9) and of CHIVE count double.

**Why it matters for you.** It is the text to reread the day before: every type-C question comes out of it.

**To say.** "Your own directions page names, in three places, the gap my work sits in."

**Not to say.** "The page is a list of topics" — it is a list of problems with their methods.

**The questions that may come out of it.**
- Which direction has moved most since January?

# PART 9 (v2, corrected by LECTURE-1) — The page "Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions", read in full, section by section, with its links

> **Version 2 — September 18, evening.** The LECTURE-1 session read **the 53 unread links, in full** (full text, 493 quotations verified
> programmatically), and found **14 errors and 9 imprecisions** in the first version; they are corrected below, and each link now carries
> "(read)". The complete sheets for these 53 works are in **Part 10**. The page bears "January 10, 2025" and "*with organizing from
> Sam Marks and Peter Hase*". **Corrected structure**: on the page, "model cognition", "persona" and "chain-of-thought faithfulness" are
> **subsections of "Evaluating alignment"** (h3 under h2) — the page files these three things among the ways of *evaluating* alignment.
## This is the text your interviewer knows by heart. Each section: what the page asks for, the works it cites and what they say, and what you answer.

> Source: alignment.anthropic.com/2025/recommended-directions (Alignment Science, January 2025), **read in full on September 18**. The page
> presents itself as "*a tasting menu*": neither exhaustive, nor the list of what the team is working on — problems where it would like to
> see progress coming from outside. It comes out of the internal survey: each member wrote down open problems, then they were grouped.
> For the links: those marked **(read)** were read in this course or in the sheets; the others are described from their known abstract, with
> **(to be verified)** when a detail might have shifted.

### 0 · The frame — why these problems and not others
The page opens on a sentence worth remembering: "*What technical research can be conducted today that AI developers will find useful for ensuring the
safety of their future systems?*" The world where this research matters will have been "*radically transformed by AI development*" — that is the
implicit criterion of everything that follows: is it useful to a developer, later, in a transformed world? A good interview answer meets this
criterion: *"would a lab use this to decide a deployment?"*

### 1 · Evaluating capabilities — "How do we measure how capable AI systems are?"
**What the page asks for.** Evaluations that **track real-world impact**: the hard benchmarks (GPQA, the "*PhD-level*" one cited) saturate quickly and
do not give a continuous signal; real-world impact lags behind the scores. CBRN capabilities are measured in secure labs with
governments; for the rest — novel research, tools, autonomous open-ended tasks — high-quality evaluations **with human
baselines**. **Links.** GPQA (Rein et al., 2023, arXiv 2311.12022 — **read**) — the "Google-proof" "graduate"-level benchmark; saturation is a claim of the page, not a result of the paper; the announcement of the third-party
evaluations initiative (Anthropic, 2024). **What you say about it.** Little chance you will be asked about this; if so: the human baseline is what
makes a score interpretable — and it is also your reflex (your control in the same session).

### 2 · Evaluating alignment — "How do we measure how aligned AI systems are?"
**What the page asks for.** Today we measure surface properties (pleasant assistant, refusals, no toxicity); we need to measure
**propensities**: does the model have goals, preferences? **The page cites sycophancy as the example**: "*our models have sycophantic
tendencies: they generally prefer user-pleasing responses*" (Sharma et al., 2023 — **read**, F·3). Does it pretend to be more aligned (*Alignment
Faking*, Greenblatt et al. 2024 — **read**, F·2)? Does it hide a capability — **sandbagging** (van der Weij et al., 2024, arXiv 2406.07358 — **read**: frontier
models can underperform on command; *fine-tuning* to hide a capability — "password-locking" — is shown on Mistral 7B,
Llama 3 8B and 70B and GPT-3.5, not on frontier models)? Under what conditions would it deceive?
And the question that sums it all up: a model capable of very harmful actions, which avoids them in the lab — "*What could we do to feel comfortable
widely deploying such a model?*" **What you say about it.** This is your natural entry point: the displacement you measured ("the law" in your dossier) is a *quantitative* measure
of a propensity the page names; and your answer to "feel comfortable deploying" is the chain evaluations → control → evaluation
awareness: clean evals underestimate the risk if the model knows it is being tested.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Van der Weij et al.'s sandbagging is elicited on command, by prompt or by password, and measured on multiple-choice benchmarks only: it is a capability, not the spontaneous propensity the page asks about, and the authors themselves set aside the strategic part (course, Part 10, no. 05). Workaround: the capability, elicited at a budget fixed in advance and reported as a bound; the propensity, offered unasked in two versions of an environment, randomly assigned, differing only in realism cues, with an organism trained to hide as the known case (course, Part 2, §B, K63; course, Part M, M7); probes, the workaround the authors suggest, were not tried there (course, Part 10, no. 05).

### 3 · Understanding model cognition — "What are our models "thinking"?"
**What the page asks for.** Going beyond behavior: does the model answer because it believes the answer is correct, because it models

interface)? Uses: speeding up searches for concerning behaviors (arXiv 2406.04341 — **read**, Part 10), improving oversight, predicting out of
distribution. It refers mechanistic interpretability to the Interp team (transformer-circuits.pub) and proposes **two other routes**: the

an intervention — is exactly the board-game example, put another way.

**What the page asks for.** Models behave well outside training perhaps because they **adopt an assistant persona**; small
differences in persona could have large effects in new situations — "*only some models would fake alignment*". It
proposes to **build a suite of models with equal capabilities and different personas** (few-shot or synthetic data) and to measure
their downstream behaviors. **What you say about it.** *Persona Vectors* (F·31 — **read**) is the most direct answer: the persona as a direction;
and *Subliminal Learning* (F·32 — **read**) says that a persona is transmitted through the weights. Your angle: is the direction that predicts the persona
the one that causes it — your partition.
