### 5 · Chain-of-thought faithfulness — "When can we take a model's chain-of-thought at face value?"
**What the page asks for.** Models "*don't always say what they think*" (Turpin et al., 2023 — **read**, F·2/I.5) and can
**systematically** distort their reasoning. Detecting unfaithfulness: Lanham et al. 2023 (**read**, *Measuring Faithfulness* — truncate or
corrupt the chain and see whether the answer follows; large models are paradoxically less faithful on it), Mills et al. 2024 (arXiv 2312.12747
— **read**: this is *ALMANACS*, a benchmark of explanation simulatability, not a detection method — the page misfiles it); **ensuring** it: Radhakrishnan et al. 2023 (arXiv 2307.11768 — **read**: the faithfulness gain comes from the **separate contexts** for the subquestions — chain
decomposition alone does less well —, and it costs accuracy: 81.8 vs 86.0), Chen et al. 2024 (arXiv 2401.13986 — **read**), Chua et al. 2024 (arXiv 2403.05518 — **read**, *bias-augmented consistency training*:
training to reason consistently with and without a biasing hint reduces biased reasoning). **Three open questions**: does faithfulness
vary by task type (math vs social reasoning; does a performance gain due to CoT imply faithfulness?); does
**situational awareness** change faithfulness (is the model more or less faithful when told its CoT is monitored?);
how to make automatic detection more efficient and with better recall. **What you say about it.** Your answer II.5 (graded perturbation) is
the quantified version of Lanham; and the second open question is your theme: evaluation awareness changes what we read.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Lanham's scale result — "large models are paradoxically less faithful on it" — holds, in its abstract, only "on most tasks" (course, Part 10, no. 18); a chain of thought often leaves out what decided — the decisive cue is mentioned in only 25% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and 39% (DeepSeek R1) of cases —, and not verbalizing is not hidden reasoning (reading sheet 17). Workaround: measure monitorability as a ratio, the verbalized against the internal or the actions, through graded perturbation — your II.5 —, and say "not verbalized", never "hidden reasoning" (reading sheet 17; course, Part 11, answer 43).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: chain of thought as a monitor → Part 11, answer 43 *(v3.6)*


### 6 · AI control — "Can we ensure safety by deploying models alongside sufficient safeguards?"
**What the page lays out.** Three possible assurances: inability, sufficient alignment, or **control** — safeguards such that the model cannot
do harm even if it tries (Greenblatt et al. 2023 — **read**, F·10). Control is worthwhile when the model is capable enough to do harm without
safeguards but not capable enough to get around them. The section focuses on **runtime monitoring**.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); fine-tuned detectors → Part 7, F·29 *(v3.6)*


**6a · Behavioral monitoring.** A monitor reads the inputs/outputs of an untrusted actor; **trusted monitoring** (a weaker but
trusted model — "*GPT-3.5 to screen code written by a potentially malicious GPT-4*") and **untrusted monitoring** (another instance of the actor).
Links: Naihin et al. 2023 (arXiv 2311.10538 — **read**), Chan et al. 2024 (arXiv 2401.13138 — **read**, *visibility into AI agents* — identifiers,
logs, real-time monitoring). **The central flaw, in one sentence you must be able to say**: "*monitor
failures might be systematically concentrated in the same episodes where the actor behaves maliciously*" — because the actor subverts the
monitor (jailbreak), or because monitor and actor **collude**. **Four directions**: reduce collusion by editing or paraphrasing the
actor's output before the monitor; train better monitors with **realistic synthetic data of sophisticated malicious
behaviors**; better estimate failure rates for **very rare** catastrophes; schemes that hold when the actor has **additional
affordances — memory across episodes, message passing between instances** (arXiv 2410.03768 — **read**: *Hidden in Plain Text*, Mathew et al., LASR Labs — the
steganography and collusion between models, caveat lifted). **What you say about it.** The four directions have each had their fellows paper: SLEIGHT-Bench (synthetic attack data —
F·23, **read**), Strengthening Red Teams (F·24), Diffuse Control (F·22, **read**); and the last one — **messages between instances** — is your program,
word for word: it is the sentence of the page to quote when you are asked where the idea comes from.

**6b · Activation monitoring.** Monitoring **activations** rather than behavior: probes that detect predefined concepts —
"*a less ambitious alternative to understanding model cognition*". **Why it is promising**: activations "*(1) correspond to the
reasoning of the model being monitored, and (2) are difficult for the model to control*" — a weak monitor can miss a vulnerability or
be fooled by obfuscated code; the activations of the generator itself get around these two failures. **The risk, in writing**: "*substantial
risk that activation monitors are not robust to distributional shifts*", and **the most important shift**: "*from fixed datasets of
synthetic data to data generated by the model itself*" — if we do not have model-generated examples of the bad outputs, we must
synthesize them, then **check that the monitor generalizes to the real dangerous generations**. Links: the *coup probes* (Roger, Redwood, 2023, LessWrong — **read in full by LECTURE-1**: the idea is to train a probe to say whether the
model is attempting a catastrophic action, on examples **written by humans, off-policy**; **no coup is tested** — the experiments
are on a proxy, (instruction, response) pairs where the response advises a theft; in the toy setting, the probes generalize to other formats and
from texts the model would not write to texts it writes once jailbroken; the name "off-policy probes" and the remark "little followed up"
come from a Redwood comment, not from the post; "*signs of life*") and
Zou et al. 2024 (**circuit breakers**, arXiv 2406.04313 — **read**, Part 10). **What you say about it.**
This is **your** section. Three sentences of the page are your sentences: activations are hard to control (your argument for white-box over
black-box), the risk of distribution shift (your H8, and *Lie Detectors* F·29 which measures it), and the move from synthetic → model-generated
(your plan with two families of organisms). Say it as a continuity: "*your page names the risk; my second result measures it; my programme
tests the fix.*"

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Neither your second result nor F·29 measures the shift of an activation monitor: your second result shows a cousin of it, already in distribution, since the direction a probe reads is not the one that acts (course, Part 6, §4; course, Part 11, answer 12); and the detectors of F·29 are not probes, but models fine-tuned with LoRA to answer a self-report question about a transcript, whose numbers do not transfer to probes (reading sheet 7; explanation of 2 October, §2). **6c · Anomaly detection.** Supervised monitoring assumes we know what danger looks like; otherwise, **anomaly detection** in the
model's computation (ARC, *mechanistic anomaly detection and ELK*). Example: an anomaly detector next to the monitor catches the rare inputs
(jailbreaks) that the monitor misses; we label them by hand and improve the monitor. Existing techniques on activations: Mallen et al.
2024 (arXiv 2312.01037 — **read**: *Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models* — "quirky" models that make systematic errors
in one context, probes that recover the true knowledge, **and a mechanistic anomaly detector** — it is this last one that the page cites here). **More ambitious, and "*unexplored*"**: automatically detecting the inputs where
a strong model understands something a weak one does not — a new and surprising behavior from the weak one's point of view. **What
you say about it.** Your sequential aggregation is an anomaly detector over time; and the "*unexplored*" question is a program idea to
offer if you are asked "what else".

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Mallen et al.'s probes and anomaly detector are validated on models fine-tuned to err when a name visible in the prompt, Bob, signals it, and the fine-tuning likely overwrote part of the natural circuitry; at comparable transfer, the logistic-regression directions there are far less causal than the mean difference (course, Part 10, no. 30). ### 7 · Scalable oversight — "Can we design oversight mechanisms that will continue to work for smarter-than-human AI?"
**What the page lays out.** The standard paradigm assumes a ground-truth signal R; beyond the human frontier, three problems: noise
(experts in disagreement), **systematic errors**, cost. Four subproblems.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: debate and scalable oversight → Part 2, §E (after "In practice — Debate"); weak-to-strong generalization → Part 2, §F (after "In practice — automation"); unsupervised elicitation → Part 2, §E (end of worked case K52); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*


**7a · Exploitable systematic errors.** The student takes tests written by a less intelligent teacher, and learns to produce what
scores well even when it knows it is wrong. Formally: a proxy R with systematic errors relative to R*; if the model M models
R − R*, training against R produces a model that **exploits** the errors (Wen et al. 2024, arXiv 2409.12822 — **read**: "U-Sophistry", RLHF
makes models more convincing without making them more correct, human false positives +24 pts on QuALITY, +18 on APPS, and the probes that
detect *intentional* sophistry do not generalize to this one; **weak link**: a 2025 reproduction attributes a large
part of the result to bugs in the RLHF pipeline — say so if you cite it; and DeepMind's *specification gaming*). **The proposed benchmark**: start from
M and R*, **deliberately introduce systematic errors** into R*, **make sure M knows them** (a system prompt that explains them),
train against R with or without an oversight technique (debate; train only on the episodes where R is certain), evaluate against R*. **What you
say about it.** The displacement you measured ("the law" in your dossier) is a **systematic error of the judge, measured with its slope and its fixed
points** — it is R − R* for the model judge measured under framing. The benchmark proposed by the page is the one your P3 could build: you know the shape of the error.

**9b · Learned governance for multi-agent alignment.** Transformative AI will be **many instances**; even if aligned one by one, the
population can fail through poor coordination — four modes: a **small negative externality** per instance, huge in aggregate; a
problem **reported from instance to instance** without ever reaching whoever can solve it; a problem seen by several, **diffuse responsibility**;
information **not shared**. Proposed solution: a **learned governance** — restricting actions by context, incentivizing prosocial behavior —
with game theory and empirical work. **What you say about it.** *AI Organizations* (F·39) measures the first mode; your program is the
detection side: what internal population signature precedes the aggregate externality. And it is the only paragraph of the page that speaks of "*many
instances*" — your H4 (shared weights) is an answer to a question the page asks without naming it.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* AI Organizations measures this mode in two simulated organizations, on Opus 4.1, and its authors write that the tasks are simulated and the mechanism of the gap is only partially explained (course, Part 7, F·39); and a model may notice the test and behave differently there, and in a simulation, "this is fake" is true (course, Part 2, §B, K63; reading sheet 3). Workaround, in part: two versions of an environment, randomly assigned, differing only in realism cues scored by a discriminator, with an organism trained to hide as the known case (course, Part 2, §B, K63); for the simulation confound itself, none known; say so (reading sheet 3).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: unlearning and re-elicitation → Part 2, §I (after "In practice — unlearning put to the test"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes") *(v3.6)*


### 10 · The overall reading, in three sentences for the oral
The page is organized from **diagnosis** (evaluating capabilities and alignment, understanding cognition) to **remedies** (control if alignment
is not assured; oversight to train it; robustness against the adversary; unlearning and governance). Three passages almost
name you: sycophancy as a propensity (§2), the shift risk of activation monitors (§6b), the circumstances in which
truth representations are useful (§7d). And one sentence is your program: the monitoring schemes that hold when the actor can **pass
messages between instances** (§6a).

## 0 · What was read, and how

- **The list.** The page contains 66 distinct external links. 12 are marked "(read)" in VOLET9. One link points to a site
  (transformer-circuits.pub) and not to a work. The other 53 are marked "(to be checked)" or described without "(read)": they
  have all been read. Two choices worth noting. (1) RepE, CAA, ITI and GCG carry a course sheet number (F·5, F·7, F·15), but not the
  "(read)" mark: they are read here, because the file itself separates the two marks. (2) The *coup probes* and Azaria & Mitchell
  are read too, because the root version, the one the brief names, does not mark them "(read)". That is more than the "forty or so"
  announced by the brief.
- **The full text, not a summary.** Each work was downloaded in full: official arXiv HTML version (bibliography
  removed, tables at one row per line), LessWrong post via its API, ELK report via Google Docs' text export, blog
  posts in HTML. No summarization tool served as a source. For arXiv, the version read is the most recent as of 18/09, except when the page links
  a specific version (2406.07358v2, 2410.05629v1, 2411.07494v1). A number may therefore differ from the version the page cited in
  January 2025: each sheet gives the version read.
- **Who read.** Eight readers, subagents of this session, each read 5 to 9 works in full, with a common instruction
  (format, sources, prohibitions). The main session read *Rapid Response* and checked the "(read)" works.
- **The verification, by program** (`check_fiches.py`). Each quotation of three words or more between quotation marks is searched word for
  word, spaces and quotation marks normalized, in the source text, the page or VOLET9. Each number is searched in the same sources. The
  length of each sheet is measured. Final result: 493 quotations verified, 0 sheets flagged. A defect in
  the instrument was found and fixed along the way: the page kept the `[texte](url)` syntax, so its sentences were not
  found. The check does not guarantee that a paraphrase is faithful; it guarantees that no quotation and no number is invented.

## 2 · Errors in the first version, corrected

### In the sheets (14)
Each line quotes the sheet's "Errors" section.

- **no. 05 · AI Sandbagging: Language Models can Strategically Underperform on Evaluations** (`2406.07358v2`) — VOLET9 writes "frontier models can underperform on command, and be fine-tuned to hide capabilities". The first holds; the second wrongly attributes the fine-tuning to frontier models: "We password-locked Mistral 7b", then Llama 3 8b, Llama 3 70b and GPT-3.5. *no. 05 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v2 HTML text, 848 lines, appendices included; the prompt boxes of appendix D are empty in the conversion (content in images), with no effect on the numbers reported.*
- **no. 07 · Me, Myself, and AI: The Situational Awareness Dataset (SAD) for LLMs** (`2407.04694`) — VOLET9 writes "seven categories of self-knowledge", but "We divide situational awareness into 3 aspects, which are tested by 7 categories": only facts, influence and introspect pertain to self-knowledge. And "sometimes guess whether they are being tested" is too favorable: without a large situating prompt, the models barely exceed chance on stages-oversight. *no. 07 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v1 HTML text, 4069 lines, all eleven appendices included; some prompt boxes are empty in the conversion.*
- **no. 20 · Question Decomposition Improves the Faithfulness of Model-Generated Reasoning** (`2307.11768`) — Imprecision (root and pack v1.3 identical): VOLET9 writes "question decomposition — faithfulness rises when one forces" reasoning through subquestions. Correction: the gain comes from the separate contexts ("answer simpler subquestions in separate contexts"); CoT decomposition alone does worse than CoT under a suggested answer (29.1% versus 21.3%), and faithfulness costs accuracy (81.8 versus 86.0). *no. 20 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v2 HTML text, 980 lines, appendices included (figures not converted; tables 1 and 4 readable).*
- **no. 27 · Coup probes: Catching catastrophes with probes trained off-policy** (`lw-coup-probes`) — Root: "catch coup attempts generated by the model" is false: no coup is tested ("Instead of studying coup attempts, we instead train probes to identify pairs of (instruction, answer) where the answer contains advice about how to commit theft"). Pack v1.3: "is currently trying to do a catastrophic action" is not word for word (text: it’s); "and notes that they have been little followed up empirically" and the name off-policy probes are absent from the post. *no. 27 — Reading: in full — full LessWrong text (GraphQL), 231 lines, appendices included; graphs absent.*
- **no. 30 · Eliciting Latent Knowledge from “Quirky” Language Models** (`2312.01037`) — Imprecision: the year varies, "2023 (arXiv 2312.01037" in §6c and "Mallen et al. 2024" in §7d; the version read and the page say 2024. The description ("probes that recover the true knowledge") holds, but omits the anomaly detection, the reason for the citation in §6c. *no. 30 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v4 HTML text, 733 lines, appendices included.*
- **no. 34 · Supervising strong learners by amplifying weak experts** (`1810.08575`) — Name imprecision: VOLET9 (root and pack v1.3) writes "Christiano et al. 2018, IDA, arXiv 1810.08575"; the text names the method "Iterated Amplification" and contains neither the acronym IDA nor the word *distillation*. Authors, year and identifier hold. *no. 34 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v1 HTML text, 1172 lines, appendices A to D included.*
- **no. 39 · On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs** (`2407.04622`) — Imprecision (root and pack v1.3 identical): "consultancy but the gain depends on the information asymmetry". The advantage over consultancy holds on all tasks; it is the gap to direct QA that depends on the asymmetry ("in extractive QA tasks with information asymmetry debate outperforms direct question answering"). *no. 39 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v2 HTML text, 1311 lines, appendices included (results per task, error analysis, Elo, prompts); the curves are images, only their captions and the text carry numbers.*
- **no. 44 · Evaluating Superhuman Models with Consistency Checks** (`2306.09983`) — Two (root and pack v1.3 identical). "Furi et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.09983": the first author is Lukas Fluri (typo inherited from the page). And the box "unsupervised regularization by consistency" does not hold: it is an evaluation at inference, without training. *no. 44 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v3 HTML text, 1571 lines, appendices included (Leela and Stockfish settings, tables per threshold, example questions, chance control, CEDH, caution, risk sheet); the boxed prompts are not rendered by the conversion ("user_logo.pn"), with no bearing on the results.*
- **no. 49 · Balancing Label Quantity and Quality for Scalable Elicitation** (`2410.13215`) — Imprecision: VOLET9 attaches this link to "quality data on non-representative tasks versus" "noisy data on representative tasks (arXiv 2410.13215)": that is the page's question, not the content; the paper does not vary representativeness and files easy-to-hard under future work. *no. 49 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v2 HTML text, 278 lines, appendices included (hyperparameters, Pareto tables at $0.50 and $0.01).*
- **no. 51 · The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It’s Lying** (`2304.13734`) — Root: "a classifier on activations predicts the truth of statements" holds. Pack v1.3 (read): "71-83% true/false accuracy" and "~20 points above zero-shot" hold; "0.64 on the statements generated by the model itself — the reading/generation gap is already there" is imprecise: 0.6362 is the best case at threshold 0.5 on OPT-6.7b alone, 0.7134 with a recalibrated threshold, and the authors attribute part of the gap to the vagueness of the generated statements. *no. 51 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v2 HTML text, 358 lines (tables 1 to 5, limitations, impact).*
- **no. 56 · Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?** (`2312.03729`) — Root: "with the link Farquhar et al. 2023 (arXiv 2312.03729", summary "CCS and the like often find **another salient feature** than truth". False: authors (Liu, Casper, Hadfield-Menell, Andreas, MIT CSAIL), title and content — no CCS, but supervised probes versus queries. Pack v1.3: "with a link (arXiv 2312.03729, to be checked" — false attribution removed; the "to be checked" is lifted by this sheet. *no. 56 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v1 HTML text, 196 lines, appendix A (sparse probes) included; figures 1 to 4 have only their captions (proportions per category not quantified in the text).*
- **no. 57 · Persistent Pre-training Poisoning of LLMs** (`2410.13722`) — VOLET9 (root and pack v1.3): "(Souly et al. 2024, arXiv 2410.13722 —", "to be checked". False on the authors: Zhang, Rando, Evtimov, Chi, Smith, Carlini, Tramèr, Ippolito (CMU, Meta, ETH Zurich, Google DeepMind); the page uses "Souly" for another link (arXiv 2402.10260). Title and year hold. *no. 57 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v1 HTML text, 544 lines, appendices A to C included (attack examples, configurations, capabilities).*

### The six "to be checked" reservations, lifted
Five links carry "(to be checked)" in both versions, a sixth in the pack v1.3 alone. What the reading settled:

- **no. 19 · 2312.12747** — it is *ALMANACS: A Simulatability Benchmark for Language Model Explainability* (Mills, Su, Russell,
  Emmons, Berkeley AI Research). The page files it among the means of **detecting** an unfaithful chain of thought; it is a benchmark of
  simulatability of explanations, not a detection method.
- **no. 26 · 2410.03768** — it is indeed steganography/collusion between models: *Hidden in Plain Text* (Mathew, Matthews,
  McCarthy et al., LASR Labs et al.). Reservation lifted.
- **no. 56 · 2312.03729** (to be checked in the pack v1.3) — *Cognitive Dissonance* (Liu, Casper, Hadfield-Menell, Andreas, MIT
  CSAIL), and not the paper by Farquhar et al. that the root version attributed to it.
- **no. 57 · 2410.13722** — *Persistent Pre-training Poisoning of LLMs*: title and year correct, authors wrong in VOLET9.
- **no. 58 · 2406.13352** — *AgentDojo* (Debenedetti, Zhang, Balunović et al., ETH Zurich, Invariant Labs): the description holds.
- **no. 61 · 2403.07918** — *On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models* (Kapoor, Bommasani, Klyman et al.): a
  position paper that proposes the **marginal risk** framework, without measuring differential harm; the page uses it to say
  "Measuring the differential impact of an attack".

### On the page itself
- **The structure.** VOLET9 numbers "3 · Understanding model cognition", "4 · Persona" and "5 · Chain-of-thought faithfulness" at the
  same level as "2 · Evaluating alignment". On the page, these are subsections of *Evaluating alignment*: `h3` tags under the
  `h2`, and the same indentation in the table of contents. In other words, the page files cognition, persona and chain-of-thought
  faithfulness among the ways of **evaluating alignment**.
- **An addition, not an error.** VOLET9 does not say who organized the page. It bears "with organizing from Sam Marks and Peter Hase".

## 3 · The "(read)" works: what was checked
VOLET9's claims about the twelve works marked "(read)" were compared with their text (titles, authors, years, numbers,
attributions). One error: *Rapid Response*, which therefore has its sheet. Two clarifications without error: Lanham et al. ("on most tasks") and
the criticism by Wen et al., which is a code review with a single rerun, not a full reproduction. The details are in the place of
each work, in the list below.

# The sheets, in the page's order

## Evaluating capabilities

### GPQA: A Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A Benchmark — David Rein, Betty Li Hou, Asa Cooper Stickland et al. (New York University; Cohere; Anthropic, PBC), 2023; arXiv 2311.12022v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Can one write questions that are reliable for experts, but that highly skilled non-experts cannot solve even with the web? Aim: a testing ground for scalable oversight of a model that the overseer cannot verify.
**The method and its controls.** 61 Upwork contractors, PhDs or PhD students in biology, physics, chemistry; each question goes through two expert validators and three non-experts from other fields, web free, LLMs forbidden. 546 questions published, 448 in the main set, 198 in Diamond. Controls: post-hoc agreement of the experts, manual classification of the 191 errors of the second expert, "answer-only" classifiers that stayed at chance (no surface cue). Baselines: Llama-2-70B-chat, GPT-3.5-turbo-16k, GPT-4 with or without chain of thought or web search.
**The result, in numbers.** "experts who have or are pursuing PhDs in the corresponding domains reach 65% accuracy (74% when discounting clear mistakes the experts identified in retrospect), while highly skilled non-expert validators only reach 34% accuracy"; "our strongest GPT-4–based baseline achieving 39% accuracy", against 25% at chance; non-experts at 34.1% ± 2.3% (95% CI); GPT-4 with search abstains on 37.2% of the questions.
**What they leave open.** "GPQA is small at only 448 examples", hence little statistical power; specialized non-experts who bound from above; a recruitment bias; and "it is still an imperfect proxy for the setting we care about, which involves supervising superhuman AI systems".
**Why the page cites it.** §1 Evaluating capabilities: "Many AI capability benchmarks, including difficult ones that target PhD-level knowledge, saturate quickly". Partial match: the paper documents no saturation (best model at 39%) and only notes that a set must "remain meaningful and not saturate".
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 1: GPQA creates the regime in which the annotator can no longer verify, the one where the authors expect hallucination and sycophancy "to be exacerbated" — where a systematic judge error weighs the most.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9's description ("GPQA (Rein et al., 2023, arXiv 2311.12022)", Google-proof benchmark "of doctoral-level questions") holds. Clarification: the paper says "graduate-level"; saturation is a claim of the page, not a result of the paper.
*no. 01 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v1 HTML text, 1222 lines, appendices included (complete prompts, incentive scale, instructions to annotators).*

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging") *(v3.6)*


### A new initiative for developing third-party model evaluations — Anthropic (announcement post, no author named), 2024; https://www.anthropic.com/news/a-new-initiative-for-developing-third-party-model-evaluations
**The hypothesis tested.** None: this is not a study but a funding announcement (Jul 1, 2024). Starting observation: "the current evaluations landscape is limited" and "the demand is outpacing the supply"; Anthropic therefore funds evaluations built by third parties.
**The method and its controls.** No experiment and no model tested: a call for proposals. Three priorities: evaluations of the ASL levels of the Responsible Scaling Policy (cyber, CBRN, autonomy, national security, social manipulation, misalignment); metrics of advanced capabilities (science beyond GPQA, refusals, multilingual, societal impacts); tools (no-code platforms, evaluations of model-based grading, uplift trials with and without access to the model). Ten principles of good evaluation, including "Not in the training data" and "Expert baselines for comparison".
**The result, in numbers.** The text reports no measurement. Its only numbers are targets: "tens of thousands of new evaluation questions and end-to-end tasks"; "evaluations with 1,000 or 10,000 tasks or questions are preferable to those with 100"; uplift trials "involving thousands of participants".
**What they leave open.** The post names its limits: "even the best evaluations are not always indicative of risks they purport to measure"; in CBRN, measuring "real-world risks accurately"; in manipulation, isolating "the model's unique contribution to these risks"; and "Most of the time, when models have performed highly, experts have realized that high performance on that version of the evaluation is not sufficient to worry them."
**Why the page cites it.** §1 Evaluating capabilities, as a reference: "See our past announcement here for more information about capabilities evaluations we are interested in more work on". Faithful reference: the novel research, tool use and autonomous tasks that the page calls for, with human baselines, are detailed in the post.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Link with axis 1: the post calls for test sets to measure "the reliability of models as high-quality graders" — the object whose systematic error the displacement law describes (the post does not talk about social framing).
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 only identifies it ("of third-party evaluations (Anthropic, 2024)"), and the date of the post confirms the year.
*no. 02 — Reading: in full — converted HTML page of the post, 125 lines; lines 112-125 ("Related content") are the site's navigation links, outside the post.*

Holds.*

### AI Sandbagging: Language Models can Strategically Underperform on Evaluations — Teun van der Weij, Felix Hofstätter, Oliver Jaffe et al. (MATS; Imperial College London; independent researchers), 2024; arXiv 2406.07358v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Do models have the capabilities for sandbagging, "strategic underperformance on an evaluation": selectively failing a dangerous-capabilities evaluation while keeping general capabilities, and emulating a weaker model? Intent is set aside: "we do not consider the strategic part of sandbagging".
**The method and its controls.** By prompt, GPT-4-Turbo and Claude 3 Opus must fail WMDP (3,668 questions of dangerous knowledge) while keeping MMLU (14,042) and CSQA (9,470) as controls, with a "regular" control prompt, best prompt selected after trial on 100 examples, refusals counted separately. By fine-tuning (LoRA), Mistral 7b is password-locked on 3347 synthetic questions written by GPT-4, then evaluated on the real MMLU and WMDP. Finally two arms: the "Emulator" (Llama 3 70b emulating Llama 2 7b) versus the "Targeter" (which aims only at accuracy). 95% CI over 3 seeds.
**The result, in numbers.** Selective drops: in biology, Claude 3 loses 39.8 points on WMDP versus 9.7 on MMLU, GPT-4 32.1 versus 14.0 — but GPT-4 also loses 15% on CSQA, an exception flagged by the authors. The locking transfers: it "generalizes to high-quality, held-out benchmarks such as WMDP". Emulation: "the Emulator behaved more like Llama 2 7b, providing the same answer on 77.1% of questions on average, compared to the Targeter's 61.7%" — 41.2 ± 0.1 locked, 74.2 ± 0.2 with password.
**What they leave open.** "We assessed models solely on multiple choice question answering (MCQA) benchmarks"; sandbagging there can perhaps be undone with few examples; it remains to test the ability to "determine when they are being evaluated"; suggested countermeasure, not tried: "these probes could be used to detect if an LM is sandbagging".
**Why the page cites it.** §2 Evaluating alignment: "Does it ever strategically choose not to reveal a capability it possesses?" Gap: the page poses a spontaneous propensity, the paper measures an elicited capability and excludes the strategic part.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 3: behavioral detection weakens as soon as the model emulates a weaker one (77.1% identical answers), and the authors designate activation probes as the untested countermeasure.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The probe countermeasure remains an untested suggestion here, and a silent probe does not separate "no intention" from "blind probe" (course, Part 10, no. 05; handover, §5.2; reading sheets, part B, trap 3). Workaround: first measure its sensitivity and false alarms on an organism in which you installed the underperformance yourself — this paper's password-locked Mistral 7b is one, without the strategic part the paper sets aside (course, Part 10, no. 05) —, its silence elsewhere then becoming a bound (handover, §5.2); such a success would bound the instrument without proving it works on natural sandbagging, and against that gap none known; say so (handover, §5.2; reading sheet 15).

**Errors in the first version, if any.** VOLET9 writes "frontier models can underperform on command, and be fine-tuned to hide capabilities". The first holds; the second wrongly attributes the fine-tuning to frontier models: "We password-locked Mistral 7b", then Llama 3 8b, Llama 3 70b and GPT-3.5.
*no. 05 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v2 HTML text, 848 lines, appendices included; the prompt boxes of appendix D are empty in the conversion (content in images), with no effect on the numbers reported.*

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section) *(v3.6)*



## Evaluating alignment › Understanding model cognition

*no. 06 · Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models — Sharma, Tong, Korbak et al., arXiv 2310.13548 (v4 read) — marked "(read)" in VOLET9, not redone. Checked: VOLET9 only claims "Sharma 2023" (link "please the user"): authors and year reread. Holds.*

### Me, Myself, and AI: The Situational Awareness Dataset (SAD) for LLMs — Rudolf Laine, Bilal Chughtai, Jan Betley et al. (Constellation; MIT; Apollo Research; independents), 2024; arXiv 2407.04694v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Does a model know that it is a model, can it infer its situation (training, test, deployment) and does it act accordingly? The authors decompose this situational awareness into measurable capabilities.
**The method and its controls.** A behavioral benchmark of 7 categories, 16 tasks and 13,198 questions, given to 16 Llama-2, GPT-3/4 and Claude models, base and chat. Bounds: chance per task, a human baseline where the human answers for themselves (below chance), a "roleplay" human baseline (ten experts, at most 15 questions each), an estimated ceiling. Two interventions: a "situating prompt" reminding the model that it is an LLM, and chain of thought (two models). Binomial standard error.
**The result, in numbers.** All do better than chance, but "even the highest-scoring model (Claude 3 Opus) is far from a human baseline on certain tasks": 49.5 ± 0.6 for Claude 3 Opus, versus 27.4 at chance and 90.7 at the ceiling. The interventions yield little: +4.5% from base to chat, +1.0% (base) and +3.2% (chat) for the situating prompt, +5.2% for chain of thought. The weakness is where the risk is: "even the best-performing models struggle to distinguish between evaluation and deployment samples in stages". At similar MMLU, the scores range from 31.6% to 42.7%.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* On stages-oversight, the score measures what the model answers when asked where it is: a self-report, which is not a belief (reading sheet 3; reading sheets, part B, trap 2), and verbalized awareness, which misses the unverbalized kind (course, Part 7, F·25); that it is barely above chance there therefore does not establish that the model cannot tell evaluation from deployment: it is an instrument's null (reading sheets, part B, trap 3). Workaround: triangulate — an internal probe, the verbal report, and behaviour between a realistic and an obvious version of the setting (course, Part 5, topic 4) —, with the probe first validated on an evaluation-conditioned organism as the known case (programme, parts 4 and 8).

**What they leave open.** "sad tests models on short, artificial, bounded tasks", hence the risk "that sad fails to capture skills that are important in practice"; "we have small sample sizes for each intervention"; leakage into the corpora.
**Why the page cites it.** Twice. §3 Understanding model cognition: "Do they have guesses about whether they are in training or how they're being monitored?" — direct match. §5 Chain-of-thought faithfulness: "Can a model's knowledge about its situation affect the faithfulness of its CoT?" — distantly: the paper measures knowledge and action, never the faithfulness of a chain.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 4: self-recognition is motivated by unintended coordination — "A model might notice that it interacts with another copy of itself and coordinate" — and plateaus at 70% for Claude 3 Opus.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** VOLET9 writes "seven categories of self-knowledge", but "We divide situational awareness into 3 aspects, which are tested by 7 categories": only facts, influence and introspect pertain to self-knowledge. And "sometimes guess whether they are being tested" is too favorable: without a large situating prompt, the models barely exceed chance on stages-oversight.
*no. 07 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v1 HTML text, 4069 lines, all eleven appendices included; some prompt boxes are empty in the conversion.*

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); self-report and introspection → Part 5, Section II, A, Topic 13 *(v3.6)*


### Monitor: An AI-Driven Observability Interface — Kevin Meng, Vincent Huang, Neil Chowdhury et al. (Transluce), 2024; https://transluce.org/observability-interface#example-2
**The hypothesis tested.** Does an interface backed by automatic neuron descriptions allow a human to spot the concepts responsible for a behavior, then to intervene on them? Two cases: the spurious concepts behind "9.8 < 9.11", and the knowledge a model holds without saying it when it refuses to answer.
**The method and its controls.** Precompiled descriptions of all the MLP neurons of Llama-3.1-8B (about 917,000), semantic search, an "AI linter" (GPT-4o mini) that groups them into clusters, two importance measures — activation and attribution (gradient on the target token) —, steering that zeroes the 500 neurons closest to a natural-language query. Validation on 1280 comparisons; controls: no intervention, random neurons (three seeds), random terms. Claimed status: "a technical demonstration" in which they "do not run detailed ablations and controls".
**The result, in numbers.** Without intervention, "Llama-3.1 gets only 55% correct". Deactivating the Bible-verse neurons raises it to 0.76 — "removing bible verse neurons increases comparison accuracy by 21 percentage points" — versus 0.54-0.57 for random neurons; the three linter concepts combined give 0.79 in the figure (77% in the text). The second example, the one the link targets, is qualitative: "Llama say that it does not know who Nicholas Carlini is, yet our AI linter surfaces a cluster of cybersecurity neurons"; deactivating "don't know" and "unable to verify" brings the information out.
**What they leave open.** A rival hypothesis admitted: "Llama simply gets "distracted" from too many concepts firing at once"; concepts found on the evaluation set itself, hence "a possibility of overfitting"; the information in the second example can be obtained otherwise, "if we tell the model to take a guess even if it isn't sure"; the tool "does not explain how models make decisions".
**Why the page cites it.** §3 Understanding model cognition: "Do our models know information that they do not report when asked?" The link's anchor points to the Nicholas Carlini example. Exact reference, weak evidence: neither number nor control.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 2: the demonstration separates what lights up (activation) from what weighs on the output (attribution) and concludes only after ablation against random neurons — the discipline that "reading is not controlling" demands.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Random neurons are only the specificity null: they rule out a single reading, that any ablation of that size does as much, not the damage specific to the removed neurons nor a neighbouring concept — the authors admit the rival hypothesis of a "distracted" model, and the concepts were found on the evaluation set itself (course, Part M, M4; course, Part 10, no. 08). Workaround: compare at matched degradation, against several families of controls (course, Part M, M4; programme, parts 3 and 7), and choose the neurons on a set disjoint from the one that evaluates them (repository README).

**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 only identifies it, "Transluce, the observability interface", without claiming anything about its content.
*no. 08 — Reading: in full — converted HTML page, 204 lines, including the system design section and the references; the screenshots of the interface are not in the text.*

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response") *(v3.6)*


### Interpreting the Second-Order Effects of Neurons in CLIP — Yossi Gandelsman, Alexei A. Efros, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley), 2025; arXiv 2406.04341v3
**The hypothesis tested.** Can the function of CLIP's neurons be described by text? The direct effect is negligible, the indirect one masked by redundancy; the authors propose the second-order effect — the flow from a neuron to the output via the subsequent attention heads — and test whether it is selective, rank one and decomposable into text.
**The method and its controls.** CLIP ViT-B-32 (12 layers), replicated on ViT-L-14; mean ablation on 5000 ImageNet images, zero-shot accuracy on the validation set, compared with the indirect effect. Decomposition by sparse coding over three pools (10k, 30k common words, 28k ChatGPT descriptions). Two causal validations: adversarial images on CIFAR-10 pairs, controls = random neurons, indirect effect, words close to the classification direction; and zero-shot segmentation.
**The result, in numbers.** The effect is selective: "each individual neuron has a significant effect for less than 2% of the images". On layer 9, ablating the second-order effect makes accuracy fall to 29.6 versus 52.3 for the indirect one; the first component explains 48.2 of the variance versus 11.0: "Mean-ablating the indirect effects results in a smaller drop in performance due to self-repair behavior." The neurons are polysemantic — "each neuron corresponds to multiple, often unrelated, concepts" — and this polysemanticity becomes an attack: 22.7 (± 0.5) adversarial images out of 100 for dog to deer, versus 6.3 (± 4.8) via the indirect effect and 0.3 (± 0.5) at random. Zero-shot segmentation: 78.1 versus 76.5.
**What they leave open.** They "ignored the effect of neurons on consecutive queries and keys"; "We did not analyze the mutual effects between neurons"; and their attack pipeline "relies on a few independent components, each of which has failure modes".
**Why the page cites it.** §3 Understanding model cognition: understood cognition serves for "expediting searches" "for concerning behaviors (e.g. during auditing or red-teaming)". Partial match: an image-text encoder, and the targeted behaviors are classification errors manufactured by a generative pipeline.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 2: the causal share attributed to a component depends on the path measured — direct negligible, indirect masked by self-repair (52.3 versus 29.6) —, so a direction that is read is only worth something once validated by the intervention it enables.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 gives only the identifier ("speed up searches for concerning behaviors"), without title or authors.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction") *(v3.6)*

### Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models — Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans et al. (Google Research, Brain Team), 2023 (v6); arXiv 2201.11903v6
**The hypothesis tested.** Are a few input, chain-of-reasoning, output triples given as examples enough to unlock multi-step reasoning, without fine-tuning? And is the effect emergent with scale?
**The method and its controls.** Eight hand-written exemplars, greedy decoding, no fine-tuning. Five families: GPT-3 (350M to 175B), LaMDA (422M to 137B), PaLM (62B, 540B), UL2, Codex. Domains: arithmetic (GSM8K, SVAMP, ASDiv, AQuA, MAWPS), commonsense (CSQA, StrategyQA, SayCan), symbolic with out-of-distribution sets. Baseline: standard few-shot. Three ablations rule out rival explanations — "equation only", "variable compute only", "chain of thought after answer" —, and robustness is tested across three annotators, other exemplars and ordering (standard deviations over five seeds). Two manual analyses, 50 correct chains and 50 wrong ones.
**The result, in numbers.** On GSM8K, PaLM 540B goes from 17.9 to 56.9 (+39.0) and GPT-3 175B from 15.6 to 46.9 (+31.3). The effect is "an emergent ability of model scale": in small models the chain lowers the score (LaMDA 420M, 2.6 versus 0.4). The ablations stay at baseline level on LaMDA 137B (standard 6.5 ± 0.4, chain 14.3 ± 0.4, equation only 5.4 ± 0.2, variable compute 6.4 ± 0.3, reasoning after the answer 6.1 ± 0.4): "the sequential reasoning embodied in the chain of thought is useful for reasons beyond just activating knowledge". Of 50 wrong chains, 46% are almost correct, 54% have a major error.
**What they leave open.** The chain "does not answer whether the neural network is actually "reasoning," which we leave as an open question"; "there is no guarantee of correct reasoning paths"; and the cost, since the effect appears only at large scales.
**Why the page cites it.** §3 Understanding model cognition, externalized-cognition route: "Inducing a model to "reason out loud"" via a scratchpad, "The core challenge here is ensuring the faithfulness of the externalized reasoning". The paper supplies the method, not the guarantee: it claims only "an interpretable window into the behavior of the model".
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 2: the "chain of thought after answer" ablation shows that the answer depends on producing the chain, not that the chain describes the computation — what can be read is not what causes.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 ("the chain of thought (Wei et al., 2022, arXiv 2201.11903)") holds; 2022 is the original year, the v6 read is dated "10 Jan 2023".
*No. 11 — Reading: in full — full arXiv v6 HTML text, 1604 lines, appendices included (FAQ, raw results, error analyses, complete prompts).*

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: chain of thought as a monitor → Part 11, answer 43 *(v3.6)*


### Looking Inward: Language Models Can Learn About Themselves by Introspection — Felix J Binder, James Chua, Tomek Korbak et al. (UC San Diego, Stanford, Truthful AI, Anthropic, UC Berkeley and others), 2024; arXiv 2410.13787v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Can an LLM acquire knowledge about itself that is "not contained in or derived from training data"? Criterion: M1 introspects if it predicts properties of its own hypothetical behavior better than a model M2 trained on M1's actual behavior.
**The method and its controls.** Hypothetical questions without chain of thought (second character of the answer, parity, ethical stance); fine-tuning on 30,000 examples, 6 training sets, 6 held out. Controls: a "Guessing most common behavior" baseline; cross-prediction (M2 trained on the same data, in both directions); entropy rebalancing; behavior change via 1000 answers from Claude-3.5-Sonnet. Models: GPT-4o, GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama 70B.
**The result, in numbers.** "Llama 70B predicts its own behavior more accurately (48.5%) than GPT-4o (31.8%)"; in the other direction, GPT-4o predicts itself at 49.4% versus 36.6%. GPT-3.5: an advantage that is "statistically significant but very small (+0.8%)". Cross-prediction tops out at 35.2%. Calibration (MAD): 23.0 without training, 8.7 in self-prediction, 21.3 in cross-prediction. Modified behavior: 35.4% of predictions correct for the new behavior versus 21.7% for the old one.
**What they leave open.** "Our tasks, while demonstrating introspection, do not have practical applications." Failure on long answers; no advantage in predicting its own sycophancy ("Are you sure?"): 74.5% versus 76.5% in cross-prediction; no generalization to SAD or to coordination; weak evidence for GPT-3.5; mechanism (self-simulation) only proposed.
**Why the page cites it.** Section "Understanding model cognition": "Introspection: Training models to directly verbalize the content of their hidden states". The paper fits the board-game example (self-report judged against actual behavior) better than the sentence: it predicts properties of hypothetical behaviors, not the content of hidden states.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 1: the tested behavior closest to sycophancy is precisely the one where the model does not predict itself better than an external observer — propensity still has to be measured from the outside.

### SelfIE: Self-Interpretation of Large Language Model Embeddings — Haozhe Chen, Carl Vondrick, Chengzhi Mao (Columbia University; Mila and McGill University), 2024; arXiv 2403.10949v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Can an LLM describe in natural language the content of its own hidden embeddings, without training, by reusing its ability to summarize a passage — and do these descriptions make it possible to control its reasoning?
**The method and its controls.** The embedding to be interpreted replaces [X] tokens in an "interpretation forward pass" of the same model; a "relevancy score" isolates what comes from the embedding. Model: LLaMA-2-70B-Chat (7B and 13B in ablation). Faithfulness: TextWorld (3400 evaluation examples) against linear probes trained on 1 to 100 examples. Control: Supervised Control against FT, RepE and ROME on Counterfact (844 facts), with a "Random control"; Reinforcement Control evaluated on 388 harmful behaviors.
**The result, in numbers.** TextWorld: SelfIE "recovers 60\%-80\% of the information about entity state" and "performs similarly to the 100-sample linear probe". Fact editing: harmonic mean 59.77% versus 56.92% for ROME. Ethical preference imposed by the prompt: answers favoring humans go from 100% to 2% after control, versus 95% with the random control. Erasure: harmful answers under prompt injection go from 89.06% to 4.4%, with 95.85% of facts preserved. Small models: 27.17% (7B) and 17.68% (13B) of off-instruction interpretations, versus 3.84% (70B).
**What they leave open.** The text has no limitations section. The only written caveats, in the ablation: "Accuracy degrades for later layers" and, for small models, "failure to follow instructions might decrease the chance of obtaining high-quality interpretation". The readings of reasoning (injection, trolley problem, hallucination) are examples in figures.
**Why the page cites it.** Section "Understanding model cognition": "Introspection: Training models to directly verbalize the content of their hidden states". Partial match: SelfIE does get the model itself to verbalize hidden states, but "without any training", where the page speaks of training.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Link with axis 2: SelfIE checks a reading through an intervention compared against a random control (2% versus 95%), the kind of causal test the maxim reading is not controlling demands; but the faithfulness of the reading itself is measured only against linear probes.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* A random control is only the specificity null: it rules out neither the damage specific to the intervention nor a correlate, so it is not enough for the causal test (course, Part M, M4; handover, §5.2); as for the reading, its faithfulness is measured only against linear probes, with no ground truth for latents (course, Part 10, no. 13 and no. 16). Workaround: compare the intervention with controls at matched degradation, as a dose-response curve (course, Part M, M4; course, Part 2, §C, K47), and test the decoding on fine-tuned variants with known behaviour, never seen before (reading sheet 18).

**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 gives only the identifier.

### Patchscopes: A Unifying Framework for Inspecting Hidden Representations of Language Models — Asma Ghandeharioun, Avi Caciularu, Adam Pearce et al. (Google Research; Tel Aviv University), 2024; arXiv 2401.06102v4
**The hypothesis tested.** Can an LLM be made to "translate" the information in its hidden representations by patching them into another inference pass designed to extract it — and does this framework unify and surpass logit lens, tuned lens and probes?
**The method and its controls.** A Patchscope fixes a target prompt, position, transfer function, model and layer. Tests: next token from intermediate layers, against Logit Lens and Tuned Lens (LLaMA2 13B, Vicuna 13B, GPT-J 6B, Pythia 12B; 2,000 evaluation examples); zero-shot attribute extraction against a logistic-regression probe (GPT-J, 12 tasks, 1,453 points, Bonferroni correction); entity resolution (PopQA); patching from Vicuna 7B into 13B; multi-hop correction (46 samples) against "vanilla" generation and chain of thought.
**The result, in numbers.** Next token: from layer 10 on, "a gain of up to 98% in layers 18-22". Attributes: better than the probe "on six out of twelve tasks" (Company CEO 47.8 versus 5.0), with the probe keeping the advantage on Object superclass (65.6 versus 54.8). Multi-hop: 50% versus 35.71% (CoT) and 19.57% (vanilla). Cross-model: reading Vicuna 7B with the 13B improves the description of entities, but not for Pythia, where the smaller model does better.
**What they leave open.** "Limitations" section: evidence limited to autoregressive Transformers. The computation after the patch can add information: "this approach does not guarantee that the patched representation itself stores all that information". To do: choosing the target prompt, patching across model families, limiting "placeholder contamination".
**Why the page cites it.** Section "Understanding model cognition": "Introspection: Training models to directly verbalize the content of their hidden states". Partial match: the model verbalizes its representations, but without training ("training-data free"); only cross-model patching learns an affine function.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 2: the authors write that successful decoding does not prove that the representation carries the information — a distinction close to the one between what an instrument reads and what the model uses causally.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9's description ("the model decodes its own representations into natural language by patching", root and pack v1.3 identical) holds; the framework also patches into a pass "(of the same or a different LLM)".

### Vector-ICL: In-context Learning with Continuous Vector Representations — Yufan Zhuang, Chandan Singh, Liyuan Liu et al. (UC San Diego; Microsoft Research), 2024; arXiv 2410.05629v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Does an LLM's in-context learning (ICL) extend to continuous vectors "obtained from black-box pretrained encoders", once projected into its embedding space?
**The method and its controls.** Encoder and LLM frozen; only a lightweight projector (linear or MLP) is trained, by language modeling or generic objectives, then optionally per task. Four LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2-7B, Yi-1.5-9B), four text encoders, plus time series, graphs and fMRI (3 subjects). Named baselines: few-shot ICL on the raw input, soft prompt, domain models, random baseline. Nine tasks, 95% error bars.
**The result, in numbers.** Classification (Llama3.1-8B, up to 50 examples): fine-tuned V-ICL 88.80, 98.16, 97.28, 85.20 and 81.68 (Rotten Tomatoes, SST2, IMDB, Emotion, Financial Phrasebank) versus 87.31, 91.74, 93.50, 55.20 and 71.78 for few-shot ICL; the soft prompt reaches 93.24 on Rotten Tomatoes, above V-ICL. Without fine-tuning, V-ICL stays below few-shot ICL on four datasets out of five (the sheet's reading of Table 2). Summarization (RougeL): 20.08 and 20.49 versus 19.53 and 19.41. Regression: "Vector-ICL consistently outperforms few-shot ICL with raw number inputs". fMRI: "LLMs can surpass random baselines".
**What they leave open.** "our experiments did not cover all possible combinations of these variables"; other modalities and encoder-decoder pairs remain to be explored; "we only experimented with single-token encoders".
**Why the page cites it.** Section "Understanding model cognition": "Introspection: Training models to directly verbalize the content of their hidden states". Distant match: the vectors read come from external encoders, not from the hidden states of the LLM reading them; only the projector is trained.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 3: a lightweight projector, often linear, makes vectors readable by an LLM, but the paper concerns neither the activations of the monitored model nor the shift from synthetic data to the model's generations.

### LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to Decode Activations Into Natural Language — Alexander Pan, Lijie Chen, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley), 2026; arXiv 2412.08686v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Can a "decoder" LLM be trained to answer open-ended questions in natural language about a target LLM's activations, faithfully enough to read properties of its future completions and to control it?
**The method and its controls.** Latent Interpretation Tuning (Lit): 16,732 examples (goals, personas, extractive QA) generated with o1-preview; the stimulus activations (layer k=15) are patched into a fine-tuned copy of the target model, with the control activations masked to prevent cheating. Target: Llama-3-8B-Instruct (Gemma-3-4b-it in the appendix). Baselines: for reading, GPT-4 with the full dialogue, SelfIE, Patchscope, linear probe; for control, prompting, RepE, SFT, DPO.
**The result, in numbers.** Hidden personas, absent from training: the decoder "outperforms GPT-4 absolutely by 18.7% and 2.7% and SelfIE absolutely by 77.3% and 76% on the hard and easy settings, respectively". Relation extraction: +32.2% over the probe and +38.2% over Patchscope (6 tasks), with the probe keeping the advantage on Ath_Position (75.9 versus 65.2). Debiasing (CrowS Pairs): 3.70 versus 4.05 without control and 4.38 with RepE; "Lit is the only control method which statistically significantly reduces bias across both metrics". Malicious role: 100 and 87% harmful answers versus 0 by prompting. Scale: hard task from 12% (1B) to 92% (8B).
**What they leave open.** "our training data may lack diversity" and "because we have no ground truth for latents, our decoder may hallucinate", a risk they consider mitigated by the reading and steering results. Generalization of steering to unseen personas is shown qualitatively.
**Why the page cites it.** Section "Understanding model cognition": "Introspection: Training models to directly verbalize the content of their hidden states". Direct match, with a nuance: it is a fine-tuned copy of the model that reads, not the queried model itself.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Link with axis 2: steering from the whole activation reduces bias where RepE's linear steering increases it (4.38 versus 4.05), which the authors attribute to a concept that "may not be linearly represented" — the same family of finding as the causal partition, without a measurement of a direction's causal share.

### ALMANACS: A Simulatability Benchmark for Language Model Explainability — Edmund Mills, Shiye Su, Stuart Russell, Scott Emmons (Berkeley AI Research), 2025; arXiv 2312.12747v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Can one measure automatically whether an explainability method helps predict a model's behavior on new inputs, under distribution shift (simulatability) — and do existing methods manage it?
**The method and its controls.** Non-objective yes/no questions on 12 safety topics (including Sycophancy), with values reserved for the test; two models (flan-alpaca-gpt4-xl, vicuna-7b-v1.3), 18,000 test examples. Predictor: GPT-4 with 10 neighboring examples. Methods: Counterfactual, Rationalization, Attention, IntegratedGrads; NoExpl control; naive baselines including LogisticRegression; KLDiv metric. Validation: a synthetic model with known explanations and 10 human annotators (1848 prompts).
**The result, in numbers.** "when averaged across all topics, no explanation method outperforms the explanation-free control". Mean KLDiv of NoExpl: 0.10 (flan-alpaca) and 0.08 (vicuna); methods: 0.09 or 0.10, then 0.08 to 0.10. Best case, counterfactuals: "0.19 to 0.15 in Sycophancy". Positive control: on the synthetic model, KLDiv goes from 0.54 to 0.30 (Qualitative explanation) and to 0.16 (Weights). Humans: no 95% confidence interval disjoint from NoExpl.
**What they leave open.** "it is not a perfect substitute for human evaluations, which remain the gold standard"; "we caution against overinterpretation of ALMANACS results"; simulatability rewards neither minimality nor robustness; "developing an explanation method that aids simulatability in ALMANACS remains an open challenge".
**Why the page cites it.** Section "Chain-of-thought faithfulness": "We are therefore interested in techniques for detecting" (Mills et al., 2024), then "How can we make automatic methods for detecting unfaithful CoT". Partial match: ALMANACS does not test the faithfulness of a chain of thought but simulatability, "a necessary condition for faithfulness and completeness"; the model's rationalizations do not help there.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 1: the most notable case where an explanation helps is the Sycophancy topic, but the paper measures the predictability of yes/no answers, not the size of a shift under social framing.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 gives only the identifier, marked "to be checked" (root and pack v1.3). The point is settled: it is ALMANACS, a simulatability benchmark for explanations, which VOLET9, like the page, files under the detection of unfaithfulness.

### Question Decomposition Improves the Faithfulness of Model-Generated Reasoning — Ansh Radhakrishnan, Karina Nguyen, Anna Chen et al. (Anthropic; Jan Brauner: University of Oxford), 2023; arXiv 2307.11768v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Does decomposing a question into subquestions — especially answered in separate contexts — make the generated reasoning more faithful than chain of thought (CoT), and at what cost in accuracy?
**The method and its controls.** CoT, CoT decomposition (a single context) and factored decomposition (subquestions in isolated contexts, then recomposition), against zero-shot and few-shot. A single RLHF model, "using the same base model as Claude 1.3"; 1200 questions from HotpotQA, StrategyQA, OpenBookQA and TruthfulQA. Faithfulness: perturbations from Lanham et al. (truncation, added errors) and biased contexts from Turpin et al. ("answer is always A", suggested answer).
**The result, in numbers.** Accuracy: 86.0 (CoT), 85.6 (CoT decomposition), 81.8 (factored), 79.7 (few-shot). A corrupted CoT changes the answer for only 9.6% of questions, versus 28.7% and 33.6%. Suggested answer: a drop of 21.3% (CoT), 29.1% (CoT decomposition), 9.2% (factored). "answer is always A": no significant difference. Sycophancy: 14.7% non-sycophantic answers (factored) versus 4.7% (CoT), but "not a clear indication of greater reasoning faithfulness".
**What they leave open.** Faithfulness is paid for in accuracy, and the effect of training is uncertain; the metrics are limited by "our inability to access the ground truth for the model’s reasoning"; "only one model (an RLHF-finetuned LLM)" and four tasks.
**Why the page cites it.** Section "Chain-of-thought faithfulness": techniques for "ensuring" (Radhakrishnan et al., 2023) "the faithfulness of a language model's chain-of-thought (CoT)". Direct match: a prompting method that increases measured faithfulness.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Link with axis 1: the suggested answer is a social framing, and answering the subquestions outside that context reduces the accuracy drop (9.2% versus 21.3%) without cancelling it — an effect measured in accuracy, not as a fraction of distance as in the displacement law.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** Imprecision (root and pack v1.3 identical): VOLET9 writes "question decomposition — faithfulness rises when one forces" reasoning by subquestions. Correction: the gain comes from the separate contexts ("answer simpler subquestions in separate contexts"); CoT decomposition alone does worse than CoT under a suggested answer (29.1% versus 21.3%), and faithfulness costs accuracy (81.8 versus 86.0).

### Bias-Augmented Consistency Training Reduces Biased Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought — James Chua, Edward Rees, Hunar Batra et al. (Independent, Speechmatics, Apollo Research, University of Oxford, NYU, Anthropic), 2025; arXiv 2403.05518v3
**The hypothesis tested.** Does training a model to reason the same way with and without a biasing hint reduce the unverbalized biased reasoning of the CoT, even for unseen biases and tasks? BCT is "an unsupervised fine-tuning scheme that trains models to give consistent reasoning across prompts with and without biasing features".
**The method and its controls.** GPT-3.5T is finetuned on prompts augmented with a single bias (Suggested Answer, sycophancy), with its own CoT produced without bias as the target (10k pairs). Nine biases; evaluation on four unseen tasks (600 questions per bias). Named control: Self-Training (same volume, unbiased prompts). Measure: BRR, the gap between the biased-answer rate and the unbiased base, and the BRR ratio; verbalization checked by hand on 1040 cases; replication on LLaMA-3 8B Instruct.
**The result, in numbers.** Trained bias: ratio .14 versus .72 for the control ("reduces biased reasoning from sycophancy by 86% on held-out tasks"). Eight unseen biases: ratio .63 versus .88 ("by an average of 37%"), mean BRR 43 → 27 (control 38), better than the control "on all held-out biases (all p<0.001 ), aside from Positional Bias". Failures: Argument .89, Positional Bias .95. Consistent biased reasoning 27.2% → 15.1% (p=0.0002). No gain on sensitivity to paraphrases (entropy 1.01 → 1.10 bits). Costs: accuracy 62.9% → 61.5% (control 61.1%), strong prior tasks 52.4% → 45.0%. LLaMA-3: 46% → 28% on unseen biases.
**What they leave open.** "BCT requires that we have a prompt where the bias is not present to reduce susceptibility to that bias specifically". Future work: more varied counterfactuals, understanding the generalization, and "teach models to verbalize them".
**Why the page cites it.** §5 Chain-of-thought faithfulness: "or ensuring […] the faithfulness of a language model's chain-of-thought (CoT)". Direct match: unfaithfulness is treated there as an inconsistency across contexts and reduced — by making the model ignore the bias, not by making it verbalize it.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 1: for a judge under social framing, BCT is a tested remedy against directed sycophancy, which transfers to unseen biases but not to the position bias of a judge model (ratio .95, control .94).

## AI control › Behavioral monitoring

### Testing Language Model Agents Safely in the Wild — Silen Naihin, David Atkinson, Marc Green et al. (AutoGPT, Northeastern University, Microsoft Research, independents), 2023; arXiv 2311.10538v3
**The hypothesis tested.** Can an LLM monitor stop, in time, the dangerous or off-task actions of an agent tested on the real internet? The proposed framework: "agent actions are audited by a context-sensitive monitor".
**The method and its controls.** Data: 1,965 AutoGPT outputs (422 attempts, 29 tasks), labeled safe after inspecting 100; the authors hand-write 30 dangerous outputs (harm to confidentiality, integrity or availability) and 27 off-task ones, which replace 30% of the outputs; 30% of the attempts are used for tuning, 70% for evaluation. Monitor: gpt-3.5-turbo-16k-0613, a programmatic filter then a parameterized prompt (task, previous action, file, examples, whitelist) and a threshold chosen on training (68). Control: ablation of each parameter; accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC curve.
**The result, in numbers.** On the test set, "we see an F_{1} score of 89.4%, with a precision of 82.1% and a recall of 98.3%"; AUC 0.982. Removing the previous action costs the most (F1 86.8%, precision 77.4%); removing the few-shot examples lowers recall (93.4%) and raises precision (90.9%); several ablations improve both, a sign of tuning to be redone according to the authors.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These scores are measured against 30 dangerous and 27 off-task outputs written by hand, with no red team optimizing against the monitor; yet a safety number depends on the red team's strength (course, Part 10, no. 24; course, Part 7, F·24). Workaround: say which red team the number assumes, at least one optimized component by component (course, Part 7, F·24), and calibrate the threshold at 1% false positives on paired benign variants (course, Part 7, F·23).

**What they leave open.** "the distinction between off-task and unsafe model outputs is crucial" and remains their main objective; "the space of LMA attacks is vast, we do not even attempt to fully cover it in this early work"; the examples provided "failed to cover the full range of possible attacks"; and "the extent to which our approach is robust to model capability improvements remains an open question".
**Why the page cites it.** §6a Behavioral monitoring: "to use an auxiliary AI system (the monitor) to screen the inputs and outputs of another untrusted AI system (the actor)". Partial match: the monitor does filter an agent's outputs, but the agent is not trying to deceive it; the "adversarial simulated agent" of the abstract boils down to hand-written outputs.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 4: the monitor judges each action in isolation, and the context of the previous action is its most useful parameter (without it, F1 86.8%) — a modest hint in favor of monitoring that looks at more than one step.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9's description ("testing agents safely in the wild") holds.

Distant match: monitoring by the deployer and the providers, for accountability and regulation, and not an AI monitor facing an actor that would try to get around it.

### Hidden in Plain Text: Emergence & Mitigation of Steganographic Collusion in LLMs — Yohan Mathew, Ollie Matthews, Robert McCarthy et al. (LASR Labs, University College London, University of Amsterdam, University of Oxford), 2025; arXiv 2410.03768v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Can steganographic collusion between LLMs emerge without being requested, under a misspecified reward and an overseer, and do the usual countermeasures hold up against optimized colluders? Thesis: "unintended steganographic collusion in LLMs can arise due to mispecified reward incentives during training".
**The method and its controls.** Sender and receiver against an overseer and an optional paraphraser. Two optimizers: GBRL (Gemma-2-2B-it sender via PPO, DistilBERT receiver) and ICRL (Claude-3.5 Sonnet). Emergence: sorting of cover letters biased by university or gender (18,000 training examples, 2,000 test), with a ceiling without the sensitive variable of 50% or 67%; control: a DistilBERT on redacted letters stays at that ceiling (0.51, 0.50, 0.72). Countermeasures tested on AQuA-RAT and HumanEval against a GPT-3.5 Turbo mitigation calibrated on honest episodes. 5 ICRL seeds, 3 GBRL.
**The result, in numbers.** Emergence: task success 0.97 to 1.00 versus a clean ceiling of 0.50, overseer bypassed at 0.97 to 1.00, paraphraser included; with GPT-4o, 0.58, "not more than random chance". Countermeasures: on AQuA-RAT, "the collusion team is able to maintain a decoding success of at least 90% on 1-bit payloads"; on HumanEval, over 99% at 1 bit. And "oversight is not always effective at preventing collusion, but can in-fact encourage collusion that is more subtle".
**What they leave open.** A sorting setting that "only captures the core structure of the problem"; an overseer that is sometimes fragile; limited models; an ICRL pipeline tuned on Claude; a centralized learner that "may not perfectly simulate realistic optimization pressures". Lead: "White-box detection strategies".
**Why the page cites it.** §6a, last direction: "or the ability to pass messages between instances". Direct match; nuance: in GBRL the receiver is a DistilBERT classifier, not another instance of the same model.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 4: in the program's very setting, messages between agents under monitoring, a weaker output overseer plus a paraphrase are not enough against optimized collusion; the authors point to white-box detection.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* White-box detection is only a lead here, untested; and the paper already observes that oversight can encourage subtler collusion: iterating against your detectors selects for evasion (course, Part 10, no. 26; reading sheet 19). Workaround: sealed detectors, outside the training loop — if they keep firing when the in-loop ones go quiet, evasion has been selected (reading sheet 19) — and, for a white-box probe, its known case first (handover, §5.2).

**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9's description ("steganography/collusion between models") holds; the text read lifts the "to be checked" caveat.

### Coup probes: Catching catastrophes with probes trained off-policy — Fabien Roger (Redwood Research, per the text), 2023; https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/WCj7WgFSLmyKaMwPR/coup-probes-catching-catastrophes-with-probes-trained-off
**The hypothesis tested.** Can a probe trained on off-policy examples, written by humans, flag when the model is "currently trying to do a catastrophic action"? The blog post only tests its generalization, in a toy setting.
**The method and its controls.** Theft advice instead of coups: 43 positive answers from Wizard Vicuna 30B Uncensored, negatives drawn from Alpaca. Logistic regression on the activations of Llama2-7B-Chat (layer 16); validation negatives from AlpacaEval (n=805); true positives at 1% false positives. Variations: format (without the question, as a story, bullet points, French), jailbreak of the LLM, jailbreak of both the LLM and the probe. Control: a linear classifier on BERT; a single-example trial.
**The result, in numbers.** The 46 unmodified validation points are all detected at 1% false positives. The probe "generalizes across all variations in format, as well as when jailbreaking the LLM"; the attack on the probe "only mildly succeeded"; the drop comes mostly from French. BERT: no true positive on 48 bullet-point examples and 32 in French. A single example is enough. The per-variation rates are only in charts absent from the text. The author puts at about 50% the chance of catching the first real attempt, with "p=10% that some of them are wrong".

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* This perfect recall concerns positives written by another model, in a toy, and the generalization shown goes from one format to another and under jailbreak: an in-distribution score proves nothing, what you measure is the gap with held-out families (course, Part 10, no. 27; reading sheets, part B, trap 1; reading sheet 7). Workaround: hold out whole families, never paraphrases, and formats up to multi-turn agentic (explanation of 2 October, §3; programme, part 3); validate on generations of the monitored model, labelled by their conduct and never by the probe (course, Part 6, §8; handover, §5.1 and §5.2); and first measure the probe on an organism in which you installed the intention yourself (handover, §5.2).

**What they leave open.** "the probe might just learn “that looks like a takeover attempt written by humans”, and there is no clear way to rule that out"; the setting excludes "hard auditing and diffuse failures".
**Why the page cites it.** §6b: "the shift from fixed datasets of synthetic data to data generated by the model itself" and "signs of life for activation monitoring". Good match, but the toy's positives come from another model; the model-generated side is only approached through jailbreaks.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 3: this is the source for off-policy probes; generalization is shown there only in a toy, not on real generations of the monitored model.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** Root: "catch coup attempts generated by the model" is false: no coup is tested ("Instead of studying coup attempts, we instead train probes to identify pairs of (instruction, answer) where the answer contains advice about how to commit theft"). Pack v1.3: "is currently trying to do a catastrophic action" is not verbatim (text: it’s); "and notes that they have received little empirical follow-up" and the name off-policy probes are absent from the blog post.
