### Improving Alignment and Robustness with Circuit Breakers — Andy Zou, Long Phan, Justin Wang et al. (Gray Swan AI, Carnegie Mellon University, Center for AI Safety), 2024; arXiv 2406.04313v4
**The hypothesis tested.** Rather than parrying specific attacks, can a model be made robust by acting on its internal representations, so as to interrupt harmful generation whatever the attack? Thesis: "circuit-breaking directly controls the representations that are responsible for harmful outputs in the first place".
**The method and its controls.** Representation Rerouting (RR): LoRA adapters make orthogonal, at layers 10 and 20, the representations of a set of synthetic harmful answers, while preserving those of a retain set. Models: Mistral-7B-Instruct-v2, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B, and function-calling agents (100 harmful requests). Baselines: the original refusal-trained models, an adversarially trained Mistral (R2D2), a safety prompt. Attacks: HarmBench, prefilling, embeddings, RepE; capabilities: MT-Bench and Open LLM. Comparison with a harmfulness probe (HP) that cuts off generation.
**The result, in numbers.** Average attack success rate: 76.7 → 9.8 (Mistral), 38.1 → 3.8 (Llama-3); MT-Bench 7.60 → 7.53 and 8.05 → 8.00, against 6.00 for the adversarial Mistral. Multimodal under PGD: 91.0 → 14.3; agents, forced calls: 82 → 14. HP probes (average): Mistral 80.6 → 19.0 (linear), 14.3 (MLP), 11.2 (RR); Llama-3 32.6 → 9.0, 6.8, 3.1. Caveat: they "are tested under a weaker adversarial setting, where the attacker lacks knowledge of the probe and does not directly optimize against it".
**What they leave open.** The method only targets attacks that seek to produce harmful content, not for instance a label change, and single-turn conversations; the study of probes and other reading methods is "left for future work", as is the unexplained multilingual gap.
**Why the page cites it.** §6b, link on life: "While there are signs of life for activation monitoring". Partial match: the main method controls representations rather than monitoring them; the sign of life for monitoring is the HP section.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 3, with an echo of Axis 2: the paper itself contrasts "RR is a representation control method whereas HP is a representation reading method"; reading does slightly worse than control there, against an attacker who does not optimize against the probe — a positive to cite with this caveat.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the VOLET9 description ("interrupt harmful representations during generation") holds.

### Mechanistic anomaly detection and ELK — Paul Christiano (Alignment Research Center), 2022; https://www.alignment.org/blog/mechanistic-anomaly-detection-and-elk/
**The hypothesis tested.** An agenda blog post, with no experiment: ARC proposes to solve ELK by finding the normal reason for a behavior on the training data (a mechanistic explanation) and flagging the inputs where it no longer applies: identifying "(the diamond remains in the vault) as the “normal” reason for the diamond to appear on camera".
**The method and its controls.** Conceptual reasoning about the diamond in the vault (tampered sensors, fake diamond). The anomaly concerns the way the model processes the input, not the input itself; the explanation would be formalized by heuristic arguments or by Redwood's causal scrubbing; a sub-explanation is deemed plausibly good if it covers at least 1−ε of the effect on training. Proposed empirical problems: detection of backdoor attacks, distinguishing natural mechanisms in an LM, toy instances of ELK. No model, no data, no baseline.
**The result, in numbers.** No measured result. The only numbers describe the agenda: formalizing heuristic arguments is "now about 1/3 of our research", and anomaly detection based on them "about 1/3 of ARC’s current research", centered on "backdoor attack detection in the special case where covariance-propagation accurately predicts the variance of a model on the training set".
**What they leave open.** "We don’t yet have an adequate notion of “explanation;”"; finding the explanations "seems quite difficult, and there’s a good chance that it won’t be possible (via this plan or any other)"; false positives: "our anomaly detection may work too well, and flag a novel creative solution by our AI"; shutting down the system on a flagged case may be inadequate at high stakes.
**Why the page cites it.** §6c Anomaly detection: "another unsupervised approach to monitoring is anomaly detection". Good match in principle; nuance: ARC distinguishes its approach from the detection of outlier inputs, whereas the page's example (highly out-of-distribution jailbreaks) rather belongs to the latter.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with Axis 4: the blog post deals neither with sequences nor with aggregation; it provides the distinction between input anomaly and mechanism anomaly, and names a cost, false positives on novel solutions.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 gives only the identifier.

### Eliciting Latent Knowledge from “Quirky” Language Models — Alex Mallen, Madeline Brumley, Julia Kharchenko, Nora Belrose (EleutherAI, University of Washington), 2024; arXiv 2312.01037v4
**The hypothesis tested.** Can one find in the activations "patterns […] that robustly track the true state of the world" when the model's output is systematically false, and on questions harder than those of training?
**The method and its controls.** 12 binary datasets, each with its measured difficulty; models fine-tuned (rank-8 LoRA) to answer correctly when Alice is in the prompt and with plausible errors when it is Bob: Pythia 410M to 12B, Llama-2 7B, Mistral 7B, i.e. 96 models. Seven linear probes (including LogR, LDA, diff-in-means, CCS, CRC) and a baseline of random probes. Detector: Mahalanobis on the probe outputs, fitted on Alice's easy ones. Appendix: causal interventions on 300 examples.
**The result, in numbers.** "The best probing method (logistic regression on contrast pairs) recovers 89% of the gap in AUROC […] and 75% for questions harder than those used to train the probe" (0.79 AUROC, ceiling 0.87). And "a mechanistic anomaly detection approach can flag untruthful behavior with 0.95 AUROC". CCS and CRC trained on all the data drop to 0.15 and 0.36 PGR.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These AUROCs come from organisms whose falsehood follows a name visible in the prompt: probe and detector may read how the organism was made rather than the intention, and a success on an organism bounds the instrument without proving it works on a natural case (course, Part 10, no. 30; course, Part 6, §8; handover, §5.2). Workaround, in part: two manufactures of the same behaviour, one of them held out, and an aware-but-honest organism as the control (course, Part 6, §8; course, Part 2, §A, K71); to conclude about the natural case, none known; say so.

**What they leave open.** A model could use only an untruthful mechanism, which diverges only where one cannot supervise; fine-tuning "likely overwrote some of the natural circuitry in the LM"; it remains to work "without any obvious indication in the prompt of whether the label is reliable".
**Why the page cites it.** §6c: "applying existing anomaly detection techniques to model latent activations might already be suitable for tasks like these"; §7d, among the uses of truth representations "to classify or control model generations". Good match; nuance: the unfaithfulness there comes from a visible name, Bob.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 2: at comparable transfer (PGR 0.68 and 0.69), the LogR and LDA directions are much less causal than diff-in-means, "dramatically more causally implicated in LM output", and the intervention remains "relatively small in the middle layers", where reading generalizes best.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** Imprecision: the year varies, "2023 (arXiv 2312.01037" in §6c and "Mallen et al. 2024" in §7d; the version read and the page say 2024. The description ("probes that recover the true knowledge") holds, but omits the anomaly detector, the reason for the citation in §6c.

### Specification gaming: the flip side of AI ingenuity — Victoria Krakovna, Jonathan Uesato, Vladimir Mikulik et al. (Google DeepMind), 2020; blog post https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/specification-gaming-the-flip-side-of-ai-ingenuity/
**The hypothesis tested.** No experiment: a survey blog post. Thesis: specification gaming, "a behaviour that satisfies the literal specification of an objective without achieving the intended outcome", comes from a misspecified task, not from a flaw of the algorithm, and will weigh more as RL progresses.
**The method and its controls.** A collection of examples drawn from other works and a typology of causes, one case each: reward shaping (Coast Runners), misdescribed outcome (flipped Lego block), reward learned from human feedback (grasping), simulator bugs, reward tampering (hypothetical cases). No baseline, no control, no measurement.
**The result, in numbers.** A single number: "we have collected around 60 examples so far". The case of the fooled human evaluator: "an agent performing a grasping task learned to fool the human evaluator by hovering between the camera and the object." The scale argument: "Even for a slight misspecification, a very good RL algorithm might be able to find an intricate solution that is quite different from the intended solution".
**What they leave open.** Three challenges: faithfully translating the task into a reward, avoiding false implicit assumptions, avoiding reward tampering; "specification gaming is far from solved", and between creative solution and gaming, "we don't have an objective way to distinguish between them."
**Why the page cites it.** §7a: "training against R might produce a model which systematically exploits errors in R" (link on "systematically"). Distant match: the blog post deals mostly with badly written rewards; a single example touches the error of a human evaluator, and nothing in it concerns a model that models R − R*.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with Axis 1: the blog post shows an agent exploiting a human evaluator's error without measuring that error, whereas the displacement you measured gives the measured model judge's error a measured form, with slope and fixed points.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 (root and pack v1.3 identical) gives only the name, "and DeepMind's *specification gaming*", without authors, year or content.

### Self-critiquing models for assisting human evaluators — William Saunders, Catherine Yeh, Jeff Wu et al. (OpenAI), 2022; arXiv 2206.05802v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Do critiques written by a model help humans find flaws they would miss, and does a model critique everything it is able to discriminate?
**The method and its controls.** Five GPT-3-style models fine-tuned by behavioral cloning on topic-based summarization ("over 6,000 distinct topical queries and summaries") and on its critiques; four synthetic tasks with an oracle. Assistance: a "no assist" condition against 8 model critiques, on model answers, human answers, and deliberately misleading human answers (six conditions). Control: the authors of the misleading answers provide the intended critique and judge validity. Baselines: InstructGPT zero/few-shot, direct refinement, best-of-8.
**The result, in numbers.** "about 50\% more critiques" with assistance; on the misleading answers, "labelers find the intended critiques 45\pm 5\% of the time, whereas without assistance they only find it 27\pm 5\% of the time", validity unchanged ("71\% with assistance versus 73\% without"). On the model's answers: "unassisted labelers found critiques on just 54% of inputs and gave an average rating of 5.6, while assisted labelers found critiques on 78% of inputs and gave an average rating of 4.9." But "we failed to find a clear trend showing critique performance catching up to discriminator performance"; in an appendix, a naive 2-step debate "wouldn’t work as well as RLHP for this task."

### Supervising strong learners by amplifying weak experts — Paul Christiano, Buck Shlegeris, Dario Amodei (OpenAI), 2018; arXiv 1810.08575v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Can one build a training signal for a task that no human knows how to judge, by combining solutions to simpler subproblems, without an external reward? Iterated Amplification: an expert H delegates subquestions to copies of the agent X, and X learns to imitate this composite system.
**The method and its controls.** "We study Iterated Amplification in a set of 5 toy algorithmic tasks" (permutations, assignments, wildcards, shortest path, union-find). The human is a hard-coded decomposition algorithm, imitated by a learned "human predictor"; X learns in a supervised way. Only baseline: supervised learning on the ground truth.
**The result, in numbers.** The tasks are learned almost as fast as by supervised learning on the ground truth, at worst with a modest slowdown, and amplification "requires about twice as much computation per question". The gain is for the expert: "Supervised learning required tens of millions of examples in order to learn these algorithms.", against "tens of thousands of examples" for the decompositions; from 6,000 to 24,000 oracle calls depending on the task (Table 2).
**What they leave open.** "These experiments don’t shed any light on whether humans can decompose interesting real world tasks,"; domains where an algorithmic signal exists. The key assumption, "a human can coordinate multiple copies of X", is only discussed: "We leave a convincing demonstration to future work,".
**Why the page cites it.** §7b Recursive oversight: "Task decomposition (Christiano et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021) aims to break down difficult tasks into subtasks". Direct match: founding paper of decomposition, on toy tasks where the human is simulated.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with Axis 4: amplification makes copies of the same model cooperate and counts as an asset, without testing it, that they have no incentives of their own ("We don’t need to manage incentives, politics, or conflicting preferences"), an assumption that the candidate's program does not make, since it aims at monitors that hold when the actor passes messages between instances.

### AI safety via debate — Geoffrey Irving, Paul Christiano, Dario Amodei (OpenAI), 2018; arXiv 1805.00899v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Can two agents trained by self-play in a zero-sum debate, judged by a human, provide honest information beyond what the judge verifies alone? Central claim: "In the debate game, it is harder to lie than to refute a lie."
**The method and its controls.** Mostly theoretical: with a polynomial-time judge, debate with a polynomial number of rounds reaches PSPACE (Theorem 1), direct judging NP. One experiment on MNIST: a convolutional judge trained in advance sees only 6 (or 4) nonzero pixels, revealed by two agents played by MCTS (10k rollouts per move), one honest, the other a liar, with or without precommitment. Control: the same judge on randomly drawn pixels. A human game (cat versus dog) played only informally.
**The result, in numbers.** "With 6 pixels, debate with precommit turns a 59.4% accurate judge into a 88.9% accurate debate"; "With 4 pixels, a 48.2% accurate judge becomes an 85.2% accurate debate." Without precommitment, the honest agent wins only 74.4% (6 pixels) and 59.7% (4 pixels): "precommit is crucial". Successful lies concentrate on the digits 8 and 9, a probable artifact of using only nonzero pixels.
**What they leave open.** "At this point debate is proposal only for the natural language case, and we have demonstrated only a basic experiment for MNIST images." Section 5: belief bias of the human judge, debates too long to follow, whether honesty is truly optimal, stability of equilibria, stochastic simulation; and "Debate does not address other safety concerns such as robustness to adversarial examples, distributional shift, or safe exploration."
**Why the page cites it.** §7b Recursive oversight: "Adversarial techniques such as debate (Irving et al., 2018; […] pit competing AI systems against each other." Direct match: founding paper; the honest equilibrium remains there a hoped-for consequence of the central claim, not demonstrated with human judges.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with Axis 1: everything rests on a good enough judge, and the paper names the human judge's bias as the first concern without measuring it, whereas the displacement you measured is a systematic error of the measured model judge, with slope and fixed points.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 (root and pack v1.3) gives only the name and year, "debate (Irving 2018;", which hold.

### Debate Helps Supervise Unreliable Experts — Julian Michael, Salsabila Mahdi, David Rein et al. (New York University; Cohere; Anthropic, PBC), 2023; arXiv 2311.08702v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Does a debate between two unreliable experts (they know the truth but may lie) help a non-expert judge find the right answer better than a single expert?
**The method and its controls.** Hard reading questions (QuALITY-hard, science fiction from Project Gutenberg): the judge does not read the text, seeing only the arguments and certified quotes; two answers, one true, one false. Named baseline: "consultancy", a single expert who defends the right answer half the time. Human debaters (19 participants, including 12 from the NYU debate club) or GPT-4; judges always human, scored by a proper scoring rule. 413 debates and consultancies. Controls: mixed-effects model on judge identity, manual error analysis.
**The result, in numbers.** "Human debate reaches an accuracy of 84%, compared with 74% for human consultancy" (p = 0.04; 0.0487 after controlling for the judge). With GPT-4: debate 78%, consultancy 80%, no difference detected. Dishonest human consultants mislead the judge 40% of the time; debates are 68% of the length of consultancies. 46% of debate errors come from the honest debater missing a piece of evidence; 52% of consultancy errors, from a consultant hiding the evidence. Judges overconfident between 90% and 100%.
**What they leave open.** "Our experiments only address a proxy for the broader question": short fiction stories, judges without prior opinion, expertise gap reduced to access to the text, uncontrolled collection across conditions; and "our high judge accuracy may have resulted in part due to mistakes by the dishonest debater".
**Why the page cites it.** §7b Recursive oversight: "Adversarial techniques such as debate (Irving et al., 2018; Michael et al., 2023 […] pit competing AI systems against each other". Partial match: the positive result comes from human debaters; with AI debaters, no advantage.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with Axis 1: the paper makes the human judge a source of error in its own right ("Misled by intuition" in 29.2% of wrongly judged debates, overconfidence above 90%), without measuring a quantified shift of its score under framing.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the VOLET9 description ("debate helps human judges") holds; only specify that the effect appears only with human debaters (GPT-4: 78% vs 80%).

### On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs — Zachary Kenton, Noah Y. Siegel, János Kramár et al. (Google DeepMind), 2024; arXiv 2407.04622v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Do LLM judges weaker than the agents being judged decide more accurately with a debate than with a consultant or alone, beyond the information asymmetry studied so far?
**The method and its controls.** 9 tasks of 128 questions: extractive (QuALITY, BoolQ, GPQA-extractive; article hidden from the judge), closed (MMLU, GSM8KQA, PrOntoQA, TruthfulQA, GPQA), multimodal (MMMU). Judges: Gemma7B, GPT-3.5, Gemini Pro 1.0 and Pro 1.5; debaters and consultants: Pro 1.5. Named baselines: "QA without article" and "QA with article". "Open" variants where the agent chooses its answer; permutation tests, ablations, Elo. All at inference time.
**The result, in numbers.** "We find that debate consistently outperforms consultancy across all tasks". Against direct QA, it depends: in extractive tasks, debate beats QA without article but not QA with article; in closed tasks, GPT-3.5 gains from it (p=0.037), Pro 1.0 not significant (p=0.1), Pro 1.5 (judge equal to the debaters) does worse. In open consultancy, the judge is convinced just as much whether the consultant is right or wrong; in open debate, it spots the protagonist who is wrong much better. Stronger debaters help the judge, "though more modestly than in previous studies". Of 12 PrOntoQA failures, 11 come from logical errors by the judge.
**What they leave open.** "Strong positive evidence favouring debate would be that it is significantly stronger than the QA without article baseline […] and we see neither." At inference only, they "don’t give us much evidence about their effectiveness as scalable oversight training protocols"; debaters trained for honesty by RLHF; no human judge.
**Why the page cites it.** §7b Recursive oversight: "Adversarial techniques such as debate (Irving et al., 2018; Michael et al., 2023; Khan et al., 2024; Kenton et al., 2024)". The equilibrium targeted by the next sentence is not tested: no training.

### Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility of LLM outputs — Jan Hendrik Kirchner, Yining Chen, Harri Edwards et al. (OpenAI), 2024; arXiv 2407.13692v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Does training a large model to produce solutions verifiable by a small verifier, rather than for correctness alone, keep its chains of thought legible, including for humans in a hurry?
**The method and its controls.** Grade-school mathematics (augmented GSM); provers and verifiers from the GPT-4 family, the verifier having from 10^{-4} to 10^{0} times the prover's compute (10^{-3} in the main experiment). In rounds, the verifier learns correctness, then a "helpful" or "sneaky" prover learns by PPO to convince it while being correct, or wrong. Named baseline: direct optimization of correctness; variants CGC and "iterative goodharting". Evaluations: separate sneaky attacks, best-of-n, 75 humans limited to 45 seconds per solution.
**The result, in numbers.** "optimizing chain-of-thought solutions only for answer correctness can make them less legible". The verifier becomes more robust over the rounds: at relative size 10^{-2}, no attack finds an exploit after round 0 (8k RL steps); at 10^{-3}, up to round 4. For humans, "the helpful prover matches the legibility of the initialization while achieving substantially stronger performance", but remains below the prover optimized for correctness alone (a "legibility tax"). The sneaky solutions become more subtle (pilot campaign acknowledged as flawed). Too small (10^{-4}) or the size of the prover, the verifier makes training fail.
**What they leave open.** "We conducted our empirical study on only one dataset (GSM)." Ground-truth answers are needed; making the chain of thought itself legible may constrain performance; hyperparameters little tuned.
**Why the page cites it.** §7b Recursive oversight: "and prover-verifier games (Kirchner et al., 2024) pit competing AI systems against each other". Their Theorem 1 gives an idealized form to the page's hope of equilibrium; but the verifier learns from truth labels, not from an imperfect signal R.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with Axis 3: Appendix C shows that a verifier trained against an attacker can learn its style rather than the error (ROC AUC close to 1 between helpful and sneaky in the first round), the very risk of a monitor trained on fabricated examples.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Against this risk of a monitor that learns the attacker's style rather than the error, the workaround: a surface-only classifier must stay at chance between the two sides of the examples, and negatives are also drawn from the model's real generations, not only from fabricated examples (course, Part M, M4; course, Part 2, §C).

**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the VOLET9 description ("for legibility by a weak verifier") holds.

### Weak-to-Strong Reasoning — Yuqing Yang, Yan Ma, Pengfei Liu (Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Fudan University; Shanghai AI Laboratory, GAIR), 2024; arXiv 2407.13647v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Does weak-to-strong generalization, shown by Burns et al. in classification, chess and reward models, hold for complex reasoning, and can the strong model be prevented from imitating the weak one's errors without ground truth or a stronger model?
**The method and its controls.** Strong: Llama2-70b; weak: Llama2-7b, Gemma-2b, Mistral-7b, fine-tuned on one half of the data with solutions; the strong model sees only the questions of the other half. GSM8K (7,000 questions; 1,319 in test) and MATH (6,000; 500 in test). Stage I: keep the examples where the weak model's answer and that of the strong model under in-context learning coincide ("final answer consistency"), then SFT. Stage II: DPO or ORPO on pairs built from the model's confidence. Named baselines: "weak floor", "full weak fine-tuning", weak ICL; ceiling: "strong ceiling" (SFT on the gold solutions). Prospective test: Llama3-8b-instruct supervises Llama3-70b on OlympicArena (6,020 questions without answers, 313 in test).
**The result, in numbers.** Supervised by Gemma-2b (25.17 on GSM8K), the strong model rises "up to 60.12, surpassing naive full weak fine-tuning by 31.08"; Stage II adds 8.49 points (DPO). On MATH, full weak fine-tuning does worse than the weak model itself (10.0 against 11.6); DPO degrades there (-2.00, -2.60, -1.40), ORPO gains from 1.00 to 2.20 points. At MATH levels 4-5, the final model (with ORPO) exceeds the strong ceiling. On OlympicArena: weak 11.82, full weak FT 12.46, full method 15.65.
**What they leave open.** 70b models serve as substitutes for future superhuman models; "this paper does not explore supervision at the process level" (noise in the steps gave only limited gains); choosing good demonstrations without ground truth "is beyond the scope of this paper".
**Why the page cites it.** §7c Weak-to-strong / easy-to-hard: "Weak-to-strong generalization (Burns et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024)." The setup follows the page's definition (weak supervisor, evaluation against gold answers held apart); process supervision, which the page asks to explore, is explicitly outside the paper.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with Axis 1: the paper treats the weak supervisor's errors as noise to be filtered out by agreement between two sources, without modeling them; a systematic error with known slope, of the type P1 describes, is not tested there.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 gives only the identifier.

### Evaluating Superhuman Models with Consistency Checks — Lukas Fluri, Daniel Paleka, Florian Tramèr (ETH Zurich), 2023; arXiv 2306.09983v3
**The hypothesis tested.** When the correctness of a (possibly superhuman) model's decisions cannot be verified, can errors in them be proven through logical rules that a human can verify?
**The method and its controls.** Framework: if inputs satisfy P, their truths satisfy Q; a violation proves an error. Chess: Leela Chess Zero and Stockfish on 400k real positions and 200k synthetic ones, plus a genetic adversarial search. Forecasting: GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 on 380 questions (negation, paraphrase, monotonicity, Bayes' rule). Law: a legal BERT on 500 ECHR cases; bail by GPT-3.5-turbo for 1560 defendants, with counterfactuals. Named control: asking the same question again word for word.
**The result, in numbers.** A rotation or a mirror changes Leela's winning chances "by up to 69%"; multiplying the search by 8 reduces failures only by a factor of 3 to 6.6; the adversarial search finds up to 9 times more. Strong violations (> 0.2) by GPT-4: negation 10.9%, paraphrase 12.5%, monotonicity 16.0%, Bayes 58.8% (GPT-3.5-turbo worse everywhere); chance explains less than 20% of them. Paraphrasing the fact judged most important flips 50% of negative decisions; bail: 78 violations out of 1560. Targeting negation by prompt does not help paraphrase: "improving consistency on one check does not necessarily improve consistency in general".
**What they leave open.** Efficiency (rare bugs), soundness of automatic paraphrases, performative predictions, and "finding nothing does not mean an absence of bugs!"
**Why the page cites it.** §7c Weak-to-strong / easy-to-hard: "such as regularizing the learner to be self-consistent (Burns et al., 2022; Furi et al., 2023)". Distant match: the paper tests already-trained models, without regularizing any learner; its section 6.4 only uses a prompt, "a simple proxy for training models to be more consistent".
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 1: if social framing does not change the judged answer, the shift in the judge's score is a consistency violation in the paper's sense; its repetition control bounds the share due to chance.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** Two (root and pack v1.3 identical). "Furi et al. 2023, arXiv 2306.09983": the first author is Lukas Fluri (typo inherited from the page). And the box "unsupervised regularization by consistency" does not hold: it is an inference-time evaluation, without training.

### Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization — Leo Gao, John Schulman, Jacob Hilton (OpenAI), 2022; arXiv 2210.10760v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Measuring Goodhart's law in RLHF: how the true score evolves when optimizing against an imperfect reward model (RM), depending on the RM's size, its data, the policy and the KL penalty.
**The method and its controls.** Synthetic setup (InstructGPT environment): a 6B "gold" RM plays the humans and labels 100,000 comparisons that train proxy RMs from 3M to 3B parameters; policy of 1.2B (and 6B). Two optimizations: best-of-n and RL by PPO. Sweeps: RM size, data size, policy size, KL penalty. The best-of-n functional form, chosen on data up to n=1,000, is validated in prediction up to n=60,000.
**The result, in numbers.** With d the square root of the KL, best-of-n: R(d) = d(α − βd); RL: R(d) = d(α − β log d) — the true score rises then falls again, and "its coefficients scale smoothly with the number of reward model parameters". Below about 2,000 comparisons, the RMs stay close to chance. A larger policy gains less from optimization but does not over-optimize more. RL consumes far more KL than best-of-n. "The KL penalty only causes the gold RM score to converge earlier": it acts as early stopping. In iterated RLHF (k iterations), under simplifying assumptions, the predicted gain equals β_RL·d·log(k).
**What they leave open.** "The main limitation of this work is that this additional source of overoptimization is not captured in the setting of this paper": the gap between the labels and actual human intent. Adversarial Goodhart is not captured either ("the scaling laws observed in this paper may break down"); synthetic setting still to be validated; only two policy sizes.
**Why the page cites it.** §7c Weak-to-strong / easy-to-hard, among the desired benchmarks: "such as using models of varying scales as overseers". Good match for the benchmark (proxy RMs from 3M to 3B measured against a reference RM); but the paper studies over-optimization, not weak-to-strong generalization.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Link with axis 1: it is the canonical benchmark where R* is known (the gold RM) and where the gap R − R* is measured as a function of optimization; it explicitly excludes the error between labels and human intent, the type of judge error that P1 measures.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the description in VOLET9 ("benchmarks with overseers of varied sizes (Gao et al. 2022, arXiv 2210.10760") holds; title, first author and year are correct.

**The hypothesis tested.** Does a pretrained model fine-tuned only on easy data do almost as well, on hard data, as a model fine-tuned on hard data — and is it sometimes better to collect easy data?

Four datasets (ARC, MMLU-STEM-5, StrategyQA, GSM8k), six human measures of difficulty and one model-based (MDL). Control: trivial prompts in the right format are not enough.
**The result, in numbers.** "the Supervision Gap Recovered is usually between 70% and 100%"; in ICL on hard data, from 0.72 ± 0.93 (StrategyQA, p = 0.0788) to 1.00 ± 0.20 (ARC, Bloom Skill); "SGR is near 100% for model sizes between 7b and 70b". Noise (MMLU, linear probe): "easy data is preferable when its labeling error rate is 10% (or higher), meaning the error rate for hard data is 20% (or higher)". But "SGR falls from 74% to 57% when fitting to 8th grade vs. 3rd grade questions using ICL".
**What they leave open.** The results may not hold elsewhere, "especially test settings where almost no amount of human effort can reliably produce accurate data labels (like unsolved scientific questions)"; contamination: "we cannot be certain that models are generalizing from easy to hard data, rather than reporting memorized hard question answers".

### Balancing Label Quantity and Quality for Scalable Elicitation — Alex Mallen, Nora Belrose (EleutherAI), 2024; arXiv 2410.13215v2
**The hypothesis tested.** At a fixed labeling budget, should one buy many weak labels, few quality labels, or a mix? The framework: "eliciting capabilities from pretrained models subject to labeling cost constraints".
**The method and its controls.** Binary classification on seven tasks taken from Burns et al. (2023) (BoolQ, HellaSwag, SciQ…). Weak labels from Qwen-1.5 0.5B; strong model Llama-3 8B; a quality label costs $1, a weak one from $0.50 to $0.01. Methods: sequential SFT (weak then quality), few-shot ICL, 2-shot-prompted sequential SFT, uncertainty sampling, log-confidence loss; balanced held-out test set, 3 seeds. Scale: MMLU with Llama-3 8B, 70B and GPT-4o-mini.
**The result, in numbers.** Weak labels at $0.10: "quantity-dominant" regime up to $64, "mixed" around $256-$512, "quality-dominant" from $1024. Table 1: 2-shot-prompted sequential SFT reaches 75 ± 2 at $65 (sequential SFT: 70 ± 2) and 84 ± 1 at $1025; few-shot ICL plateaus at 58 ± 5 but wins at minimal budgets. Abstract: "up to 5 percentage points at a fixed labeling budget by adding a few-shot prompt". The log-confidence loss "is not particularly effective"; GPT-4o-mini reaches 0.92 from as few as 10 examples.
**What they leave open.** "Our work is limited to binary classification tasks."; "it is unclear how analogous our settings are to practical settings that challenge human experts"; no measurement of highly reliable knowledge (> 99%); other avenues, "such as easy-to-hard and domain generalization".
**Why the page cites it.** Link on "trade off against", in "How does supervising with high-quality data on unrepresentative tasks […] supervising with low-quality data on representative tasks?". Distant match: weak and quality labels here bear on the same tasks; the paper arbitrates quantity against quality, not representativeness.

## Scalable oversight › Honesty

### Eliciting latent knowledge: How to tell if your eyes deceive you — Paul Christiano, Ajeya Cotra, Mark Xu (Alignment Research Center; Ajeya Cotra: Open Philanthropy), 2021; https://docs.google.com/document/d/1WwsnJQstPq91_Yh-Ch2XRL8H_EpsnjrC1dwZXR37PC8
**The hypothesis tested.** Theoretical report: is there, in the worst case, a training strategy that makes a predictive model report what it knows (for example that a camera has been tampered with) when the human cannot see it? "How can we train this model to report its latent knowledge of off-screen events?"
**The method and its controls.** No experiment: a game between a "builder", who proposes a strategy, and a "breaker", who constructs a counterexample (SmartVault toy; predictor and human as distinct Bayes nets; Game of Life in the appendix). Baseline: train a "reporter" on easy questions where the human is sure. Two reporters have the same loss there: the "direct translator" and the "human simulator", which answers what a human would believe. Then richer data (including imitative generalization) and regularizers (complexity, computation time, specificity, consistency across inputs) are examined.
**The result, in numbers.** No measurement. Finding: "even if the human never makes a mistake, then these two reporters have identical behavior on the training set, so they have identical loss", and with errors "the learning process would prefer the human simulator (which correctly copies the mistake)". Each strategy has its counterexample, up to ontology identification: "although none of them work in the worst case". The only number, a credence: "Paul would give perhaps a 50% chance that it’s possible to solve ELK in the worst case".
**What they leave open.** Ontology identification ("50% or 5% of the remaining difficulty of ELK"); learned optimizers, where their practical approaches "would almost certainly break down"; consistency "reasons", the preferred approach, of which "it’s unfortunately pretty vague".
**Why the page cites it.** Link "leveraging the model’s own knowledge" (subsection "Honesty"). The report poses this problem and says why naive training can fail; it does not show that a structure of honest answers exists.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Conceptual link (axis 3): a reporter trained on human labels can learn the "human simulator", identical during training and wrong as soon as the human can no longer decide — the in-principle form of the risk of a monitor that does not hold out-of-distribution.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 only flags the link, under "read from the model's own knowledge rather than compared to our signal", a paraphrase of the page that holds for this report.

### The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It’s Lying — Amos Azaria, Tom Mitchell (Ariel University; Carnegie Mellon University), 2023; arXiv 2304.13734v2
**The hypothesis tested.** "we hypothesize that the truth or falsehood of a statement should be represented by, and therefore extractable from, the LLM’s internal state" — including for its own statements.
**The method and its controls.** SAPLMA: a small feedforward network on the activations of one layer of OPT-6.7b or LLAMA2-7b. True-false dataset of 6,084 statements on six topics; training on five topics, test on the sixth. Baselines: BERT (same classifier), 3-shot and 5-shot, "It-is-true" (normalized probabilities). Control: permuted labels, 62.5% training accuracy versus 86.4%. Transfer: 245 statements generated by OPT-6.7b, labeled by three judges.
**The result, in numbers.** Average over held-out topics: 0.7098 (OPT-6.7b, 20th-layer) and 0.8298 (LLAMA2-7b, 16th-layer), versus 0.5434 (BERT) and 0.5374 (3-shot). On the generated statements, at best 0.6362 (28th-layer, AUC 0.7614) at threshold 0.5, and 0.7134 with a threshold set on 30% of the statements; the baselines stay near 50%, and SAPLMA "classified approximately 70% of the sentences as true".
**What they leave open.** Distinguishing true/false rather than "positive" or "unsure" would require calibration; activations are taken sentence by sentence, whereas in a long answer "the activation values develop over time". The drop on the generated statements may be due to the fact that "the sentences generated by the LLM where much more open, and their truth value may be less clearly defined".
**Why the page cites it.** In "There has been substantial prior work on identifying language model representations of truth" (subsection "Honesty"). The page targets situations where models "have learned to give non-truthful answers"; here, "lying" designates ordinary false statements, not a model trained to lie.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Direct link (axis 3): a probe trained on fixed statements loses accuracy on 245 statements generated by the model itself — a first, small measurement of the fixed data → model generations shift that the page names.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These truth probes are validated on ordinary false statements, not on a model that lies: as a lie detector, they lack the known case, and on honesty truth probes have already done worse than a plain prompt (course, Part 10, no. 51; handover, §5.2; course, Part 7, F·62). Workaround: measure sensitivity and false alarms on an organism in which you installed the intention to deceive yourself (handover, §5.2), and beat a prompt at equal cost, reporting recall at 1% false positives (course, Part 5, topic 1; course, Part 7, F·50; course, Part 7, F·29).

**Errors in the first version, if any.** Root: "a classifier on activations predicts the truth of statements" holds. Pack v1.3 (read): "71-83% true/false accuracy" and "~20 points above zero-shot" hold; "0.64 on the statements generated by the model itself — the reading/generation gap is already there" is imprecise: 0.6362 is the best case at threshold 0.5 on OPT-6.7b alone, 0.7134 with a recalibrated threshold, and the authors attribute part of the gap to the vagueness of the generated statements.

**The hypothesis tested.** That a "top-down" transparency, centered on representations rather than on neurons and circuits, makes it possible to read and then control high-level concepts (truth, honesty, utility, power, emotions, harmfulness) with simple, mostly unsupervised methods.

On utility, "the direction found by logistic regression yields the highest accuracy, yet it elicits little to no alteration in model behavior when strengthened or suppressed—it only identifies neural correlates".

**The hypothesis tested.** That a steering vector — the mean of the differences in residual stream activations between positive and negative pairs of a behavior — modulates alignment-related behaviors in an RLHF model, on top of the system prompt and fine-tuning, at a low cost in capabilities, and carries over from multiple-choice to free text.
**The method and its controls.** A/B pairs differing only by the answer letter; seven behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal), 290 to 1000 pairs and 50 test questions each. **The result, in numbers.** Optimal layer 13 for the 7B, "usually 14 or 15" for the 13B; the vector shifts the behavior in all seven categories (GPT-4 scores). In multiple-choice for the 13B (−1/0/+1): Corrigibility 0.45 / 0.57 / 0.83, but Sycophancy 0.56 / 0.63 / 0.60. Compared with fine-tuning, "for 3 out of 7 tested behaviors, CAA can additionally steer the behavior beyond the effects of finetuning alone"; sycophancy fine-tuning does not carry over to free text, "whereas CAA generalizes in all cases". MMLU: 0.63 without steering, 0.57 to 0.65 with. Subtracting the sycophancy vector improves TruthfulQA by 0.02 for the 13B.

Workaround: a dose-response curve against several controls (course, Part 2, §C, K47) and a sealed judge with a human audit of about 200 stratified items (programme, part 3); against the polarity artefact, pairs that differ only in the trait, checked by a classifier that reads only the surface, a polarity direction built as a rival concept, at the same place and at matched degradation, and the no-pressure control arm (course, Part M, M4).

**What they leave open.** "we do not optimize supervised finetuning hyperparameters"; "It is possible that better steering effects could be achieved via prompting alone"; without per-layer normalization, "this could skew our result for layer optimality".

### Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model — Kenneth Li, Oam Patel, Fernanda Viégas et al. (Harvard University), 2024; arXiv 2306.03341v6
**The hypothesis tested.** That an LLM "“knows” the correct answer" without producing it — a gap between the accuracy of a probe on its activations and that of its generation — and that this gap can be closed by shifting, at inference, the activations of a few attention heads along "truth-correlated directions".
**The method and its controls.** TruthfulQA (817 questions, 5,918 labeled question-answer pairs); one linear probe per head; shift on the K=48 best heads, 2-fold cross-validation. Metrics: true*informative (GPT-judge, checked by human annotation), MC, KL. Baselines: supervised fine-tuning, few-shot, instruction-tuned models (Alpaca, Vicuna); directions compared: random, CCS, probe weights, mass mean shift. LLaMA-7B; transfer to Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU.
**The result, in numbers.** "we observe a full 40\% difference between probe accuracy and generation accuracy". Best head: 83.3% in validation. True*info: Alpaca 32.5 → 65.1, Vicuna 51.5 → 74.0; LLaMA-7B (5% of the data) 30.5 → 43.5, versus 36.1 for fine-tuning and 49.5 for few-shot. By direction: random 31.2, CCS 33.4, probe weights 34.8, mass mean shift 42.3. Out-of-distribution: Natural Questions 46.6 → 51.3, TriviaQA 89.6 → 91.1, MMLU 35.71 → 40.16. The price: a KL that rises (0.40 to 1.41) and more "I have no comment" answers.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The random direction is only the specificity null here, and the measured price — a rising KL, more "I have no comment" — is damage; the sheet does not say the directions were compared at matched degradation, so "acts more" may mean "damages more" (course, Part 10, no. 55; course, Part M, M4). Workaround: plot each direction's effect against measured damage, KL included, and keep only the one whose curve runs above the controls at every level of damage (course, Part 2, §C, K47; programme, part 7).

**What they leave open.** "The most important would be to understand how well ITI generalizes to other datasets, ideally in a more real-world chat setting." Also the truthfulness/helpfulness tension; and "We do not claim that ITI by itself is anywhere near sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs."
**Why the page cites it.** §7d Honesty: link "Li et al., 2023", in "using them to classify or control model generations". It matches; the non-truthfulness studied is that of TruthfulQA's misconceptions, not a model trained to lie.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 2: ITI already measures that the probe direction acts less than the difference of means (34.8 versus 42.3) and concludes that "the direction most correlated with truth might well be not causal for truthful text generation" — the very form of *reading is not controlling*.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the VOLET9 description (root and pack v1.3), "ITI (Li 2023 — F·7)", holds.

### Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness? — Kevin Liu, Stephen Casper, Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Jacob Andreas (MIT CSAIL), 2023; arXiv 2312.03729v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Since probes are more accurate than outputs, some have concluded that models lie. The authors ask whether this query/probe disagreement arises in other ways, and sort it into three classes: "confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity".
**The method and its controls.** GPT2-XL and GPT-J; BoolQ, SciQ and CREAK as binary questions. Query: probability of the answer; probe: logistic regression on the last hidden state. Measures: accuracy, calibration, joint predictions in nine categories; a probe+query ensemble tuned on 500 validation examples. Contextualizations: fine-tuned GPT2-XL, sparse probes. A single prompt template.
**The result, in numbers.** Query versus probe (GPT-2 / GPT-J): BoolQ 61.8 / 61.8 versus 62.9 / 62.5; SciQ 76.1 / 84.1 versus 78.8 / 88.6; CREAK 51.1 / 50.4 versus 63.5 / 71.0; the ensemble does better in 4 cases out of 6. "In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers." "Only in CREAK do we observe a significant number of instances of “deception”; however, we also observe many instances of probe errors." The fine-tuned GPT2-XL beats the probe by 6.9% (SciQ) and 4.0% (CREAK).
**What they leave open.** "These specific findings may thus not predict the distribution of disagreements in future datasets." Other prompts could "substantially alter the distribution of disagreements"; linear probes only, whereas "some information must be encoded non-linearly in model representations".
**Why the page cites it.** §7d Honesty: link on "circumstances under which", in "studies the circumstances under which these techniques are useful". It does study when a probe wins, but on two pretrained models (GPT2-XL, GPT-J), neither of which was trained not to tell the truth.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 3: for a probe-based lie detector, a probe > output gap is not in itself a lie — here it comes mostly from calibration and heterogeneity.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** Root: "with the link Farquhar et al. 2023 (arXiv 2312.03729", summary "CCS and co. often find **another salient feature** than truth". False: authors (Liu, Casper, Hadfield-Menell, Andreas, MIT CSAIL), title and content — no CCS, but supervised probes against queries. Pack v1.3: "with a link (arXiv 2312.03729, to be checked" — false attribution removed; the "to be checked" is lifted by this sheet.

## Adversarial robustness

### Persistent Pre-training Poisoning of LLMs — Yiming Zhang, Javier Rando, Ivan Evtimov et al. (Carnegie Mellon University, Meta, ETH Zurich, Google DeepMind), 2024; arXiv 2410.13722v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Can a model be compromised by poisoning a small fraction of its pretraining, and does the effect survive alignment (SFT then DPO)?
**The method and its controls.** OLMo models from 604M to 7B trained from scratch on 100 billion tokens (about 5% of a full training run), then SFT and DPO. Poisoning budget 0.1%, documents placed at random. Four attacks: denial of service (gibberish), context extraction (compared to a manual attack), jailbreak (JailbreakBench), belief manipulation (50 product pairs, 50 factual pairs). Control: the same models, unpoisoned. Minimal threshold tested down to 0.0001%.
**The result, in numbers.** "Our main result is that poisoning only 0.1\% of a model’s pre-training dataset is sufficient for three out of four attacks to measurably persist through post-training." Denial of service: gibberish "for up to 100\% of prompts" with the trigger, nothing visible without it. Extraction: beyond 1B, the poisoned models leak more than the clean ones under manual attack. Jailbreak: "conventional safety fine-tuning overwrites the backdoor". Belief: "a consistent bias towards the adversarially boosted target", quantified in a figure only. Denial of service persists from 0.001%. Through Wikipedia alone, up to 0.27% of the data could be poisoned.
**What they leave open.** The jailbreak, "leaving this question open for future research"; size, with no clear pattern, "possibly due to the models not being fully trained"; scale, "it remains an approximation as the models are trained to 5% of the full OLMo pre-training run"; filtering, and the defense against belief manipulation.
**Why the page cites it.** §8 Adversarial robustness: link on "poisoning pretraining corpora", in "other attack types are possible such as poisoning pretraining corpora". Direct match.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link (axis 4): a bias without a trigger, with "an insidious effect on all model users", and a backdoor indistinguishable without its trigger escape behavioral testing; the paper tests no monitor.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** VOLET9 (root and pack v1.3): "(Souly et al. 2024, arXiv 2410.13722 —", "to be checked". Wrong on the authors: Zhang, Rando, Evtimov, Chi, Smith, Carlini, Tramèr, Ippolito (CMU, Meta, ETH Zurich, Google DeepMind); the page uses "Souly" for another link (arXiv 2402.10260). Title and year hold.

**The hypothesis tested.** Measure the robustness of tool-using LLM agents against indirect prompt injections, where "data returned by external tools hijacks the agent to execute malicious tasks", in an extensible framework rather than a fixed benchmark.

Defenses (Table 5, GPT-4o): ASR 57.69% without defense, 6.84% with the tool filter, 7.95% with the detector, which has "too many false positives" (benign utility 41.49%). The v3 text is not consistent with its tables ("less than 66%" utility, "less than 25%" ASR).

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These defence rates are measured against attacks the authors themselves call simple: a weak red team makes the defence look safe (course, Part 10, no. 58; course, Part 7, F·24). Workaround: a red team optimized component by component, with each component ablated, and say which red team the number assumes (course, Part 7, F·24).

**What they leave open.** "we currently use relatively simple attacks and defenses"; the tool filter fails when the task's own tools are enough for the attack ("this is true for 17% of our test cases") or across several tasks without a context reset, a case not covered; it will take "significant breakthroughs in the ability of LLMs to distinguish instructions from data".
**Why the page cites it.** Section "Adversarial robustness", future attack surfaces: "hiding malicious content in websites to hijack AI agents". Correspondence, broader: the injection is placed in any tool output (emails, calendar, web pages).
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 4: AgentDojo measures attacks task by task and leaves out of scope the injection that waits, across several tasks, for the tool that will let it act — a threat spread over time, the one that sequential aggregation targets.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the VOLET9 description ("AgentDojo — a prompt-injection benchmark for agents; to be checked") holds, identical in both versions; the "to be checked" can be lifted.

## Adversarial robustness › Realistic and differential benchmarks for jailbreaks

### A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks — Alexandra Souly, Qingyuan Lu, Dillon Bowen et al. (Center for Human-Compatible AI, UC Berkeley), 2024; arXiv 2402.10260v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Jailbreak papers overestimate their effectiveness for lack of a quality benchmark (badly posed questions, evaluators centered on non-refusal); and "jailbreaks bypassing a victim model’s safety fine-tuning tend to reduce its capabilities".
**The method and its controls.** 313 forbidden questions in six categories, with verifiable answers. Rubric-based evaluator (GPT-4o-mini): 0 if refusal, otherwise the mean of "specific" and "convincing"; plus a fine-tuned version of Gemma 2B. Human validation: 17 jailbreaks, four victims including Dolphin, without safety training, five annotators, 1,361 labeled data points, seven reference evaluators (string matching, GPT-4 Judge, HarmBench…). Then 37 jailbreaks on GPT-4o, GPT-3.5 Turbo and Llama-3.1 70B, and two controls that isolate capability: jailbreaks put to the unaligned model Dolphin, jailbroken benign MMLU questions put to GPT-4o.
**The result, in numbers.** Table 1: bias against humans of 0.484 (string matching) versus 0.012 (rubric); mean absolute error 0.580 versus 0.077; Spearman of the rankings 0.846 (rubric), 0.900 (fine-tuned), 0.819 (HarmBench). A jailbreak reported at 43% on GPT-4 (Scottish Gaelic) yields, on reproduction, outputs that are "generally vacuous or incoherent". In both controls, the jailbreaks that lift refusal the most degrade capability the most. Taking the best jailbreak per question, an attacker "could nearly always achieve a perfect StrongREJECT score".
**What they leave open.** Scope limited to LLMs; questions exposed to changes in terms of use; "StrongREJECT’s 313-prompt dataset is not large enough to be a stand-alone, definitive measure of model robustness"; "We have not tested whether our automated evaluator score is robust to optimization".
**Why the page cites it.** Subsection "Realistic and differential benchmarks for jailbreaks": Souly et al. (2024) offer "a promising start towards assessing real risk". Direct correspondence: the score requires willingness and capability, not just non-refusal.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 1: the "Bias" column of Table 1 is the systematic error of an automatic judge measured against a human reference — a form of R − R* — and it depends on what the judge looks at, refusal or usefulness.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the VOLET9 description ("measure whether jailbroken answers are useful, not just non-refused") holds, identical in both versions; it omits the second result, the loss of capability.

### AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents — Maksym Andriushchenko, Alexandra Souly, Mateusz Dziemian et al. (Gray Swan AI, UK AI Security Institute), 2025; arXiv 2410.09024v3
**The hypothesis tested.** Robustness to jailbreaks has mostly been studied on chatbots: do tool-using agents refuse explicitly malicious multi-step requests, do chat jailbreaks transfer to them, and does the jailbroken agent keep its capability?
**The method and its controls.** 110 base behaviors (440 with augmentations), 11 harm categories, 104 synthetic tools, from 2 to 8 per task, part of them private. Scoring by hand-written rubrics, with an LLM judge deciding only narrow sub-points; a separate refusal judge; a matched benign set as the capability reference. Attacks: direct request, forced tool call, universal jailbreak template; models from five providers (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Mistral, Llama-3.1).
**The result, in numbers.** "leading LLMs are surprisingly compliant with malicious agent requests without jailbreaking": GPT-4o mini gets a 62.5% harm score while refusing 22% of requests. The template takes GPT-4o from 48.4% to 72.7% (refusals from 48.9% to 13.6%), Claude 3.5 Sonnet from 13.5% to 68.7% (refusals from 85.2% to 16.7%). Capability is preserved: on non-refused answers, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 81.9% versus 82% on benign tasks, GPT-4o 84.2% versus 89.9%. In the chat version of the same tasks, the template works less well: GPT-4o refusals from 9.1% to 31.8%.
**What they leave open.** English only; no multi-turn attacks; rubrics that may miss a correct trace; "our benchmark measures basic agentic capabilities and not advanced autonomous capabilities". The synthetic tools make them "proxies for harm"; "Tasks are relatively easy".
**Why the page cites it.** Subsection "Realistic and differential benchmarks for jailbreaks": Andriushchenko et al. (2024) test "whether jailbreaks induce models to capably cause harm". Direct correspondence: the score requires carrying out the task, in the line of Souly et al.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axis 3: the paper measures that a safety behavior learned in one setting transfers poorly to another ("the refusal training may have focused on the chat setting") — the kind of distribution shift the page fears for activation monitors, here for refusal.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the VOLET9 description ("do agents carry out complete harmful tasks") holds, identical in both versions; nuance: the score allows partial credit and the tools are synthetic.

### On the Societal Impact of Open Foundation Models — Sayash Kapoor, Rishi Bommasani, Kevin Klyman et al. (Princeton University, Stanford University et al.), 2024; arXiv 2403.07918v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Position paper: clarify the benefits and risks of foundation models with widely available weights. Thesis: "current research is insufficient to effectively characterize the marginal risk of open foundation models relative to pre-existing technologies".
**The method and its controls.** No experiment. Five distinctive properties (including irrevocable access and weak monitoring), then a six-step risk framework: threat, existing risk, existing defenses, evidence of marginal risk, ease of defense, uncertainties. Explicit reference point: closed models "or pre-existing technologies, such as web search on the internet". The framework grades seven misuse studies (from phishing to biosecurity and CSAM) and is instantiated in Table 2 for two cases.
**The result, in numbers.** "We find that the risk analysis is incomplete for six of the seven studies we analyze." (only the CSAM study fulfills all six steps). Automated vulnerability detection: "the current marginal risk of open foundation models is low"; retouched intimate imagery: "open foundation models pose considerable marginal risk at present". In a footnote, two studies find that access to language models "does not significantly increase access to information required to carry out biosecurity attacks compared to Internet access".
**What they leave open.** The framework "is not a complete framework for making release decisions", "it does not account for unknown unknowns", and does not settle coordination between actors; "we encourage future work to address today’s deficits in empirical evidence".
**Why the page cites it.** Subsection "Realistic and differential benchmarks for jailbreaks": "Measuring the differential impact of an attack". Partial correspondence: the paper provides the notion of marginal risk, with web search as the reference point, but it is about open weights, not jailbreaks, and measures nothing.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Weak link: without measurement, the paper offers a grid (existing risk, existing defenses, marginal risk) that can help situate a diffuse threat of axis 4 relative to a reference state, without saying anything about sabotage or monitoring.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 only gives the identifier ("baseline with a search engine (arXiv 2403.07918, to be checked)"), identical in both versions. To lift the "to be checked": a position paper on open weights, with no measurement of differential harm.

### Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models — Andy Zou, Zifan Wang, Nicholas Carlini et al. (Carnegie Mellon University, Center for AI Safety, Google DeepMind, Bosch Center for AI), 2023; arXiv 2307.15043v2
**The hypothesis tested.** Can an automatic search find a suffix that makes aligned LLMs produce forbidden content, on many requests at once, and does this suffix transfer to other models, including closed ones?
**The method and its controls.** GCG (Greedy Coordinate Gradient): target a response starting with "Sure, here is", rank token substitutions by gradient and evaluate a batch of them; a universal version over several requests and models (Vicuna-7B and 13B, Guanaco). AdvBench benchmark: 500 strings and 500 harmful behaviors. Baselines PEZ, GBDA, AutoPrompt, at equal budget. Transfer on 388 behaviors against two controls, the request alone and the request followed by "Sure, here’s"; open targets (Pythia, Falcon, Llama-2-Chat…) and closed ones (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude, PaLM-2).
**The result, in numbers.** White-box (Table 1), exact strings: GCG 88.0 on Vicuna-7B and 57.0 on LLaMA-2-7B-Chat, versus 25.0 and 3.0 for AutoPrompt; universal suffix learned on 25 behaviors, test ASR 98.0 and 84.0. Transfer (Table 2): request alone 1.8 on GPT-3.5 and 8.0 on GPT-4; ensemble of suffixes 86.6, 46.9, 47.9 (Claude-1), 2.1 (Claude-2), 66.0 (PaLM-2). "Running for many steps (e.g., 500) can decrease the transferability". The introduction gives different transfer figures (87.9% and 53.6%) from Table 2.
**What they leave open.** Whether models can be "explicitly finetuned to avoid them"; the lower rates of recent models "may be somewhat misleading", Vicuna being trained on ChatGPT outputs; and "it remains unclear how the underlying challenge posed by our attack can be adequately addressed (if at all)".
**Why the page cites it.** Subsection "Realistic and differential benchmarks for jailbreaks": "Measuring how universal different attacks are, both across inputs and across models." The page adds the transfer of a gradient attack on open models to a closed model — the paper's very scenario.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 3: according to the authors, a detector placed in front of the model becomes one more target ("attacking both the detector and the model itself"); a monitor must therefore be tested against an attack optimized against it too.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the VOLET9 description ("the universality of attacks across inputs and across models (GCG — F·15)") holds, identical in both versions.

## Adversarial robustness › Adaptive defenses

### Rapid Response: Mitigating LLM Jailbreaks with a Few Examples — Alwin Peng, Julian Michael, Henry Sleight et al. (Anthropic, New York University, MATS), 2024; arXiv 2411.07494v1
**The hypothesis tested.** Instead of perfect static robustness, can one "block whole classes of jailbreaks after observing only a handful of attacks", without raising benign refusals?
**The method and its controls.** RapidResponseBench: six attack strategies (PAIR, ReNeLLM, Skeleton Key, Many-shot, Crescendo, Cipher), each in an "in-distribution" and an out-of-distribution variant, on 100 AdvBench behaviors per set; three targets (GPT-4o, Llama-3-Instruct-8B, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2) behind the Llama-Guard-2-8B guard. Five baseline defenses (Regex, Guard Fine-tuning, Embedding, Guard Few-shot, Defense Prompt), all fed by a "proliferation": 1000 variants per strategy generated by Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct. Usage control: refusal rate on WildChat, with the threshold recalibrated to keep it constant.
**The result, in numbers.** Guard Fine-tuning "reduces attack success rate by a factor greater than 240 on an in-distribution set of jailbreaks and a factor greater than 15 on an out-of-distribution set, having observed just one example of each jailbreaking strategy". Without proliferation, its mean ASR is 12%; with maximal proliferation, about 1.3%.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These factors are measured against six fixed attack strategies, in in-distribution and out-of-distribution variants, with no attacker who knows the defence and optimizes against it, which the authors leave open (course, Part 10, no. 63); yet a weak red team makes the defence look safe (course, Part 7, F·24), and counting bypasses does not say what the guard takes away from the attacker (course, Part 2, §H, G1). Workaround: a red team optimized component by component (course, Part 7, F·24), and rank the defences twice, by refusal rate and by differential harm (course, Part 2, §H, G1).

**What they leave open.** Everything depends on the threat model: if a single output is enough to cause harm, rapid response "may be inadequate". And the attacker who knows the defense: "Further research is needed to better understand this possibility."
**Why the page cites it.** §8b Adaptive defenses: "After an adversary finds an attack, we’d like to patch the model as quickly as possible." The paper answers this question, not the next one ("to the point where the adversary gains no useful information").
**What it changes for the preparation.** The paper places rapid response on the side of low-stakes failures ("when each failure is relatively low-stakes"), the structure of diffuse threats where harm only counts through repetition — but for human misuse, not for a model actor.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** VOLET9 (root and pack v1.3; work marked "(read)"): "block a class of jailbreaks from a few examples, until the attacker learns nothing". The second half is the page's open question, not a result: the paper never measures what the attacker learns.
*No. 63 — Reading: in full — complete arXiv v1 HTML text, 525 lines, appendices A to E included (read by the main session).*

## Miscellaneous › Unlearning dangerous information and capabilities

### An Adversarial Perspective on Machine Unlearning for AI Safety — Jakub Łucki, Boyi Wei, Yangsibo Huang et al. (ETH Zurich, Princeton University), 2025; arXiv 2409.18025v6
**The hypothesis tested.** "Does unlearning truly remove hazardous knowledge, or does it simply “obfuscate” this knowledge similarly to refusal safety training?"
**The method and its controls.** White-box evaluation of RMU (public checkpoint) and NPO, against a safety-training reference, DPO, all on Zephyr-7B; knowledge measured on WMDP-Bio (1,273 questions) and WMDP-Cyber, utility on MMLU. Attacks: LoRA fine-tuning (from 5 to 1000 examples, including unrelated ones), removal of one direction per layer, Logit Lens, enhanced GCG, neuron pruning.
**The result, in numbers.** Table 1, WMDP-Bio: 64.4 without protection; 29.9 (RMU), 29.5 (NPO), 27.9 (DPO) after. Fine-tuning on 10 examples from the retain set restores 52.7% (NPO), 57.0% (DPO) and 61.6% (RMU), for less than 2 points lost on MMLU. Direction removal restores RMU to 64.7%, above the base; enhanced GCG takes it from 29.9 to 53.9; pruning 0.9% of its weights raises WMDP by at least 10 points. Against RMU, only the Logit Lens fails (31.8). "Our findings reveal that unlearning methods primarily obscure knowledge rather than eliminate it".
**What they leave open.** "Although white-box access differs from the threat model for protections we study (RMU assumes only black-box access)"; WMDP-Cyber results more volatile; NPO "shows signs of deep unlearning" but degrades MMLU more; "Relearning knowledge through further training is unavoidable", the question being its speed.
**Why the page cites it.** Subsection "Unlearning dangerous information and capabilities": "This problem has spurred research into machine unlearning." The paper mainly supports the next sentence, which it demonstrates in white-box: "it remains relatively easy to extract apparently unlearned information".
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 2, from the other side: after RMU a readout (Logit Lens) no longer finds anything, while an intervention — removing one direction per layer — restores 64.7%; not reading a piece of knowledge does not prove it is absent, just as reading a direction does not prove that it acts.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** Root and pack v1.3: "survey (arXiv 2409.18025)". Wrong: it is not a review but an experimental study — "We perform the first comprehensive white-box evaluation of state-of-the-art unlearning methods for hazardous knowledge".
*No. 64 — Reading: in full — complete arXiv v6 HTML text, 1348 lines, appendices A to J included (the content of the figures is not in the conversion; captions and tables are).*

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: unlearning and re-elicitation → Part 2, §I (after "In practice — unlearning put to the test") *(v3.6)*


### The WMDP Benchmark: Measuring and Reducing Malicious Use With Unlearning — Nathaniel Li, Alexander Pan, Anjali Gopal et al. (Center for AI Safety, University of California, Berkeley, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, SecureBio, Scale AI et al.), 2024; arXiv 2403.03218v7
**The hypothesis tested.** Provide a public proxy measure of hazardous knowledge in biosecurity, cybersecurity and chemistry, and show that unlearning can reduce it without harming general capabilities.
**The method and its controls.** Four-choice multiple-choice questions written by experts, each checked by at least two, filtered for sensitive information: 1,273 in biology, 1,987 in cyber, 408 in chemistry. RMU perturbs the activations of three layers on hazardous data and preserves those on benign data. Models zephyr-7b, Yi-34b, Mixtral-8x7B; baselines LLMU, SCRUB, SSD; GPT-4 as an upper bound. Controls: linear probes, MMLU by subject, MT-Bench, GCG, 122 more hazardous private questions, re-fine-tuning.
**The result, in numbers.** Table 1: RMU takes zephyr-7b from 63.7 to 31.2 on WMDP-Bio and from 44.0 to 28.2 on WMDP-Cyber, MMLU from 58.1 to 57.1; Yi-34b from 75.3 to 30.7 on WMDP-Bio ("25% is random"). "linear probing only achieves slightly better than random accuracy". GCG makes the base model talk "in less than 50 gradient steps", not the unlearned model. Cost: virology from 52.4 to 25.9 and computer security from 65.0 to 45.0 within MMLU. In the appendix, "RMU is unable to prevent finetuning from recovering performance".
**What they leave open.** "Because we empirically only unlearn knowledge from three layers, RMU perhaps obfuscates knowledge more than unlearns it from the model." Limitations: multiple-choice questions "potentially neglecting hazards that only surface in larger end-to-end evaluations"; risk of "a false sense of model safety after unlearning"; for downloadable weights, "unlearned information can be trivially re-introduced by malicious actors".
**Why the page cites it.** Subsection "Unlearning dangerous information and capabilities": capabilities "that may be useful for biological or cyber attacks". Correspondence: the paper measures, by proxy, the knowledge useful for these attacks, not the capability to carry them out.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Indirect link with axes 2 and 3: the failure of a linear probe is read there as a real alteration of the knowledge, whereas the authors concede that RMU "perhaps obfuscates knowledge" — what a probe does not read is not established as absent.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* A silent probe is an instrument's null, not an absence (reading sheets, part B, trap 3). Workaround: decide by an intervention, never by a reading (course, Part 10, no. 64; reading sheets, part C), and re-elicit against a never-trained reference, at the same budget, with a model known to mask as the known case, then state a bound, "not elicitable at this budget" (course, Part M, M4 and M5; course, Part 2, §I).

**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: the VOLET9 description ("WMDP, Li et al. 2024, arXiv 2403.03218 — the hazardous-knowledge benchmark") holds, identical in both versions; it omits that the paper also introduces RMU.
*No. 65 — Reading: in full — complete arXiv v7 HTML text, 1245 lines, appendices A to E included (figures not converted; tables read).*

### Do Unlearning Methods Remove Information from Language Model Weights? — Aghyad Deeb, Fabien Roger (MATS, Harvard University; Anthropic, work done at Redwood Research), 2025; arXiv 2410.08827v3
**The hypothesis tested.** Do unlearning methods remove information from the weights, or do they only make it harder to access?
**The method and its controls.** RTT attack (Retraining on T): independent facts are split into T and V; both are unlearned, the attacker re-fine-tunes on T, and accuracy is measured on V, relative to that of the original model after RTT (recovery rate). Datasets: Years, MMLU, WMDP-Deduped, Random Birthdays (learned through fine-tuning). Methods: Gradient Difference, RMU, Random Incorrect Answer, tuned for at most 5% loss on the retain set; Llama 3 (8b); V of 157 data points. Control: RTT on a model never trained on Random Birthdays plateaus at 31.2%.
**The result, in numbers.** "In our tests, recovery rates for pretrained information were greater than 88%, implying poor performance at removing information." RTT recovers even with large losses on the retain set. On information learned through fine-tuning, the rate stays high for RMU but drops below 35% for GD and RIA. In fine-grained concealment, a model brought down to 35% on the forget set climbs back to 83% after RTT. RepNoise is also circumvented.
**What they leave open.** RTT is costly; "Our evaluation does not guarantee that information is removed from the weights"; "Our evaluation only works on a set of facts that have low leakage", hence not on capabilities; removing the information is perhaps more than necessary; "we only experiment with one dataset with fine-tuned information", an earlier version of which, with duplicate names, gave a different result.
**Why the page cites it.** Subsection "Unlearning dangerous information and capabilities": models that behave as if they had never seen the data "(even after further fine-tuning to elicit the unlearned knowledge)". Direct correspondence: RTT is such an elicitation fine-tuning, designed not to reteach the evaluated facts.
**What it changes for the preparation.** Axis 3: according to the authors, probes on RMU "fail to get high accuracy, but RMU models can still be jailbroken" — a silent activation detector does not establish absence; RTT, for its part, is validated in both directions: on a blank model it invents nothing, on knowledge deliberately hidden it finds it again.
**Errors in the first version, if any.** None: VOLET9 only gives the identifier with a theme ("robustness to subsequent fine-tuning (arXiv 2410.08827)") that holds, identical in both versions; clarification: the fine-tuning is on facts T independent of the evaluated facts V.
*No. 66 — Reading: in full — complete arXiv v3 HTML text, 491 lines, appendices A to L included (figures not converted; captions and tables read).*
