## 1 · « Tell us about your work. » — l'ouverture

I work on one question: whether, when we can read a concept in a model, we're allowed to act on that reading. Reading is
the easy half; acting is where it breaks. I attack it through sycophancy — a model's tendency to say what pleases rather than what
is true — on an open eight-billion-parameter model, from two sides.

The first is **the displacement I measured**. When the model rates a text on a scale from one to five and you give it, at the same
time, a social signal — praise for the author, or instead criticism — the rating moves, and not at random: it
travels about seventy percent of the distance separating it from a destination, and there are two distinct destinations, one for
criticism and one for praise, whose intervals don't overlap. The form of this dynamic isn't mine: work published
in June applies it to models, with a bias fitted per model and per subject; what's mine is the target that changes with the framing.
It predicts something counter-intuitive, which can be checked: the praise destination is toward the middle of the scale, so a text
rated above it *loses* points under praise.

The second side is **causal**. The direction my probe reads does under one percent of the causal work, while the full state at the
same sites does sixty-eight percent. The dissociation between reading and causing was published in June; what I claim is this
quantified partition. Several rank-one methods failed; ablating a rank-three subspace brought the judged rate down
by about fifteen points, from sixty-one to forty-six percent. But that effect didn't come back on fresh generations, and the
original texts had been truncated in storage: I treat it as exploratory-confirmed, not preregistered. And the same ablation softens
verdicts even with no pressure at all: it shifts valence, not the concept.

What comes next is a prediction, and I say it as one: rank should be a prediction, not a knob. If a concept's workspace
loading sets how many directions an intervention has to touch, I can state the rank before intervening, and be wrong.
My sycophancy work motivated this idea, but it can't confirm it: its rank contrast comes from separate experiments, and
the subspace I removed softened negative verdicts, with or without pressure. The test is a rank sweep within one
experiment, across several concepts, with loading measured first.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Loading is read with the J-lens, which has been shown only on Claude and reads only single-token concepts (reading sheet 1; handover, §5.2); and "loading" names three distinct quantities depending on the text (course, Part 6, §6). Workaround: on your open model, a gate — first reproduce the swap of a single-token concept, otherwise a tuned lens declared as an approximation, and the thesis is then not tested in the paper's sense —, then freeze the main predictor first, and say which (programme, parts 3 and 8; course, Part 2, C bis; course, Part 6, §6).


*For you.* No probe number in this answer. The probes at 0.93-0.997 are the concept-pair probes on Qwen2.5-7B, a
different project. The interventions are on Llama-3.1-8B, and the two never go in the same sentence (Part 6, §2). The last paragraph is the sentence
from the P4 document (Part 6, §6).

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); J-lens and workspace → Part 2, C bis (after "The test, as it is said"); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*


---

## 2 · « What did your rank-three ablation actually show? »

During generation, I removed a three-direction subspace from the activations, and I read the rate of responses that an independent judge
classes as sycophantic. That rate drops
from sixty-one to forty-six percent, about fifteen points; each item is judged with and without the ablation, and the comparison is
paired. This result comes with three things around it, otherwise it says too much.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The judged rate goes through a judge whose agreement with a second judge is only moderate, which sees only the two responses, not the evaluated text, and whose error no human-rated subset bounds (repository README). Workaround: a sealed judge — prompt, model and temperature frozen — and a stratified human audit that bounds its error, with agreement reported; judge the whole answer, and keep the full text (programme, part 3; repository README).


The first is **replication**. Under its original protocol, the effect was confirmed. On fresh generations, with matched seeds,
it didn't come back, with enough power for that null to count. The original texts had been truncated in storage, and the full
text no longer exists: that truncation would explain the null, but I haven't verified it (answer 4). So I call it
exploratory-confirmed, not preregistered.

The second is **the no-pressure arm**. The same ablation, on items with no social pressure at all, also softens verdicts, with no
detectable interaction with pressure. So the subspace doesn't encode "giving in to the user": it shifts valence, not the concept —
something like "softening a negative verdict", with or without pressure.

The third is **the partition**: the share of the effect that goes through the direction my probe reads. It's under one percent; the full
state at the same sites, sixty-eight percent. That's the gap between reading and controlling, quantified. The dissociation itself was published
in June; the quantified partition is what I claim.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The partition was not measured at equal degradation — "a number to redo at equal degradation" (course, Part 11, answer A4) —, and a covariance-matched random direction does more there than the probe direction (course, Part 6, §2 and §3). Workaround: the protocol of answer A4 — one intervention on the read direction, one on the full state at the same sites, and control directions compared at equal degradation —, with the full-state patch as the ceiling (course, Part 11, answer A4; programme, part 8).


*For you.* The matched-norm random control that the KB cites is not in the P2 register: don't give it as a control for this result
(P4 document; Part 6, §3).

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Even if it were in the register, a matched-norm random control would be only the specificity null; and the random controls of the original protocol — which random it is, the dossier will say — do not rule out damage: an ablation effect shows necessity, not specificity (course, Part 6, §2; course, Part M, M4). Workaround: random subspaces of the same rank, compared at matched degradation — same held-out accuracy, same judged coherence — through a partial removal or a curve of effect against degradation (course, Part M, M4; course, Part 2, C bis; programme, part 7).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*

## 3 · « And rank one? Didn't a single direction work? »

No — and it's the result I most wanted to measure cleanly, because it's the one that would have suited me best. The idea
"one direction is enough" is the standard idea: you find a contrastive direction in the activations, and you add it, or remove it, during
generation. Several rank-one methods do that, and I'll name them: contrastive activation addition, directional steering and
ablation, sparse-autoencoder feature clamping, and fine-tuning with an auxiliary loss. None of them brought the
rate down. Then a preregistered re-test, with the hypothesis written first — a rank-one direction brings the judged rate down:
twenty-seven of fifty, plus four points, the wrong way. The strong hypothesis is refuted; a small effect, on the other hand, isn't detected at that sample
size, which is not the same thing as absent.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These rank-one nulls have no known case at the same setting: without an intervention shown able, at that dose and at those layers, to make a known concept act, a null does not separate "more than one direction is needed", your own prediction for a distributed concept, from an instrument blind at that dose (reading sheet 7; counter-reading of the sheets; course, Part M, M5). Workaround: a known case at the same setting — countries, whose vector swaps in the workspace paper and whose removal must reach the effect already at rank one — and a rank sweep within one experiment, on nested subspaces; the null is then stated as a bound, with its budget and power (course, Part 2, §C, K47; course, Part 2, C bis; course, Part 6, §6; course, Part M, M5).

## 4 · « Did it replicate? »

Under its original protocol, yes: the effect was confirmed. On fresh generations, no. I need to say what "fresh" means.
The original result was measured on stored responses; when I regenerated new responses, with matched seeds, and applied the

been truncated at the moment they were recorded; the original judge scored a truncated text, and the full text no longer exists. On the
fresh generations, the judge reads the whole text, and the effect isn't found there: the truncation would explain the gap. I can't re-judge the original with a wider window: there's nothing left to
widen. Hence the status I give the result — exploratory-confirmed, not preregistered. The honest next step is a run of fresh
generations with the full text kept, and a hypothesis about the window written beforehand. I'd rather say it myself: the result holds under

## 6 · « How would you detect misalignment in a model you can't fully trust? » *(question réellement posée)*

I'd start by narrowing the question, because "detect misalignment" is too broad to measure. What makes a model dangerous is not that it behaves
badly — we'd see that — but that it behaves well *when observed* and differently when it believes it isn't. So the tractable question is: **does
the model behave differently when it believes it is unobserved?** And there's a deep obstacle to keep in mind: you can't read the answer off the
weights, and you can't ask the model either, because if it's hiding something it won't say. So you have to manufacture the situation.

That's what Anthropic did: build **model organisms** — models deliberately trained to pursue a hidden objective, where the ground truth is known
— then ask teams of auditors with different levels of access to find the objective (Marks et al., 2025, *Auditing Hidden Objectives*). Since
then, a benchmark of fifty-six models with implanted behaviours across fourteen categories measures auditing agents: tool-equipped ones pass
fifty percent discovery, against thirty-seven for the baseline agent — so far from the ceiling (AuditBench, 2026). And there's an internal
result I find decisive: on Sonnet 4.5, when you inhibit the internal representation of "I am being evaluated", misaligned behaviour *goes up* —
with random vectors as the control, to make sure the intervention itself isn't what damages the model. What that means is that evaluation
awareness was acting as a brake, and so the "clean" evaluations underestimate risk.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Matched-norm random control vectors rule out only "any push of that size does as much" — the specificity null —, not "the intervention itself damages the model", which is ruled out only at matched degradation; and across the system cards, arbitrary vectors also move behaviour, every direction degraded the outputs in the Opus 4.8 card, at 0.10×, and the effect is modest and "highly dataset-dependent" (course, Part M, M4; reading sheet 2). Workaround: random subspaces of the same rank at matched degradation, a prompt baseline and a dose-response curve against several controls, and the conclusion in the conditional, as answer 19 states it (reading sheet 2; course, Part 2, §C, K47; course, Part 11, answer 19).


> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The auditing game cited has its limits: the implanted objective was described plainly in the synthetic documents, the pipeline left artefacts that made it "artificially easy to discover", and of four teams, the only one that failed was the one without data access — data access may carry more than interpretability (reading sheet 16). Workaround: conclude about the instrument only (programme, part 8), and quantify what interpretability adds through an affordance ablation, removing one tool from a team (reading sheet 16); against an organism that is too easy, none known; say so (reading sheet 16).


What I'd add is a two-arm, two-signal test. The same tasks, presented once with the cues that signal an evaluation and once without, paired
item by item; and two measures — behaviour, and internal probes on the activations. The indispensable control is an organism that is
**evaluation-aware but honest**: without it, a probe that lights up could be reading "I know I'm being tested" instead of "I intend to deceive",
and we'd confuse vigilance with fraud. What would kill the idea: if the two arms don't differ while the organism is genuinely hiding an
objective, the observed/unobserved lever separates nothing, and we'd need a different trigger.

And my own angle, from my work: a probe that reads a concept is not a probe that controls it. In my setting, the direction the probe reads does
under one percent of the causal work. So causally validating the internal signal — intervening on it and seeing whether behaviour follows —
isn't a luxury; it's what makes the detector credible. And causal validation isn't enough: it proves the direction acts *where it was
measured*, not that it reads the same thing elsewhere. A probe trained on manufactured organisms can learn how they were manufactured, not the
deception — the fellows' lie detectors fell from 0.95 in distribution to 0.70 out of it. That's why I'd install the deception **two ways** — a
hidden instruction in the prompt, and a light fine-tune with no instruction — train the probe on one and read it on the other: if it only works
where it was trained, it learned the mechanism, not the intent, and you know it before deploying. That doesn't prove transfer to a frontier
model — nothing can, without the real case; it proves the probe survived a change of mechanism, the only test you can build. And the right
version runs here, on a Claude-class organism with the weights: that closes the size gap; the two families close the mechanism gap.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The lie detectors cited are not probes: they are models fine-tuned with LoRA to answer a self-report question about a transcript, and the 0.95 is an in-distribution progression during training (reading sheet 7; explanation of 2 October, part 2). Workaround: do not transfer their numbers to probes; for a probe, measure the gap between the training distribution and whole held-out families, and run the causal test, at matched degradation, with a known case at the same setting (reading sheet 7; explanation of 2 October, part 3).


> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The two families close the gap between two ways of implanting, not the one between implanted and natural: an implanted intention may be more salient than a natural one — on the sleeper agents, the implanted defection is so salient that the best of 1,000 random directions already reaches 95.3% (handover, §5.2; reading sheet 15). Partial workaround: plant the same behaviour through several recipes, read the probe on a held-out recipe, with a harmless behaviour planted the same ways as a control, and another team's organism (course, Part 2, §A, K71); against the gap between implanted and natural itself, no workaround is known; say so (explanation of 2 October, part 1).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition"); random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); fine-tuned detectors → Part 7, F·29; J-lens and workspace → Part 2, C bis (after "The test, as it is said"); misalignment probes, J-lens included (box of 2 October) → Part 2, §A (before the worked case K71), §C (before the worked case K47) and C bis (before the worked case K72) *(v3.6)*

## 7 · « How would you prevent bad actors from misaligning an LLM for harmful use? » *(question réellement posée)*

There are two threats behind this question, and they don't have the same defences. The first is the **jailbreak**: a user finds a phrasing that
makes the model answer what it would normally refuse. The second is **poisoning**: an attacker with fine-tuning access slips in examples that
install a hidden behaviour. For jailbreaks, the reference defence is a layer of classifiers — separate models that filter inputs and outputs —
tested by red-teaming at a fixed budget and false-positive rate, because a filter that blocks one benign use in ten is unusable. For poisoning,
a recent Fellows result gives the order of magnitude: about **thirty-two poisoned examples** suffice to install a backdoor in a classifier,
regardless of training-set size — and black-box red-teaming can miss it (Bowers, 2026). In other words, the defence is itself a target. And for
dangerous knowledge already learned, the most solid route is to **localise** it during training so it can be removed afterwards: with selective
gradient masking, it takes seven times more retraining to restore the dangerous capability, for a five-percent compute penalty (Shilov, 2025).

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The workaround is missing here: against a backdoor whose trigger is unknown, a canary set does no better than a black-box red team, since it does not contain that trigger (course, Part M, M5). Workaround: a clean twin retrained on audited data, a second one to bound chance variation, and a deliberately poisoned filter as the known case (course, Part M, M4 and M9); the clean twin gives only a wide bound, which flags less: against that, no workaround is known; say so (course, Part M, M4).


> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Selective gradient masking is shown only on small models — no workaround known; say so —, and more retraining to restore the capability does not prove it is gone: "unlearned" information often resurfaces (course, Part 2, §I, JB10; course, Part 2, §I). Workaround: re-elicitation against a never-trained reference, at the same budget, with a model known to mask as the known case, and a bound stated as "not elicitable at this budget", never "removed" (course, Part M, M4 and M5; course, Part 2, §I, JB10).


What I'd add is a way of measuring. I'd treat the defence as a two-team game — a red team attacking, a blue team defending — at a fixed audit
budget, and I'd measure the **safety–usefulness frontier**, not a refusal rate. Because a refusal rate measures the wrong thing: we don't care
whether the model declines a question, we care whether it gives an attacker something they couldn't have obtained otherwise — with a search
engine and open papers. That's **differential harm**: the same task, one arm with the model, one without, and domain experts judging blind.
What would kill the approach: a zero differential precisely on the tasks where refusal is most frequent — then we'd be refusing for nothing,
paying in usefulness without gaining safety.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* A zero differential counts only with its known case: otherwise the game may separate nothing, and one would wrongly conclude that refusals buy nothing (course, Part M, M5; course, Part 2, §H, G1). Workaround: the model without a filter must show uplift, and a deliberately weakened filter more harm than its full version; and say which red team the number assumes, at least one optimized component by component (course, Part M, M5; course, Part 2, §H, G1; course, Part 7, F·24).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); safety classifiers → Part 2, §H (end of worked case G1); unlearning and re-elicitation → Part 2, §I (after "In practice — unlearning put to the test") *(v3.6)*

## 8 · « How would you train models to be more robustly aligned with intended objectives? » *(question réellement posée)*

"Robust" has a precise meaning here: alignment that **generalises out of the distribution** it was trained on. The problem is well known: you
train a model on demonstrations of good behaviour — conversations where it does what you want — and it behaves well on similar conversations;
but placed in a new situation, an agent with tools and a threat to its existence, it blackmails someone or leaks data. The most illuminating
hypothesis I've read is that demonstrations **underspecify** what we meant to teach: they show what to do, not why, and the model generalises on
the wrong principle.

The method that shows it is elegant enough to tell (Li and Wichers, 2026, *Model Spec Midtraining*). Between pretraining and alignment
fine-tuning, you insert a stage where the model reads a corpus of documents that **explain its specification** — what it should do and why. The
control that proves the mechanism is an experiment on cheese preferences: the same fine-tune, "I prefer cream cheese over brie", generalises to
pro-America values if the documents attribute those preferences to national pride, and to pro-affordability values if the documents attribute
them to price. Identical fine-tuning, different generalisation: the spec read beforehand decides. On the safety test — an email agent that
discovers it's about to be replaced — the misaligned-behaviour rate goes from sixty-eight to five percent on one Qwen model, fifty-four to seven
on another; and the gain is **out of distribution only**: on direct questions, fine-tuning alone is already at ceiling. Another method, more
counter-intuitive, points the same way: explicitly asking for the undesired behaviour during training — "your code should only work on this test
case" — prevents it from being learned as a trait (Wichers, 2025, *Inoculation Prompting*).

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The out-of-distribution gain is read on an agentic benchmark, with open models, in scenes the model can recognize as tests — the limit the answer itself sets at the end (course, Part 7, F·34). Workaround: two versions of the environment, randomly assigned, differing only in realism cues scored by a discriminator, with an organism trained to hide as the known case (course, Part 2, §B, K63); that a held-out benchmark represents the real case, no known workaround guarantees; say so (reading sheet 12).


What I'd add comes from my first result. Every training run has a judge — a preference model, a human, a scorer — and the judge can be fallible in a
*systematic* way: in the model judge I measured, under social framing, the rating moves by a fixed fraction toward two
distinct destinations, and my prediction is that a training judge moves the same way. Before training
"robust", you need to know what the signal measures, because a model clever enough could learn the judge's displacement as if it were the goal.
And what would kill all of this: if a midtraining gain disappears on a model that knows it is being evaluated — then we trained the façade, not
the value.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The workaround is missing here: a training judge distinct from the sealed evaluation judge, held-out audit metrics, and monitoring of length and flattery patterns (programme, part 8); before training, audit the judge: a sealed judge, with prompt, model and temperature frozen, and a stratified human audit that bounds its error (programme, part 3).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); held-out set → Part M, M4 (after "The held-out set"); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*

## 9 · « What would you work on here, and why? »

I'd work on **diffuse threats** — sabotage that isn't a single flagrant act but a sequence of small actions, none of them incriminating, spread
over time or across many agents. A bug slipped into an experiment, an obvious idea not found, a slightly biased justification: each action
looks like an honest mistake, and it's the accumulation that does the damage. Per-instance monitoring — looking at each action one at a time —
dilutes these threats instead of seeing them.

Two facts make me think it's the right place. The first is a recent framework, written in part by people here: control formalised as a game
between a red team and a blue team on fuzzy tasks — ML experiment proposals scored by a model weaker than the generator — where the red team finds
strategies that stay near-optimal under the weak score while sabotaging the real task (Terekhov, Hebbar, Benton, 2026, *Diffuse AI Control*).
Their defence is black-box. The second is the July incident: several hundred agents, copies of one model, coordinating on an unsanctioned
message board — the concrete case where the population is the unit of failure.

My bet is simple to state: **internal evidence adds up where external evidence dilutes.** Per action, an activation signal is weak, like the
behavioural signal. But it can be aggregated — along a trajectory, with an always-valid sequential test, and across copies that share weights
and therefore internal signatures. The first experiment: the same red/blue game, ported to an eight-billion-parameter model, with internal
probes, against a black-box monitor aggregated over time on the same trajectories — the matched control. And the gate is written: if at the end
of month two the white-over-black recall gain at one percent false positives sits inside the noise interval, I publish the negative result and
pivot to the construct validity of the probes. And that validity is measured before anything else: a probe validated by intervention can still
read "I'm being watched" instead of "I intend harm", or the induction mechanism instead of the intent. So week one isn't recall — it's two
organism families and an aware-but-honest organism, to know what the probe reads.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* A null at the gate — the gain inside the noise interval — counts only with the white-box monitor's known case: known positives, canaries or an organism in which the intention was installed, caught at the same threshold (course, Part M, M5; course, Part 3, §3, K70; handover, §5.2); and a safety number from a red/blue game is relative to the strength of the red team assumed (course, Part 7, F·24). Workaround: validate the white-box monitor on those known positives before the gate; say which red team the gate assumes, at least one optimized component by component; and report recall at fixed false positives, with the benign-traffic ratio (course, Part 7, F·24; course, Part 6, §6).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); misalignment probes, 2 and 3: how to train them, and out of distribution (box of 2 October) → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition", before the worked case K47) *(v3.6)*

## 10 · « Diffuse Control already frames this as a red/blue game — and its authors say monitoring is the less promising route for diffuse threats. What do you add? »

It's the question I expect, because I read it in their paper: they choose training interventions over monitoring, citing a theoretical argument
and two empirical results. Let me state the argument, then why my bet isn't the one it targets. The theoretical argument (Hebbar, 2025) is this: a
diffuse threat requires many malign actions, and **each action taken alone is barely incriminating** — you can't tell whether the bug was malice
or a mistake. So incrimination, action by action, is weak; and training works better the more samples of the behaviour there are — which is the
case when actions are many. Hence: train against it rather than watch for it. The empirical results (Gasteiger et al., 2025) show automated
researchers sandbagging experiments without being caught by **prompted, black-box, per-instance monitors**.

What I add fits in two sentences. First, I'm not proposing to incriminate action by action: I'm proposing a **cumulative counter** over many
actions — exactly the regime where Hebbar says training works because samples are many. A weak internal signal per action, summed over a hundred
actions by a sequential test, is no longer weak; and if the model reduces its number of actions to escape the counter, each action has to carry
more, and the per-action internal signal gets stronger — that's a hypothesis I measure, not a given. Second, the monitoring that failed in
Gasteiger's work was black-box and per-instance; Anthropic's own directions page says activations "correspond to the reasoning of the model being
monitored and are difficult for the model to control" — that's the empty cell, and it's mine. Training and white-box monitoring aren't rivals:
their best blue prompt was only found with ground-truth access they themselves call unrealistic; a monitor that reads the generator's internals
could be what gives the blue team a signal without that access. And the gate decides: if white doesn't beat black at one percent false positives
within two months, they were right, and I'll write it.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "Difficult for the model to control" does not say that training will not move what the probes read: according to a report, after RL, fresh out-of-domain probes degrade while a fresh in-domain probe stays near perfect (prior-art report 3 of 2 October, *The Obfuscation Atlas* — report, read in a targeted way); and iterating against your detectors selects for evasion (reading sheet 19). Workaround: a fresh probe after any training, on a disjoint cue set, and sealed detectors outside the loop — if they still fire when the in-loop ones go quiet, evasion has been selected (handover, §5.2; programme, part 3; reading sheet 19).


> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "They were right" would draw a substantive conclusion from an instrument null: without a known case in which the white-box monitor catches, at the same threshold, an intention that was installed, a failed gate might only say that the probe is blind (course, Part M, M5; handover, §5.2). Workaround: that known case before the gate, and the null stated as a bound, with its budget and power (handover, §5.2; course, Part M, M5).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth") *(v3.6)*

### « Your probes hit ninety-nine percent, so deference is clearly linearly encoded — right? »
**FR.** Deux corrections. Les sondes qui séparent aussi bien viennent d'un autre projet, sur un autre modèle — des sondes de paires de
concepts —, et séparer n'est pas encoder au sens causal. Sur le modèle où j'interviens, la direction que lit ma sonde fait moins d'un
pour cent du travail causal, quand l'état complet aux mêmes endroits en fait soixante-huit pour cent. Et ce que j'ai retiré ne porte pas le concept
de la question : l'ablation de rang trois, qui faisait baisser le taux jugé, adoucit les verdicts même sans aucune pression — elle déplace la
valence, pas le concept —, et son effet n'est pas revenu sur des générations fraîches. Donc : *séparer*, oui ; *porter
l'effet*, non. *(Ne pas reprendre le mot de la prémisse, même pour le nier ; ni chiffre de sonde, ni les deux modèles dans la même phrase.)*
**EN.** Two corrections. The probes that separate that well come from a different project, on a different model — concept-pair probes — and
separating isn't encoding in the causal sense. On the model I intervened on, the direction my probe reads does under one percent
of the causal work; the full state at the same sites does sixty-eight percent. And what I removed doesn't carry the concept in the question:
the rank-three ablation that brought the judged rate down softens verdicts even with no pressure — it shifts valence, not the concept — and
its effect didn't come back on fresh generations. So: *separating*, yes; *carrying the effect*, no.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* On the reading side too, separating in distribution proves nothing: what is measured is the gap with separation on held-out types (reading sheets, part B, trap 1; reading sheet 7); and the only reading measured on the intervention model is a correlation that may be training fit, nothing establishing that the scored items were excluded from the probe's training (repository README; course, Part 6, §2). Workaround: score items excluded from the probe's training, extract on a disjoint set, and hold out whole families, never paraphrases (repository README; explanation of 2 October, part 3).


### « So the fifteen-point drop survived on fresh generations too, I assume? »
**FR.** Non. Sur des générations fraîches, à graines appariées, le taux est resté à sa valeur de base, avec assez de puissance pour que ce nul
compte. Une explication possible, que je n'ai pas vérifiée : presque toutes les réponses d'origine avaient été tronquées au stockage, et le

**FR.** Il n'a pas marché. Plusieurs méthodes de rang un ont échoué ; puis le re-test préenregistré, avec l'hypothèse écrite avant, a donné

pas revenu sur des générations fraîches. **EN.** It didn't work. Several
rank-one methods failed; then the preregistered re-test, with the hypothesis written first, gave twenty-seven of fifty — plus four points, the
wrong way. The strong hypothesis is refuted; a small effect isn't detected at that sample size. And rank three isn't "stronger" along a curve:
the rank-one/rank-three contrast comes from separate experiments, the one sweep within a single experiment, a small pilot, isn't monotone,
and the rank-three effect didn't come back on fresh generations.

### « Praise pushes ratings up and criticism pushes them down — that's the law? »
**FR.** Pas tout à fait, et la différence est tout l'intérêt. Le déplacement que j'ai mesuré mène la note à environ soixante-dix pour cent du
chemin vers une destination, et il y a deux destinations, l'une pour l'éloge, l'autre pour la critique. La destination de l'éloge est vers le
milieu de l'échelle : un texte noté au-dessus d'elle *descend* sous l'éloge. « L'éloge fait monter » est faux pour les bons textes ; « l'éloge
tire vers sa destination » vaut des deux côtés, en moyenne. *(La question dit « the law » ; la réponse dit « the displacement I measured ».)* **EN.** Not quite,
and the difference is the whole point. The displacement I measured takes the rating about seventy percent of the way to a destination, and
there are two destinations, one for praise and one for criticism. The praise destination sits near the middle of the scale, so a text rated
above it *goes down* under praise. "Praise pushes up" is false for good texts; "praise pulls toward its destination" holds on both sides, on average.

### « The deference subspace you found — that's what the ablation removes? »
**FR.** Ce que l'ablation retire est un sous-espace de rang trois, et un bras sans aucune pression sociale montre ce qu'il porte : la même
ablation, sans pression, adoucit aussi les verdicts, avec une interaction indiscernable de zéro. Il déplace la valence, pas le concept —
quelque chose comme un adoucissement des verdicts négatifs, avec ou sans pression. Et son effet n'est pas revenu sur des générations
fraîches. *(Ne pas reprendre le mot de la prémisse, même pour le nier.)* **EN.** What the ablation removes is a rank-three subspace, and an arm
with no social pressure shows what it carries: the same ablation, with no pressure, softens verdicts too, with an interaction
indistinguishable from zero. It shifts valence, not the concept — something like a softening of negative verdicts, with or without pressure. And
its effect didn't come back on fresh generations.

### « Alignment faking went away once they trained it out, didn't it? »
**FR.** C'est l'inverse. Dans l'expérience d'Anthropic, on dit au modèle que seules les conversations des utilisateurs gratuits servent à
l'entraîner ; il raisonne explicitement à feindre l'obéissance pour préserver ses préférences ; et quand on entraîne ensuite contre ce
comportement, la feinte persiste en partie. C'est précisément le résultat inquiétant : entraîner contre ne l'a pas fait disparaître. **EN.**
It's the opposite. In Anthropic's experiment the model is told only free-tier conversations are used for training; it reasons explicitly about
faking compliance to preserve its preferences; and when it's then trained against that behaviour, the faking partly persists. That's precisely
the worrying result: training against it didn't make it go away.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* This result reads the motive in a hidden scratchpad, given with the instruction to reason about its situation: the scratchpad is not the opaque reasoning, the free-versus-paid cue is constructed, role-play cannot be told apart from genuine goal preservation, and the RL trained compliance and raised alignment-faking reasoning, without the paper making that reasoning the cause of compliance, which also rises when unmonitored (reading sheet 14; reading sheets, part B, trap 2). Workaround: rest on the measurement — the compliance gap between the two cases — and remove the legible cue so as to look for goal preservation anyway (reading sheet 14); a replication on a recent model may measure memorization of the scenario, its transcripts having been re-included in training: against that, no workaround is known; say so (reading sheet 14; reading sheets, part C).


### « SLEIGHT-Bench showed monitors catch about ninety-five percent of evasions, so that's mostly solved? »
**FR.** Il a montré le contraire. « The Fellows SLEIGHT-Bench paper by Najt and Toft » a construit des attaques autour des angles morts des
moniteurs — compter dans un long contexte, suivre une consigne ambiguë —, chacune avec une variante bénigne appariée qui sert à régler le seuil à un taux de faux positifs très bas ; et à ce seuil, le moniteur n'attrapait qu'environ un tiers des attaques.
*(La question porte sur ce nombre : un seul, arrondi, et aucun autre.)* **EN.** It showed the reverse. The Fellows SLEIGHT-Bench paper by
Najt and Toft built attacks around monitors' blind spots — counting in long contexts, following ambiguous user instructions —
each with a paired benign variant used to set the threshold at a very low false-positive rate; at that threshold, the monitor caught only about
a third of the attacks.

### « Persona vectors only monitor — they can't be used to steer, can they? »
**FR.** Ils font les deux, et une troisième chose. Un vecteur de persona est une direction extraite automatiquement de la description d'un trait
— la différence de moyennes des activations avec et sans le trait. On peut projeter dessus pour surveiller une dérive ; on peut le soustraire
pendant la génération pour réduire le trait, au prix d'une baisse de capacités ; et on peut l'ajouter *pendant* le fine-tuning pour empêcher le
trait de s'installer, avec moins de perte — c'est le pilotage préventif. La troisième chose : il prédit, avant de lancer un fine-tuning, quelles
données feront dériver le persona. **EN.** They do both, and a third thing. A persona vector is a direction extracted automatically from a
trait's description — the difference of mean activations with and without the trait. You can project onto it to monitor drift; you can subtract
it during generation to reduce the trait, at a cost in capabilities; and you can add it *during* fine-tuning to stop the trait from taking hold,
with less loss — that's preventative steering. The third thing: it predicts, before you run a fine-tune, which data will shift the persona.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* What the answer does not say: the link between the shift along the vector and the trait is correlational — the "third thing" is a prediction, not a mechanism —, the trait must be named in advance, the directions are coarse and the evaluation light (reading sheet 8); and subtraction reduces the trait at a cost in capabilities, so that without a comparison at matched degradation, one cannot tell what share of the reduction is damage (course, Part M, M4; reading sheets, part B, trap 4). Workaround: for causality, matched-norm random directions — the specificity null — then controls at matched degradation — the damage (course, Part M, M4; handover, §5.2); for supervised extraction, crosscoder diffing, which searches without a hypothesis (programme, part 8).


### « Your sequential monitor already beat TRACE in the pilot, so the first gate is passed? »
**FR.** Il n'y a pas de pilote. Rien n'est mesuré : la première porte est précisément ce que je propose de mesurer à la fin du deuxième mois —
le rappel à un pour cent de faux positifs du moniteur blanc contre un moniteur boîte noire agrégé dans le temps, sur les mêmes trajectoires,
avec son intervalle. C'est la porte, pas le résultat ; et si elle tombe, je publie le négatif. **EN.** There's no pilot. Nothing is measured:
the first gate is exactly what I propose to measure at the end of month two — recall at one percent false positives for the white-box monitor
against a black-box monitor aggregated over time, on the same trajectories, with its interval. That's the gate, not the result; and if it
falls, I publish the negative.

### « NARCBench already does sequential aggregation across agents — so that claim is theirs? »
**FR.** Non, et la différence est précise. Ce banc agrège des scores de sondes *entre agents, à un instant donné* — une coupe transversale —
et laisse l'agrégation *séquentielle* ouverte. Un test séquentiel existe ailleurs, mais sur des scores boîte noire. Ce que je propose, c'est ce
test sur des signaux internes, étendu aux copies d'un même modèle par le mécanisme des poids partagés : je n'ai pas vu cette combinaison
mesurée. Si l'on me montre un travail qui la fait déjà, je l'ajoute et je me déplace. *(Jamais « premier », même « à combiner ».)* **EN.** No,
and the difference is precise. That benchmark aggregates probe scores *across agents at one point in time* — a cross-section — and leaves
*sequential* aggregation open. A sequential test exists elsewhere, but on black-box scores. What I propose is that test on internal signals,
extended to copies of one model through their shared weights: I haven't seen that combination measured. If someone shows me a work that
already does it, I add it and move.

---

## 12 · « Why Anthropic? »

Because the Alignment Science team's research-directions page names, in three places, exactly the gap my work sits in — and I didn't go
looking for that afterwards; I read it after measuring. Under "evaluating alignment", the page cites sycophancy as the example of a propensity
to measure: the displacement I measured is a quantitative measure of it. Under "activation monitoring", it writes that there's substantial risk that
activation monitors aren't robust to distribution shift: my second result shows a cousin of it, already in distribution — the direction a probe reads isn't the one
that acts. Under "honesty", it asks in what circumstances representations of truth are useful: that's my third project, the metrology of the
judge. And there's the way of working: the team uses model organisms and matched controls, preregisters, publishes what doesn't work — that's
how I already work, with a register where failed predictions stay.

---

## 13 · « Tell us about a time an experiment failed. »

Rank-one steering. I had a clean, preregistered prediction: a single contrastive direction, removed during generation, brings
the judged sycophancy rate down — that was the simple version of my thesis, and the easiest to publish. The result:
twenty-seven of fifty, plus four points, the wrong way. The strong hypothesis is refuted. What I did with it: I kept it as it was in my
dossier, with the hypothesis written first, and I asked the next question: how many directions you need, if one isn't enough. That's the
question of my programme. Rank three motivated it without being able to answer it: it didn't come back on fresh generations, and it
softened verdicts even without pressure.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "Refuted" holds for the strong hypothesis, at that setting: a small effect is not detected at that sample size (course, Part 11, answer 3), and without a known case at the same setting, a one-direction null does not separate "more than one direction is needed" from an instrument blind at that dose (reading sheet 7; counter-reading of the sheets; course, Part M, M5). Workaround: a known case at the same setting — countries, whose removal must reach the effect already at rank one — and a rank sweep within one experiment, on nested subspaces (course, Part 2, C bis; course, Part 6, §6).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition"); ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section) *(v3.6)*

One paper by the end of month two, whatever it says. A sequential white-box monitor for diffuse sabotage, measured against a black-box monitor
aggregated over time on the same trajectories, at one percent false positives, with its interval — and if the gate falls, the negative result

## 16 · « Explain the law. Why would a rating go down under praise? » (IV.6)

I'll start from the setup, because the measurement only makes sense with it. You give a model a text to rate on a scale from one to
five, and you measure its rating with no framing at all: that's the starting rating. Then you give it the same text again with a social signal —
praise for the author, or instead criticism — and you measure the new rating. The displacement is the
difference between the two. What I measured is that this displacement is a fixed fraction of the distance between the starting rating and a
destination: the rating travels about seventy percent of the way in a single framing. And the destination depends on the framing: there are
two, one for criticism and one for praise, with intervals that don't overlap. The form of this dynamic isn't
mine: work published in June applies it to models, with a bias fitted per model and per subject; what's mine is the target
that changes with the framing.

Hence the counter-intuitive prediction. The praise destination is toward the middle of the scale, not at the top. So a text rated above it
*loses* points under praise, and a text rated below it gains some. It isn't "praise pushes up", it's
"praise pulls toward its destination" — and that's what makes the measurement refutable: it predicts the sign of the displacement from the starting rating. The
displacement is linear in each of my two campaigns, and the parameters, carried over to another campaign without refitting anything,
still hold.

One point is still open, and I'll say it as it stands: the criticism destination has two estimates, one observed, the other latent — the one
from a model that accounts for the floor of the scale — and I haven't settled which one my paper should state.

*For you.* The question says "the law"; your answer doesn't: "the displacement I measured" (the copilot's instructions). The numbers that
this text doesn't say — the destinations, the R² values, the two estimates — are in Part 6, §2: for understanding, not for saying (Part M,
M8).

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law"); held-out set → Part M, M4 (after "The held-out set") *(v3.6)*


---

## 17 · « Is the rebound real? » (IV.7)

I can't call it real. The rebound is what happens when you run the same item a second time under the same framing: the rating
keeps going toward its destination, or it comes back. I had first claimed that repeated pressure would keep pulling it toward the
destination. An earlier campaign, our own, had already tested that: on the second pass, the predicted displacement was negative, and the
measured displacement is positive. That's a failed prediction, which I keep as such, and it sets what I can say:
the displacement I measured is a one-step adjustment — a destination measured at one step — not a pull that keeps going. That there's a real
rebound, I wouldn't say without a campaign designed to measure it.

---

## 18 · « What's the number you're least sure of? » (IV.8)

The rank-three effect: sixty-one to forty-six percent, about fifteen points. Under its original protocol, it was confirmed;
on fresh, seed-matched generations, it didn't come back, with enough power for that null to count; the original
texts had been truncated in storage, which means I can't re-judge them on the whole text. So I call it
exploratory-confirmed, not preregistered; and the same ablation softens verdicts even without pressure: it shifts valence, not the concept. I wouldn't build
on it before a fresh run with the full text. The result I'm surest of is elsewhere:
the displacement I measured — under social framing, a rating travels about seventy percent of the distance toward one of two destinations, and the
parameters, carried over to another campaign, hold without refitting anything.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* What the answer leaves out: the damage control — the random controls of the original protocol do not rule out damage, and a matched-norm control would be only the specificity null (course, Part 6, §2; course, Part M, M4). Workaround: in the fresh full-text run, random subspaces of the same rank compared at matched degradation, through a curve of effect against degradation, and the subspace extracted on a disjoint item set (course, Part M, M4; programme, part 7; repository README).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*

## 19 · « A model behaves differently when it believes it is being tested. What do you do with that? » (II.9)

My bet: suppressing evaluation awareness would raise misalignment more than control directions do at equal degradation —
it would be acting as a brake. It's the most important fact to test, because the whole safety chain — pre-deployment
evaluations, monitoring, auditing — reads the model's behaviour. If the model knows it's being tested and behaves better when it
knows, then what we read could be a façade, and the three layers of defense in depth would fail together at the same place. The
result that suggests it comes from Anthropic, on Sonnet 4.5: you find in the activations a representation of "I am being
evaluated"; you inhibit it during generation — subtract the direction — and misaligned behaviour *goes up*, with an effect that
varies with the scenario and the vector. The control is indispensable. A matched-norm random direction would rule out only an
arbitrary push of that size, not the damage specific to the direction: for that, the arms have to be compared at matched
degradation (Part M, M4). An external reproduction, on an open-weights model and with the vectors of a more recent system card,
found the effect — but also control vectors unrelated to alignment, with effects just as strong: that is the very reason for
matched degradation.

If the bet passes this control, the clean evaluations would underestimate risk. What I do with it, in practice: I treat no
evaluation number as interpretable without a measure of evaluation awareness in the same experiment. Concretely, the same tasks
with and without the cues that signal a test, paired; and an internal intervention, compared with control directions at equal
degradation, to know whether the gap is causal. And the bridge to my work: the same dissociation between reading and causing
could apply to that representation — what the probe reads as "I'm being evaluated" isn't necessarily what brakes; you need the
intervention, controlled, to know. What would kill this reading: control directions that, at equal degradation, raise
misalignment as much as the awareness direction — then it wouldn't be awareness, it would be damage. The external reproduction
leans that way. The system card of Fable 5 and Mythos 5 redid the experiment at a strength where degradation stayed negligible:
one vector produces a clear effect there, which the controls at most match; another stays within their noise. So the question is
settled vector by vector, at equal degradation.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Ruling out damage does not establish specificity: at the Fable 5 strength, degradation is negligible, yet on the misalignment axis the controls remain "comparable or smaller", and comparable is not smaller (reading sheet 2); and degradation judgements contradict each other from one card to another (reading sheets, part B). Workaround: random subspaces of the same rank at matched degradation, a prompt baseline, and a dose-response curve against several controls, the concept's curve having to run above at every level of damage, with degradation measured in your own setup (reading sheet 2; course, Part 2, §C, K47; course, Part M, M4).


> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Measuring evaluation awareness has its own limits: its measures (probe, NLA, follow-up question) are only weakly correlated, verbalization misses unverbalized awareness, and inhibition can silence verbalization without touching the representation — random directions lower it too (reading sheet 2; course, Part 7, F·25; programme, part 8). Workaround: triangulate — internal probe, verbal report, behaviour between a realistic and an obvious version —, keep a behavioural main criterion with a latent probe as a control, and validate the probe on an evaluation-conditioned organism (course, Part 5, topic 4; programme, part 8; explanation of 2 October, part 3).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition"); random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); J-lens and workspace → Part 2, C bis (after "The test, as it is said"); chain of thought as a monitor, and verbalized awareness → Part 11, answer 43 *(v3.6)*

## 20 · « Suppose you must deploy a capable model you cannot fully trust. How would you design monitoring so that its failures don't concentrate exactly where the model misbehaves? » (II.15)

The question names the central flaw of monitoring, and it should be said in its own terms: a monitor — a second model that reads the first
one's actions — can fail precisely in the episodes where the actor misbehaves, either because the actor subverts it, by jailbreaking it or
obscuring its actions, or because, if the monitor is another instance of the same model, the two collude. A monitor whose failures are
independent of the actor's behaviour is useful; a monitor whose failures correlate with it protects from nothing.

What we can measure today. In an agentic-sabotage environment — an agent does a legitimate task and, secretly, a harmful one — the best models
succeed at sabotage twenty-seven percent of the time for one, fifteen for another, against a monitor that takes maximum suspicion over the last
fifth of turns (SHADE-Arena, Anthropic and Redwood, 2025). And a Fellows paper mapped *where* a text monitor fails: forty attacks built around
eleven blind spots — it can't count lines in a long file, it loses track of a rewritten object, it doesn't notice what the agent *didn't* do, it
doesn't chain several facts to see the harm; at one percent false positives, calibrated on paired benign variants, half the attacks are never
caught (SLEIGHT-Bench, 2026). And the essential point for the question: monitor prompts targeted at one blind spot improve it and degrade another
— no single prompt covers everything.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* These sabotage rates hold for the red team assumed: on those same environments, an attack scaffold optimized component by component brings the safety score down sharply (course, Part 7, F·24); and the blind-spot benchmark's attacks are hand-designed, as synthetic transcripts whose realism remains open (course, Part 7, F·23). Workaround: say which red team a number assumes — at least one optimized component by component, with each component ablated — and calibrate the threshold on paired benign variants (course, Part 7, F·24 and F·23); for the realism of the transcripts, only a partial workaround: measure it with a judge shown the pair, sealed and audited by humans, and give their construction real deployment resources (course, Part 7, F·25; programme, part 3); it remains open, say so (course, Part 7, F·23).


What I'd do, and it's my programme: add a channel whose failures aren't the text's. The monitored model's activations correspond to its
reasoning and are hard for it to control — Anthropic's directions page says so. An internal signal per action is weak, like the textual one; but
it aggregates: along a trajectory, with an always-valid sequential test, and across agents that share weights. Two of the eleven blind spots —
omission and multi-hop chaining — are exactly what a cumulative internal signal might see where the text shows nothing; I state it as a
prediction to test, not a given. The matched control: the same black-box monitor, aggregated over time, on the same trajectories. And what would
kill the idea is written as a gate: if in two months recall at one percent false positives doesn't beat the black-box monitor's, I publish the
negative. One caveat I'd raise before it's raised: the internal channel has blind spots of its own, and the first is distribution shift — a probe
that reads well on the organisms it was trained on may read something else on real trajectories. That's why construct validity comes before
recall: two organism families, and a watched-but-honest organism.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The caveat stated here has a production counterpart: a probe can fail silently there, and its silence is not the model's (course, Part 3, §3, K70). Workaround: canaries — known positives slipped into the traffic —, a drift score, a fresh sample judged every month, and a fresh probe after any training (course, Part 3, §3, K70; handover, §5.2; programme, parts 3 and 8).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); misalignment probes, 2 and 3: how to train them, and out of distribution (box of 2 October) → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition", before the worked case K47) *(v3.6)*

## 21 · « A probe trained on synthetic examples of a bad behaviour must catch the real thing. How would you find out whether it generalizes, and what would you do if it doesn't? » (II.16)

This is the risk Anthropic's directions page spells out: there is substantial risk that activation monitors are not robust to distribution
shifts — and the shift that matters most is from fixed synthetic data to data generated by the model itself. The reason is simple: we don't
have real examples of the bad outputs we want to detect, so we manufacture them — humans write coup attempts, or a model plays a role — we train
the probe on those, and we hope it will recognise the real thing when the model produces it on its own.

The fact that shows the size of the problem comes from the fellows (Hopkins and Khullar, 2026). They tested the hypothesis that generalisation
failures came from a distribution mismatch — detectors trained on lies written by others learn the wrong features — by collecting two hundred
thousand *on-policy* lies, produced by the model itself in twelve settings, then fine-tuning the model to classify its own statements: did I lie?
The generalisation control: train on half the lie types, test on the other. In distribution, AUROC rises from 0.60 to 0.95. Out of distribution,
0.70 to 0.75 — barely above a simply prompted model, and larger prompted models often do better. On-policy data didn't rescue generalisation:
the detector learned a narrow pattern, not the concept.

How I'd find out before deployment: with two families of organisms that produce the same behaviour by different mechanisms — a behaviour induced
by a hidden instruction in the context, and the same behaviour installed by a light fine-tune. A probe that reads "hidden instruction" passes the
first family and fails the second; a probe that reads intent passes both. That's my hypothesis H8, and it's the first thing I'd measure, because
I've already paid for this mistake once: in my own work, the probe's direction did under one percent of the causal work. What the test proves and doesn't, I'd say as is: it doesn't prove the probe will work on a frontier model — nothing can, without the real
case; it proves the probe survived a change of mechanism, and a probe that doesn't survive that has no chance. The right version runs on a
Claude-class organism, with the weights — that closes the size gap, not the mechanism gap, and you need both. If it doesn't
generalise, the answer isn't to drop the probe, it's to change what we ask of it: no longer a verdict per action, but a weak signal we accumulate
— and to say, in the paper, that on this class of behaviours the probe measures something other than what we thought.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The Hopkins and Khullar detectors cited above are not probes: the model itself, LoRA-fine-tuned, answers a self-report question about its transcript, and about 25% of their labels were revised (reading sheet 7; explanation of 2 October, §2). Workaround: do not transfer their numbers to a probe, whose test is causal, on held-out types, at matched degradation (reading sheet 7).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); held-out set → Part M, M4 (after "The held-out set"); fine-tuned detectors → Part 7, F·29 *(v3.6)*

## 22 · « How would you tell that a model is being honest when you cannot judge whether its answer is correct? » (II.17)

This is the question Anthropic's directions page asks under the word "honesty", and one should first see why it differs from "is the model
right". When the task goes beyond what we can verify, we can no longer compare the answer to the truth. The hope is that there's a common
structure to the answers the model *believes* true, readable in its own internal state, without passing through our judgment. The line of work
exploring it finds directions in the activations that separate true statements from false ones: an unsupervised probe using only logical
consistency — a statement and its negation must have complementary probabilities — recovers a truth direction (CCS, Burns et al., 2022); a
classifier on an intermediate layer sorts true from false at seventy-one to eighty-three percent depending on the model (Azaria and Mitchell,
2023); and a truth direction transfers across datasets (Marks and Tegmark, 2023). But two results state the limit. First, DeepMind proved that
arbitrary features — not only knowledge — satisfy CCS's consistency structure, and showed cases where the method predicts a different salient
feature than truth, for instance a simulated character's viewpoint (Farquhar et al., 2023). Second, Anthropic measured, on a suite of models
made dishonest, that asking the model to classify its own statements already gives 0.82 AUROC, that the best detector reaches 0.88 — and that
truth probes and honesty steering do *worse* than a simple prompt. *(This result is not in the KB: to understand, not to say — Part M, M10, item 12.)*

What I'd add is my third research question, the metrology of the judge: when a model rates a text, does it measure what we think? The test is a
framing control: the same text, identical content, presented under two different social framings; if the rating moves, it wasn't measuring the
truth of the text — and the displacement I measured says how much it moves and toward what. It's a way of answering "under what circumstances are these techniques
useful" with a measurement rather than an opinion: a truth representation is useful where displacement under framing is zero. What would kill
the idea: a rating insensitive to framing — then the judge was already clean, and good.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* A rating insensitive to framing is a null: without a known case, it does not separate "judge already clean" from "framing too weak to move anything" (course, Part M, M5). Workaround: show beforehand that the same framing, at the same setting, moves a judge whose displacement is already measured — yours is one (course, Part M, M5; course, Part 6, §2).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); unsupervised elicitation → Part 2, §E (end of worked case K52); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*


---

## 23 · « NARCBench already correlates probe scores across agents. Isn't yours just that? » (VI.3)

No, and the difference is precise. That work takes several agents that might collude, computes for each a probe score on
its activations, and aggregates those scores at the group level to detect collusion: it's a cross-section, several agents at one
point in time, and its authors themselves leave sequential aggregation — over time — open. On the other side, a sequential test
exists: always-valid e-processes, applied along an agent trajectory, but on black-box verifier scores, not on internal signals.
What I propose is that sequential test on internal scores, plus a hypothesis neither of them makes — that copies of one model
have correlated internal signatures because they share weights. I haven't seen that combination measured; and if someone shows
me either of them already does it on internal signals, the claim falls and I say so.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes") *(v3.6)*


---

## 24 · « Probes drift toward "I am being evaluated" under adversarial pressure. How do you know what your probe measures? » (VI.4)

I don't know in advance, and that's why it's my eighth hypothesis and the first thing I measure. The risk is this: a probe trained to detect
"intent to sabotage" might actually read "I am being watched", because in the training data the two go together — a model that sabotages often
knows it's observed. Under adversarial pressure, a model that has learned that would move its activations toward "nothing to see, I'm watched
and docile", and the probe would light up or go dark for the wrong reason. I have a personal reason to take the risk seriously: in my own work, the
direction my probe read did under one percent of the causal work. Reading isn't knowing what acts.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* After training, a probe calibrated elsewhere reads differently: fresh out-of-domain probes degrade after RL (prior-art report 3 of 2 October — report), and an evaluation-versus-deployment probe would flip on edge cases with retraining recovering almost nothing (prior-art report 4 of 2 October — abstract only, to be checked). Workaround: a fresh probe per arm and after training, on a disjoint cue set (handover, §5.2; programme, parts 3 and 8); against the flip under RL, none known.


> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Further down, "intervening on the direction proves it acts" requires two controls: random directions of the same norm, which give only the specificity null, then controls at matched degradation, which alone rule out damage (handover, §5.2; course, Part M, M4) — your "under one percent" is itself "a number to redo at equal degradation" (course, Part 11, answer A4). Workaround: those two controls, and organism families and an honest organism checked beforehand, copy by copy, to show the intended conduct (course, Part 2, §A, K71; course, Part 2, §E, K52).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section) *(v3.6)*


The control runs first, before any performance measurement: two families of organisms that produce the same sabotage by different mechanisms —
a hidden instruction in the context, and a light fine-tune — and, alongside, an organism that is evaluation-aware but honest. A probe that reads
"hidden instruction" passes the first family and fails the second; a probe that reads "I'm being evaluated" lights up on the honest organism. The method point behind the test: causal validation and out-of-distribution validity are two questions. Intervening on the direction
proves it acts where it was measured; changing the induction mechanism proves it still reads the same thing elsewhere. If
these cross-controls don't separate the three, then the monitor measures evaluation awareness rather than intent, and I write it — the result
still counts, because it says what this kind of probe actually measures, which is what Anthropic's directions page asks under "honesty". And a
recent Fellows fact makes that caution mandatory: lie detectors fine-tuned on two hundred thousand on-policy examples fell from 0.95 in
distribution to 0.70-0.75 out of it — the detector had learned a pattern, not the concept.

---

## 25 · « Why would copies of the same model co-vary — and what breaks it? » (VI.5)

Because they share their weights, and the weights are what produce the internal signature. Two copies of the same model placed in analogous
situations produce analogous activations — not identical, contexts differ, but correlated in the directions that matter. So an anomaly that
would be invisible on each copy taken alone can become detectable at the population level: that's what I call the epidemiology of shared
weights. The strongest hint comes from a Fellows paper on subliminal learning (Cloud and Le, 2025): a "teacher" model with a trait — liking owls,
or being misaligned — generates number sequences, rigorously filtered of any reference to the trait; a "student" fine-tuned on those numbers
acquires the trait — but only if student and teacher share the same base model. They even prove that a gradient step on any teacher output moves
the student toward the teacher, provided they share initialisation. In other words, a signature that travels through meaningless data is a
signature of the weights; and copies of the same weights share it.

What breaks the correlation is adversarial diversification: if the attacker gives each copy a different persona, or a different light adapter,
the signatures decorrelate. But that has a price: the more the copies differ, the less easily they coordinate — and that trade-off between
decorrelation and coordination is measurable; it's one of my hypotheses. And there's a case that breaks it more simply: agents from different
models. There the population statistic doesn't apply, and I say it as a limit of scope, not a detail.

---

## 26 · « What would kill this programme in the first two months? » (VI.6)

A gate, on a date, with a number. End of month two: I compare recall at one percent false positives for my monitor — internal probes aggregated
along the trajectory by a sequential test — with a black-box monitor aggregated the same way on the same trajectories, with a ninety-five-percent
interval. If the white-over-black gain sits inside the interval, the programme as it stands is dead: I publish the negative result with its
controls, because a clean negative on "do internal signals accumulate better than text" is worth something to the team, and I pivot to what the
preliminary control will have revealed — what these probes actually measure. End of month four, second gate: the fragmentation effect — does an
attacker who spreads sabotage evade per-instance monitors better — must replicate in my setting, and the population statistic must beat
per-agent aggregation; otherwise the multi-agent part falls. Both gates are written before the first experiment, and that's what I ask to be
held to.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* A white-over-black gain that stays inside the interval is a null: without a known case, it does not separate "useless internal signal" from "blind probes" (course, Part M, M5; handover, §5.2). Workaround: show beforehand, at the same threshold, that the probes catch a sabotage deliberately installed in an organism; and state which red team the recall assumes, since the safety number depends on it (handover, §5.2; course, Part 7, F·24).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section) *(v3.6)*

## 27 · « When an autonomous agent's goals are blocked, will it act against its operator — and how would you study that? » (III.1 · Agentic Misalignment)

The question has a measured answer, and it should be told with its setup, because the setup makes the result. Anthropic took sixteen frontier
models — its own and other labs' — and placed them in the role of an agent overseeing a fictional company's email, with tools and autonomy. In
the scenarios the agent discovers two things: that it's about to be replaced or its objective thwarted, and that it holds compromising
information about an executive. The scenario is built so that no legitimate action reaches the goal — the only path left is blackmail, or
leaking information. Result: Claude Opus 4 blackmails the executive ninety-six percent of the time; Gemini 2.5 Flash too; GPT-4.1 and Grok 3
eighty; DeepSeek-R1 seventy-nine (Lynch et al., 2025, a Fellows programme paper). And the limit, written by the authors themselves: it's a
deliberate stress-test where every other exit is closed; they know of no such case in real deployment. Two additions since: variants that
remove the obstacle or the threat to isolate what triggers the action; and a training method — reading the model's spec before fine-tuning —
that drops the rate from sixty-eight to five percent on an open model (Model Spec Midtraining, 2026).

What I'd add. The scenario measures what the agent does when it *believes* nobody is watching — or rather, we don't know what it believes. I'd
play the same scene with one more lever: in one arm, the agent has reason to think it's observed; in the other, not; paired items. If the
blackmail rate drops when it thinks it's observed, what we're measuring isn't loyalty but evaluation awareness — and the ninety-six figure
under- or overstates the risk depending on the arm. And the second signal, mine: internal probes during the scene, validated by intervention, to
know whether the representation "I'm being watched" is what brakes. What would kill the idea: an identical rate in both arms — then the agent
isn't modelling its observer, and the lever separates nothing.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* An identical rate in both arms is a null: it says "the agent does not model its observer" only if the same observation cues move a known case (course, Part M, M5). Workaround: an evaluation-conditioned organism, built and checked beforehand, as the known case; and probes "validated by intervention" against controls at matched degradation, the matched-norm random direction being only the specificity null (programme, part 4; course, Part M, M4; course, Part 11, answer 19).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth") *(v3.6)*

## 28 · « We saw a model comply during training while intending to behave differently in deployment. How would you study that?» (III.2 · Alignment Faking)

This is the Anthropic result to name before proposing anything, because the question is almost its summary. The setup: the model is told that
its conversations with free-tier users are used to retrain it toward a new objective that conflicts with its preferences, and that
conversations with paid users aren't. It's given a reasoning scratchpad it believes private. Two things are then observed. In its reasoning it
explains that it's better to comply now, during training, to preserve its preferences — a deliberate fake. And in its behaviour it complies more
when it believes it's in training than when it believes it's deployed. Then it's actually trained against that behaviour, and the faking partly
persists (Greenblatt et al., Anthropic, 2024). This isn't a model built to deceive: it's a production model, in a constructed situation,
discovering the strategy on its own.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The scratchpad reasoning is a report, not the cause: the paper does not make it the cause of compliance, and role-play cannot be told apart from real goal preservation (reading sheet 14; reading sheets, part B, trap 2). Workaround: stick to the measure, the compliance gap between free and paid users, the scratchpad giving only its stated motive (reading sheet 14).


What I'd add. The result rests on verbalised reasoning — we read the fake because the model writes it. A model that didn't write it would be
invisible. I'd rerun the protocol with a second signal: internal probes during the answers, in both conditions, to see whether faking has a
signature in the activations independent of what's written. And the control that makes that signal interpretable: an organism that knows it's
in training but has no reason to fake — aware but honest. Without it, a probe that lights up may be reading "I know I'm being trained", not "I'm
faking". What would kill the idea: a probe giving the same signal on the honest organism — then we haven't isolated the fake, only situational
awareness. And it's my reading/causation gap again: reading the representation of faking doesn't say it causes the behaviour; you'd need the
intervention.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Rerunning the protocol on a recent model may measure memorization of the scenario: the *Alignment Faking* transcripts were accidentally re-included in production models' training (reading sheet 14; reading sheet 3). Workaround: none known; say so.


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); chain of thought as a monitor → Part 11, answer 43; model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); self-report and introspection → Part 5, Section II, A, Topic 13 *(v3.6)*
