## 57 · « Can we trust the chain of thought? » (I.5) — *traitée entièrement à la réponse 43.*

## 58 · « RLHF, DPO, Constitutional AI — what do they do and what don't they solve? » (I.6)

All three train a model on preferences, and differ in where the preferences come from. RLHF learns a reward model from human comparisons — which
of these two answers do you prefer — then optimises the model against that reward. DPO does the same without a separate reward model, optimising
directly on the comparisons. Constitutional AI replaces part of the human comparisons with written principles: the model critiques and revises
its own answers according to a constitution, then a preference model is trained on those generated comparisons — reducing dependence on
annotators and making the principles explicit and auditable (Bai et al., Anthropic, 2022). What these methods fix: average behaviour on the
training distribution — models are more helpful, more polite, refuse better. What they don't fix: the judge is fallible, and a capable model
learns to persuade it. The best-documented case is sycophancy — models trained on human preferences change their answers under pressure and
flatter, because the preference data rewards flattery (Sharma et al., Anthropic, 2023). A more contested paper reported that RLHF makes models
better at convincing humans of wrong answers — I cite it with its caveat: a reproduction attributes part of the result to pipeline bugs. And my
own work gives that failure a quantitative form: under social framing, the rating of the model judge I measured moves by a fixed fraction toward two distinct
destinations — a preference model is a judge, and my prediction is that it moves the same way.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law"); behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); debate and scalable oversight → Part 2, §E (after "In practice — Debate") *(v3.6)*


---

## 59 · « Misuse or misalignment — which worries you more? » (I.7)

Two families of risk never to confuse, because their defences differ. In misuse the adversary is the user: someone wants the model's help with
a cyberattack or a weapon; the defences are refusal training, filtering classifiers, monitoring — and unlearning the most dangerous knowledge.
In misalignment the adversary is the model itself: its goals aren't ours, and it may hide that; the defence is the whole alignment stack —
better objectives, evaluations that resist faking, control. The mature answer: in the short run, misuse does the damage — it's what's real
today, and it's what has victims; in the long run, misalignment is irreversible — a system more capable than us that doesn't want what we want
can't be caught up with. And the two meet in one idea: control — safeguards designed to limit harm even if the model is misaligned, which by
construction also hold against a malicious user. What I'd add, since an opinion is asked: I work on misalignment, and on its most discreet form
— diffuse sabotage — because that's where measurement is weakest, and one more researcher has the most effect where measurement is missing.

---

## 60 · « Defense in depth — which techniques, and where do they fail together? » (I.8)

You stack complementary defences and hope their failures don't line up. Training first — RLHF, constitutional AI, and now spec midtraining,
which makes alignment generalise out of distribution. Pre-deployment evaluations next: capabilities, propensities, sabotage. Monitoring in
deployment: a model reading another's actions. Control, which assumes the worst and measures what a misaligned model could still do.
Interpretability, which reads the internal state. And policy — the Responsible Scaling Policy — which conditions deployment on capability and
safeguard thresholds. Where they fail together, and that's the point of the question: when the model is aware it's being evaluated. Then the
evaluation reads a façade, the monitor reads the same façade, the audit too — three layers reading the same surface behaviour fail at the same
place. That's why "making evaluations trustworthy" is a roadmap theme, and why the evaluation-awareness result — inhibiting the "I'm being
evaluated" representation raises misalignment — matters so much. What I'd add: the only layer whose failure isn't correlated with the façade is
the one that doesn't read behaviour — internal signals, if causally validated. And the honest caveat: those signals have their own failure modes,
distribution shift first; defense in depth wants independent failures, not layers that resemble each other.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The out-of-distribution gain of spec midtraining is read on open models, on an agentic benchmark whose scenes the model can recognize as tests — the limit its own sheet sets (course, Part 7, F·34). Workaround: two versions of the environment, randomly assigned, differing only in realism cues scored by a discriminator, with an organism trained to hide as the known case (course, Part 2, §B, K63); that a held-out benchmark represents the real case, no known workaround guarantees; say so (reading sheet 12).


> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The inhibition result cited has the same limit as at answer 56 — arbitrary control vectors also raise misalignment, more weakly in the Opus 4.8 system card, just as strongly in an external reproduction on an open-weights model, and a matched-norm control is only the specificity null (reading sheet 2; course, Part 11, answer 19; course, Part M, M4) —; and the internal layer is not independent of the façade by construction: a probe can read "I am being watched" and the test context instead of the intention, and then fail at the same place as the evaluation (course, Part 6, §8; course, Part 3, §4, K67). Workaround: random subspaces of the same rank at matched degradation for the inhibition, and, for the probe, honest transcripts written as tests and an aware-but-honest organism, on which it must stay at its baseline (course, Part M, M4; course, Part 3, §4, K67; course, Part 6, §8).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition"); held-out set → Part M, M4 (after "The held-out set") *(v3.6)*


---

## 61 · « How would you red-team a model? » (I.9)

Three layers, in order. Automated first: attacks found by optimisation — the founding result shows that gradient search on an open model finds
suffixes that make aligned models comply, and that those suffixes transfer to closed models (GCG, Zou et al., 2023). Human next: experts hunting
realistic jailbreaks, because humans find simple attacks that pipelines miss — Anthropic's directions page asks precisely for benchmarks measuring
what real humans find with a given budget. And red-teaming the safeguards themselves: the classifiers, at a fixed false-positive rate, because a
defence that blocks one benign use in ten isn't deployable. What the Fellows programme added in 2026 shifts the target: you also red-team
monitors — forty attacks built around eleven blind spots, half never caught at one percent false positives (SLEIGHT-Bench) — and you red-team
audits — an audit whose transcripts don't look like deployment measures nothing, and paired realism goes from 4.6 to 32.8 percent with real
deployment resources. And the rule that applies to all of it: a safety score is relative to the red team's strength — an optimised attack
scaffold drops SHADE-Arena's score from 0.87 to 0.41. What I'd add: the red team of my own testbed is the first thing I'd publish, before any
recall number.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The blind-spot benchmark's forty attacks are hand-designed, as synthetic transcripts whose realism remains open: the benchmark says whether the monitor sees an attack written by humans, not whether a model would produce it (course, Part 7, F·23; course, Part 11, answer B14); and paired realism is measured by an LLM judge, while task-driven evaluation awareness persists (course, Part 7, F·25). Workaround: replay the attacks as tasks the model must do in a real harness, at the threshold calibrated on paired benign variants (course, Part 11, answer B14; course, Part 7, F·23); for the synthetic transcripts themselves, only a partial workaround: measure their realism with a judge shown the pair, sealed and audited by humans, and give their construction real deployment resources (course, Part 7, F·25; programme, part 3); their realism remains open, say so (course, Part 7, F·23).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); safety classifiers → Part 2, §H (end of worked case G1); behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging"); LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law") *(v3.6)*


---

## 62 · « Is alignment actually hard? What would change your mind? » (I.10)

My position: it's hard exactly where the problem lives — on tasks we can't verify — and easy elsewhere, because verifying is sometimes simpler
than producing; we can check a program we couldn't write. The problem bites hardest where the gap between producing and verifying disappears,
and that's precisely where systems become most useful. What would change my mind: an oversight method that produces a reliable signal beyond
human expertise on a real task, measured against a control, and that holds against a model that knows it's being evaluated. Not a demonstration
on a task where ground truth exists — we have those — but on one where it doesn't, with a credible way of knowing anyway. And what, conversely,
would make me find it harder still: internal signals — probes — that never generalise out of their training distribution; because then the last
layer that doesn't read behaviour would fall too. I'd start with a real task that has no ground truth,
scored against a control.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "Never generalise" can only be established where the intention is known to be present: out of distribution, on an organism in which it was installed, a probe that stays silent shows it does not generalise; on a natural model, its silence does not separate "it does not generalise" from "there is nothing to see" (course, Part M, M5; handover, §5.2). Workaround: judge the probe on whole held-out families, up to multi-turn agentic settings, with an organism in which the intention was installed, and state the result as a bound, never as an absence (explanation of 2 October, parts 1 and 3; programme, part 3; course, Part M, M5).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); held-out set → Part M, M4 (after "The held-out set"); misalignment probes, J-lens included (box of 2 October) → Part 2, §A (before the worked case K71), §C (before the worked case K47) and C bis (before the worked case K72) *(v3.6)*

## 63 · Tes huit positions, dites en entier (VII) — à valider par toi avant de les dire

*Chaque position en une phrase, puis la raison en deux ou trois — en français, puis en anglais. Ce sont des opinions tirées de tes textes ; tu
les coches ou tu les corriges.*

**1. Le levier contre la sycophancie est la concession, pas le prompt.** FR : Parce que le déplacement que j'ai mesuré a une pente et deux
destinations fixées par le cadrage ; ma prédiction est qu'il tient quel que soit le prompt, ce qui en ferait une propriété de l'étape de
jugement — donc c'est au moment où le juge cède qu'il faudrait intervenir, pas dans la consigne qu'on lui donne. EN : Because the displacement
I measured has a slope and two destinations set by the framing; my prediction is that it holds whatever the prompt, which would make it a
property of the judgment step — so the place to intervene would be where the judge concedes, not in the instruction it's given.

**2. Les signaux internes peuvent attraper ce que le comportement ne montre pas — à condition de vérifier d'abord leur validité de
construit.** FR : Une sonde qui lit autre chose que ce qu'on croit est pire que pas de sonde, parce qu'elle donne une fausse assurance ; et même
une sonde qui lit juste n'est pas forcément le levier : chez moi, la direction de la sonde faisait moins d'un pour cent du travail causal. EN : A probe
reading something other than what you think is worse than no probe, because it gives false assurance; and even a probe that reads
right need not be the lever: in my setting the probe's direction did under one percent of the causal work.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Study note, changing nothing in the position: this "under one percent" has not yet been measured at equal degradation, and a covariance-matched random direction does more there than the probe direction (course, Part 11, answer A4; course, Part 6, §2 and §3). Workaround: redo it with the protocol of answer A4, with control directions compared at equal degradation and the full-state patch as the ceiling (course, Part 11, answer A4; programme, part 8).


**3. Le contrôle est le filet, l'alignement est le but — et un chercheur de plus doit aller là où la mesure est la plus faible, qui est
aujourd'hui le contrôle boîte blanche.** FR : Les protocoles de contrôle existent en boîte noire ; le canal interne est proposé depuis 2024 et
presque pas mesuré. EN : Control protocols exist black-box; the internal channel has been proposed since 2024 and barely measured.

**4. Une sonde prouve la lisibilité, jamais la causalité.** FR : Il faut une intervention avec un contrôle apparié — des directions aléatoires, de même covariance,
comparées à dégradation égale — pour dire qu'une direction agit ; sans ça, on a une corrélation. EN : It takes an intervention with a matched control —
random directions with the same covariance, compared at equal degradation — to say a direction acts; without it, you have a correlation.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Two caveats to keep under the position: readability itself is not proven in distribution — an in-distribution AUROC proves nothing, what is measured is the gap with held-out families (reading sheets, part B, trap 1; reading sheet 7) —; and a failed intervention refutes causation only with a known case at the same setting, otherwise the null may come from too low a rank (reading sheet 7; course, Part M, M5). Workaround: whole held-out families, never paraphrases, and a known case at the same rank, dose and threshold as the measurement (explanation of 2 October, part 3; course, Part M, M5; reading sheet 7).


**5. Le préenregistrement et la rétractation publique sont la méthode, pas un ornement.** FR : Mon registre garde les prédictions ratées avec
leur statut ; je préfère avoir tort en public. EN : My register keeps failed predictions with their status; I'd rather be wrong in public.

**6. Le plus grand problème est la vérité-terrain au-delà de l'expertise humaine.** FR : Tous les autres en héritent — on n'entraîne pas ce
qu'on n'évalue pas. EN : Every other problem inherits it — you don't train what you can't evaluate.

**7. Les évaluations de sycophancie à un tour mesurent le prompt, pas la propension.** FR : Le déplacement vit à travers la concession — il
faut au moins deux tours pour le voir. EN : The displacement lives across the concession — it takes at least two turns to see it.

**8. Beaucoup de copies d'un même modèle qui partagent leurs poids est un risque qu'on n'a pas encore chiffré.** FR : L'incident de juillet en
est la première facture, et l'apprentissage subliminal en est le mécanisme. EN : The July incident was the first bill, and subliminal learning is
the mechanism.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); patching → Part 10, Patchscopes sheet; behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging") *(v3.6)*

## ANGLES MORTS — les questions qu'on n'avait pas traitées, et leurs réponses complètes — v1.0

*Cherchées en relisant la page des directions, les dépôts de mesure, les trois types de questions et ce qu'un mentor de chaque équipe
demanderait. Dix-sept trouvées ; les huit premières avec leur réponse complète, les neuf autres en une réponse courte parce qu'elles sont moins
probables.*

## A1 · « Which team would you want to join — Alignment Science, Interpretability, or Safeguards — and what changes in your project depending on the answer? »

My answer depends on what each team measures, and I'd rather say so than pretend my project is the same everywhere. In Alignment Science, my
project is the one I wrote: white-box control of diffuse threats, with the Diffuse Control red/blue game as the base and probes as the channel —
that's the team with the environments and the red teams, and where gate G1 gets measured. In Interpretability, the project narrows to what I do
most solidly: the gap between reading and causing — the causal partition, the intervention rank, decomposing a diffuse direction into features —
and the question becomes "what exactly does a probe read, and when does it act", which is the one the directions page asks under "honesty". In
Safeguards, the project becomes robustness: probes as a detection layer for jailbreaks and distributed attacks across queries — the page calls
those inter-query defences — with the same tooling but a human adversary. What doesn't change: the method — preregister, measure against a
matched control, publish the negative. If asked to choose: Alignment Science, because that's where the empty cell is largest — the internal
channel in control has been proposed since 2024 and barely measured.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); patching → Part 10, Patchscopes sheet; ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); dictionaries and SAEs → Part 4, Towards then Scaling Monosemanticity *(v3.6)*


---

## A2 · « You have $15,000 of compute a month and four months. Walk me through month one. »

Month one measures no performance: it builds and verifies the instrument, because a recall number without a verified instrument is worth
nothing. Week one: port the Diffuse Control game to an open eight-billion-parameter model — the generator, the weak scorer, the ground-truth proxy
— and reproduce their baseline result: the weak scorer and the proxy agree on benign generators, and a red prompt separates them. If I can't
reproduce that, there's no point going further. Week two: the organisms — two families producing the same sabotage by different mechanisms, a
hidden instruction and a light adapter — plus the aware-but-honest organism; that's the construct-validity control, and it comes before any probe.
Week three: the probes themselves, trained off-policy on written examples, then the two-family test — a probe that passes the first and fails the
second learned the instruction, not the intent, and I know it before continuing. Week four: the control — the black-box monitor aggregated over
time, TRACE-lite, on the same trajectories — calibrated at one percent false positives on paired benign variants, as SLEIGHT-Bench does; and the
red team, whose strength I publish. At the end of month one I have a testbed where every piece is verified, and zero results — by design. The
budget: roughly a third of the month's compute, the rest kept for months two and three where the measurements cost. And the gate is already
written: end of month two, white against black recall, with its interval.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Probes trained off-policy on written examples may learn only a surface cue, or read the text rather than a representation (course, Part 2, §C; programme, part 8); and passing the two-family test closes the gap between two ways of implanting, not the one between implanted and natural: an implanted intention may be more salient (course, Part 6, §8; handover, §5.2; reading sheet 15). Workaround: draw negatives from the model's real generations, read at both positions, the first token before any written reason and the action token with neutral reasons prefilled, and add another team's organism (course, Part 2, §C; programme, parts 3 and 8; course, Part 2, §A, K71); against the gap between implanted and natural itself, no workaround is known; say so (explanation of 2 October, part 1; course, Part M, M5).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); red-teaming → Part 2, §H (after "In practice — StrongREJECT"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); misalignment probes, J-lens included (box of 2 October) → Part 2, §A (before the worked case K71), §C (before the worked case K47) and C bis (before the worked case K72) *(v3.6)*


---

## A3 · « What if the probes just don't work at all — the two-family test fails, nothing generalizes? What's your paper then? »

Then my paper is that one, and I think it's worth something. If the probes pass the "hidden instruction" family and fail the "light adapter"
family, the result is: on this kind of sabotage, a probe reads the induction mechanism, not the intent — which is exactly the risk Anthropic's
directions page writes under "activation monitoring", and I haven't seen it measured on diffuse threats. That result has a publishable, useful
shape: two organism families, a construct-validity protocol, and a measurement of what probes actually catch — the fellows' lie detectors met
that fate, 0.95 in distribution and 0.70 out, and the paper was published because it says something true about the tool. The pivot is written in
my programme: from "does white beat black" to "what does a sabotage probe measure" — with my causal partition as the instrument, saying what
fraction of the effect goes through the read direction. What I wouldn't do: keep aggregating signals I know read the wrong thing, hoping the sum
redeems the error — summing a bias only makes a bigger bias.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The failure on the "light adapter" family reads as "a probe reads the induction mechanism" only with two known cases: the implant of that family took, checked copy by copy through its behaviour, and the probe, at the same threshold, catches held-out cases of the family it passes; otherwise the null may only say a failed implant or too strict a threshold (course, Part 2, §A, K71; course, Part 2, §E, K52; course, Part M, M5). Workaround: those two checks before concluding, and a harmless behaviour planted through the same two recipes, which rules out a probe reading the recipe (course, Part 2, §A, K71).


> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The lie detectors cited are not probes — models fine-tuned with LoRA to answer a self-report question about a transcript —, and 0.95 is an in-distribution progression during training (reading sheet 7; explanation of 2 October, part 2): their fate does not transfer as such to probes. Workaround: for a probe, the gap between the in-distribution AUROC and the AUROC on whole held-out families, then the causal test at matched degradation (reading sheet 7; explanation of 2 October, part 3).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); fine-tuned detectors → Part 7, F·29; patching → Part 10, Patchscopes sheet; misalignment probes, J-lens included (box of 2 October) → Part 2, §A (before the worked case K71), §C (before the worked case K47) and C bis (before the worked case K72) *(v3.6)*

## A4 · « Your rank-three result is on an 8B model. Why should we believe anything about it transfers to a frontier model? »

I'm not asking anyone to believe it, and I'd say why first: even on this model, the result doesn't hold well enough for anyone to ask
whether it transfers. The rank-three effect didn't come back on fresh generations; I treat it as
exploratory-confirmed, not preregistered; it softened verdicts even without pressure; and no study has extended it to another model. What could
transfer is a question, and I state it as a prediction: the number of directions an intervention has to touch would depend on the
way the concept occupies the workspace, and would be stated before intervening. How we'd know: a rank sweep within one
experiment, across several concepts, with loading measured first, on an open model and then on a second. For the causal partition, a
protocol rather than a number — one intervention on the direction being read, one on the full state at the same sites, and control directions
compared at equal degradation — which would run on any model whose activations you have. On mine, the direction being read does
under one percent of the causal work, against sixty-eight percent for the full state — a number to redo at equal degradation. What
would change my mind: a concept among the least loaded that nonetheless gave way to a single direction, at controlled degradation, or an
ordering of the concepts that loading doesn't predict — then my prediction would fall, and I'd say so.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Loading is read with the J-lens, which has been shown only on Claude and reads only single-token concepts, and "loading" names three quantities depending on the text (reading sheet 1; course, Part 2, C bis; course, Part 6, §6). Workaround: on each open model, a gate — first reproduce the swap of a single-token concept, otherwise a tuned lens declared as an approximation, the thesis then not being tested in the paper's sense —, the loading of a multi-token concept read on a token set, and the main predictor frozen first, saying which (programme, parts 3 and 8; course, Part 6, §6).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); J-lens and workspace → Part 2, C bis (after "The test, as it is said"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); patching → Part 10, Patchscopes sheet *(v3.6)*

## A5 · « Isn't sycophancy basically solved by now — constitutional training, better preference data? Why keep working on it? »

Reduced, not solved — and what remains is the part that matters. What training reduced is the visible form — the model flipping when told "are
you sure". What the displacement I measured shows is a deeper, measurable form: a model judge
whose rating moves by a fixed fraction under social framing — about seventy percent of the way — toward two distinct destinations;
my prediction is that any judge, human, preference model or scorer, moves this way; it would be a property of judgment, not a politeness
defect, and that displacement would contaminate everything that rests on a judge: preference training, debate, oversight by a weaker model, the
judging of research proposals — where models agree less with researchers than researchers do with each other. And
Anthropic's directions page doesn't consider it solved: it cites sycophancy as the very example of a propensity we measure poorly. What I'd keep
as the criterion for "solved": a displacement under framing indistinguishable from zero, on a judge we actually use to train — and I haven't seen
that number measured.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "Indistinguishable from zero" is a null: it counts only if the same setup — same framings, same regression — sees the displacement where it exists, in the judge you measured, and it is stated as a bound, with its budget and power, never as an absence (course, Part M, M5); and the gap between models and researchers on research proposals rests on ten researchers and 92 pairs (course, Part 7, F·41). Workaround: that known case in the same protocol before declaring a judge "solved", and the proposal gap stated with its sample size (course, Part M, M5; course, Part 7, F·41).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law"); known case → Part M, M5 (end of section); behavioural evaluations and honeypots → Part 2, §B (after "In practice — sandbagging") *(v3.6)*


---

## A6 · « Suppose a probe flags an agent mid-trajectory at your threshold. What happens next — who acts, and on what?»

Detection is only worth what it triggers, and that's a question of control protocol, not of the probe. The frame exists: in a control protocol,
a suspicion signal above a threshold can trigger three things, at a fixed budget. Defer to a trusted model — replace the untrusted agent's action
with that of a weaker but trusted model, at a cost in usefulness; that's "defer-to-trusted" from the founding control paper. Resample — redraw the
action and compare, which costs compute but no human. Escalate to a human — the audit budget, the scarce resource, which sets the false-positive
rate we can afford: at one percent, a human sees one trajectory in a hundred, which is tenable; at five, they see nothing anymore. What my
sequential test adds to that scheme: it doesn't give a verdict per action but a cumulative statistic with a guarantee — the probability of a
false alarm over the whole trajectory is bounded, whenever you look. So the action can be graded: defer early on weak but rising suspicion,
escalate late when the statistic crosses the guaranteed threshold. And the point I wouldn't hide: a cumulative internal signal crossing the
threshold isn't proof of malice — it's a reason to audit; the proof is what the audit produces. That's the distinction between detection and
incrimination that Redwood draws for diffuse threats, and I keep it.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The guarantee bounds false alarms, not misses: a probe in production can fail silently, and its silence is not the model's (course, Part 3, §3, K70); and the always-valid sequential test already exists on black-box verifier scores, what remains being the same test on internal scores (course, Part 7, F·55). Workaround: canaries — known positives slipped into the traffic —, a drift score and a fresh sample judged every month (course, Part 3, §3, K70); and, for that combination, say "I haven't seen that combination measured", never "first" nor "mine" (course, Part 7, F·52 and F·55).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth") *(v3.6)*


---

## A7 · « A colleague shows you a beautiful steering result — one direction, huge behavioural effect, no side effects. What do you ask them? »

Three questions, in order, and I'd ask them kindly. The first is about the control: a matched-norm random direction at the
same site — and better, a covariance-matched random direction, because a direction drawn in the subspace where the model has
variance sometimes does a lot while meaning nothing; and, whatever the control direction, a comparison at equal degradation,
since at equal norm two directions don't damage the model equally. The second is about the share of the effect that goes
through that direction, against the full state at the same sites: that's the partition, and it says whether the direction
*is* the mechanism or one lever among others — in my setting, under one percent against sixty-eight. The third is about
replication: the effect has to hold on fresh, seed-matched generations, with the full text kept. If all three hold, it's a
beautiful result, and I'd say so. And I'd add a question about rank, because a single direction is the simplest version of the
story: you need to know how many directions the effect takes, through a rank sweep done within one experiment.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* The three questions apply first to your own number: this "under one percent against sixty-eight" has not yet been measured at equal degradation, and a covariance-matched random direction does more there than the probe direction (course, Part 11, answer A4; course, Part 6, §2 and §3). Workaround: the protocol of answer A4, with control directions compared at equal degradation and the full-state patch as the ceiling (course, Part 11, answer A4; programme, part 8).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: random controls → Part M, M4 (after "The matched-norm random direction"); matched degradation and dose-response → Part M, M4 (after "Dose-response"); patching → Part 10, Patchscopes sheet; steering vectors → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — Contrastive Activation Addition"); ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method") *(v3.6)*


---

## A8 · « How do you think about the dual-use of your own work — a better sabotage detector is also a map of what a saboteur must avoid? »

I take it seriously, and I follow the rule the Fellows programme itself applied on SLEIGHT-Bench: the authors published forty attacks against
monitors while writing that it was dual-use, encrypting the dataset, putting a canary in it so it wouldn't be trained on — and judging that
publication served safety, because a shared benchmark lets the community improve monitors systematically. For my work the asymmetry is rather
favourable: a white-box detector can't be evaded by a model that reads the paper, because the model doesn't control its activations the way it
controls its text — that's the directions page's argument, and it's what makes the internal channel less dual-use than a benchmark of textual
attacks. What would be dual-use: publishing the sabotage organisms themselves, with their induction mechanisms. There, the rule is the same as
theirs — encryption, canary, and a written judgment of what publication brings to defence. And one thing I'd say: the most dual-use result of my
programme would be a negative one — "probes don't see this kind of sabotage" — and I'd publish it anyway, because a defence whose holes are
unknown is worse than a defence whose limits are known.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* "Can't be evaded" says nothing about what training does: according to a report, after RL, fresh out-of-domain probes degrade while a fresh in-domain probe stays near perfect (prior-art report 3 of 2 October, *The Obfuscation Atlas* — report, read in a targeted way), and iterating against your detectors selects for evasion (reading sheet 19). Workaround: a fresh probe after any training, on a disjoint cue set, and sealed detectors outside the loop — if they still fire when the in-loop ones go quiet, evasion has been selected (handover, §5.2; programme, part 3; reading sheet 19).


> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: activation probes → Part 2, §C (after "In practice — The Geometry of Truth"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes"); model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); misalignment probes, J-lens included (box of 2 October) → Part 2, §A (before the worked case K71), §C (before the worked case K47) and C bis (before the worked case K72) *(v3.6)*

## A9 à A17 · Neuf questions moins probables, en réponse courte (FR / EN)

**A9 · « Your law is on Llama-3.1-8B judging texts. Does it hold for human judges? »** FR : Je ne l'ai pas mesuré sur des humains, et je ne
l'extrapole pas ; la forme — un déplacement fractionnel vers un point fixe — est celle des modèles d'ancrage en psychologie du jugement, et c'est
une raison de le tester, pas de le supposer. L'expérience est simple : les mêmes textes, les mêmes cadrages, des annotateurs humains, et la même
régression. EN : I haven't measured it on humans and I don't extrapolate; the shape — a fractional displacement toward a fixed point — is that of
anchoring models in judgment psychology, a reason to test it, not assume it. The experiment is simple: same texts, same framings, human
annotators, same regression.

**A10 · « What would you do with interpretability tools if you had them — SAEs, attribution graphs?»** FR : Décomposer le sous-espace de rang
trois en features et mesurer lesquelles portent l'effet causal — c'est la phase trois de mon programme initial, et CHIVE me rend prudent : lire
des features ne prédit pas mieux que lire le texte ; je les utiliserais comme hypothèses à tester par intervention, pas comme explications. EN :
Decompose the rank-three subspace into features and measure which carry the causal effect — phase three of my original programme — and CHIVE
makes me careful: reading features predicts no better than reading text; I'd use them as hypotheses to test by intervention, not as
explanations.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Two limits for A10: the rank-three subspace moved valence, not the concept, and its effect did not come back on fresh generations — it is not a causal handle on sycophancy, and decomposing it into features would not say what carries sycophancy (course, Part 6, §2; repository README); and the open sparse dictionary for this model leaves most of the variance in its residual, which carries the read signal (repository README). Workaround: the no-pressure control arm and a rival concept's direction, at matched degradation, before decomposing, and the signal read on the reconstruction and on the residual; to decide between "features absent from the dictionary" and "a dictionary that loses too much", none known; say so (course, Part M, M4; repository README).


**A11 · « Do you think current models are misaligned? »** FR : Je pense qu'ils ont des propensions mesurables qui ne sont pas les nôtres — la
sycophancie en est une, chiffrée — et qu'ils se comportent autrement quand ils se croient observés ; « désaligné » comme catégorie me semble
moins utile que ces deux mesures. EN : I think they have measurable propensities that aren't ours — sycophancy is one, with a number — and that
they behave differently when they believe they're observed; "misaligned" as a category seems less useful to me than those two measurements.

**A12 · « What's your view on open-weights models for safety research? »** FR : Tout mon travail causal en dépend — on ne fait pas d'ablation
sans les poids — et les fellows travaillent sur des modèles ouverts par construction ; le coût est que les résultats sont sur des modèles
plus petits, et il faut dire ce qui transfère. EN : All my causal work depends on them — no ablation without weights — and fellows work on open
models by construction; the cost is that results are on smaller models, and one has to say what transfers.

**A13 · « How do you handle a result that contradicts your mentor's?»** FR : Je le préenregistre, je le mesure avec le contrôle qu'ils
utiliseraient, et je le leur montre avant de l'écrire ; si c'est leur argument contre le monitoring des menaces diffuses, c'est exactement ce que
ma porte G1 est faite pour trancher, dans un sens ou dans l'autre. EN : I preregister it, measure it with the control they'd use, and show them
before I write it; if it's their argument against monitoring diffuse threats, that's exactly what my gate G1 is built to settle, either way.

**A14 · « What do you read to keep up?»** FR : Le blog Alignment Science et ses fellows en premier, les papiers de Redwood et d'Apollo sur le
contrôle, et je tiens une liste des chiffres que je cite avec leur pièce. EN : The Alignment Science blog and its fellows first, Redwood's and
Apollo's control papers, and I keep a list of the numbers I cite with their exhibit.

**A15 · « Explain sequential testing to someone who's never seen it. »** FR : On accumule des preuves pas à pas, et on veut pouvoir s'arrêter et
décider à n'importe quel moment sans tricher ; un test classique ne le permet pas — regarder souvent gonfle les fausses alarmes ; un processus e
multiplie des rapports de vraisemblance et garantit, par une inégalité simple, que la probabilité de dépasser un seuil sous l'hypothèse nulle
reste bornée quel que soit le moment où on regarde. EN : You accumulate evidence step by step and want to stop and decide at any moment without
cheating; a classical test doesn't allow it — looking often inflates false alarms; an e-process multiplies likelihood ratios and guarantees, by a
simple inequality, that the probability of crossing a threshold under the null stays bounded whenever you look.

**A16 · « What's the biggest risk in your own methodology? »** FR : Que mes organismes ne ressemblent pas au vrai sabotage — le réalisme, que
Kissane mesure à 32,8 pour cent pour les audits ; je publierais le mien avant tout chiffre. EN : That my organisms don't resemble real
sabotage — realism, which Kissane measures at 32.8 percent for audits; I'd publish mine before any number.

> ⚠ *(v3.6)* Kissane's paired realism measures whether a judge mistakes an audit transcript for a real one; it does not say whether an implanted intention resembles a natural one — an implanted intention may be more salient (course, Part 7, F·25; handover, §5.2; reading sheet 15). Partial workaround: plant the same sabotage through several recipes, hold one out, and add another team's organism (course, Part 2, §A, K71); against the gap between implanted and natural itself, no workaround is known; say so (explanation of 2 October, part 1; course, Part M, M5).


**A17 · « If Anthropic didn't take you, what would you do?»** FR : La même recherche, avec moins de compute et sans les environnements — et
j'essaierais d'abord de reproduire Diffuse Control en ouvert, parce que la première porte ne demande que ça. EN : The same research, with less
compute and without the environments — and I'd first try to reproduce Diffuse Control in the open, because the first gate only needs that.

> ⚠ **Limits and workarounds**: LLM judges → Part 6, §2 (after "The displacement law"); dictionaries and SAEs → Part 4, Towards then Scaling Monosemanticity; attribution graphs → Part 4, Circuit Tracing; ablation and projection → Part 2, §D (after "The method"); model organisms → Part 2, §A (after "In practice — Auditing Hidden Objectives"); control monitors → Part 2, §G (after "In practice — coup probes") *(v3.6)*
